5.3.1. Background on Priority in RFC 7540
RFC 7540 defined a rich system for signaling priority of requests. However, this system proved to be complex, and it was not uniformly implemented.
The flexible scheme meant that it was possible for clients to express priorities in very different ways, with little consistency in the approaches that were adopted. For servers, implementing generic support for the scheme was complex. Implementation of priorities was uneven in both clients and servers. Many server deployments ignored client signals when prioritizing their handling of requests.
In short, the prioritization signaling in RFC 7540 [RFC7540] was not successful.
5.3.2. Priority Signaling in This Document
This update to HTTP/2 deprecates the priority signaling defined in RFC 7540 [RFC7540]. The bulk of the text related to priority signals is not included in this document. quotes.whole:
Ensuring that processing time is not dependent on the value of a secret is the best defense against any form of timing attack.
11. IANA Considerations
This revision of HTTP/2 marks the HTTP2-Settings header field and the h2c upgrade token, both defined in [RFC7540], as obsolete.
Section 11 of [RFC7540] registered the h2 and h2c ALPN identifiers along with the PRI HTTP method. RFC 7540 also established a registry for frame types, settings, and error codes. These registrations and registries apply to HTTP/2, but are not redefined in this document.
IANA has updated references to RFC 7540 in the following registries to refer to this document: "TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs", "HTTP/2 Frame Type", "HTTP/2 Settings", "HTTP/2 Error Code", and "HTTP Method Registry". The registration of the PRI method has been updated to refer to Section 3.4; all other section numbers have not changed.
IANA has changed the policy on those portions of the "HTTP/2 Frame Type" and "HTTP/2 Settings" registries that were reserved for Experimental Use in RFC 7540. These portions of the registries shall operate on the same policy as the remainder of each registry.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

1) Current specification of HTTP/2: **RFC 9113**, "HTTP/2", Standards Track, June 2022 (ISSN 2070-1721). Editor: Cory Benfield (Apple Inc.). It is the document the RFC Editor currently marks as the active HTTP/2 specification.

2) RFCs it obsoletes: **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** — exactly two.
   - RFC 7540, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Belshe/Peon/Thomson, May 2015 (the original HTTP/2 specification).
   - RFC 8740, "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", Benjamin, February 2020.

PRIMARY EVIDENCE (verbatim from the fetched records)

- RFC 9113 header block: "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" — https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html (fetched 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z, sha256 82697578db79). The same "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" line is carried on the RFC Editor info page and the Datatracker record.
- RFC 9113 Abstract: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." — https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ (sha256 fa8ab6496754) and https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ (sha256 ad12a3569026).
- RFC 9113 Appendix B (Changes from RFC 7540), first bullet: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." — confirms RFC 8740 is folded in, not merely updated.
- RFC 9113 §11 (IANA Considerations): "This revision of HTTP/2 marks the HTTP2-Settings header field and the h2c upgrade token, both defined in [RFC7540], as obsolete." — consistent with 7540 being superseded.
- Corroboration that RFC 7540 is the superseded original: RFC 7540's own text describes it as an alternative to, but not an obsoleter of, HTTP/1.1 message syntax (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/, sha256 488ead20743d), i.e. it is the base document that RFC 9113 replaces.

HOW TO RE-VERIFY (procedure, ~2 minutes)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/.
2. In the document header metadata, confirm the line reads exactly `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`. The count must be 2; if any additional number appears, the answer to ask 2 changes accordingly.
3. Confirm there is **no** `Obsoleted by:` line and no `Updated by:` line that would displace RFC 9113 as the current base specification. As of the fetch date 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z, none appeared in the retrieved record.
4. Cross-check the same fields on https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ ("Obsoletes" / "Obsoleted by" / "Updates" boxes). Datatracker and rfc-editor.org are generated from the same RFC metadata and must agree.
5. Do not accept secondary sources (vendor docs, Wikipedia, MDN) as authoritative for the obsoletes relationship; use them only as sanity checks.

SCOPE NOTES AND DISAMBIGUATION (what is deliberately NOT in the answer)

- "Obsoletes" vs "updates": the answer counts only the formal `Obsoletes:` relationship. RFC 9113's relationship to RFC 7540/8740 is obsolescence (full replacement), not an update. This is why the answer is a set of two, not a longer list.
- HPACK: RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2) is **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113 and is **not** part of the answer to ask 2. RFC 9113 continues to reference HPACK as a separate, still-current companion specification. Anyone reading "HTTP/2 specification" broadly should treat RFC 9113 (framing/connection/streams/TLS) + RFC 7541 (field compression) as the pair — but only RFC 9113 answers ask 1, and RFC 7541 is not in the ask-2 set.
- Extensions: documents such as RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2) and other HTTP/2 extensions were not obsoleted by RFC 9113 either; they remain in force on top of the base specification. They are excluded from ask 2. (Worth a glance at each one's own "Updates:" header if the reader needs the full dependency picture; that is outside the two asks.)
- HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) does not obsolete HTTP/2; it is a separate protocol. It is excluded.
- Date sensitivity: "current" is asserted as of the source fetch time, 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z. RFC statuses change only when a new RFC is published with an `Obsoletes:` line naming 9113; the step-3 check above is the guard. Errata against RFC 9113, if any are recorded, correct text but do not alter the obsoletes relationship and do not change either answer.
- RFC 7540's own `Obsoletes:` list (i.e. what the 2015 document itself superseded) is a separate historical question and is not part of either ask; the retrieved passages do not show that header, so nothing is asserted about it here.

ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

RFC 9113 (June 2022) is the current HTTP/2 specification; per its own header and abstract it obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ ("Obsoletes: 7540, 8740").

Statutory Instruments

2026 No. 357

TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT

The Secretary of State makes these Regulations in exercise of the powers conferred by section 1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 (“the 1998 Act”)(1).



Citation, commencement and extent

1.—(1) These Regulations may be cited as the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026.

(2) These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.

(3) These Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Amendments to the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015

2.—(1) The National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015(2) are amended as follows.

(2) In regulation 4 (the national living wage) for “£12.21” substitute “£12.71”.

(3) In regulation 4A(1) (workers who qualify for the national minimum wage at a different rate)—

(a)in sub-paragraph (b) for “£10.00” substitute “£10.85”;

(b)in sub-paragraph (c) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”;

(c)in sub-paragraph (d) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”.

(4) In regulation 16(1) (amount for provision of living accommodation) for “£10.66” substitute “£11.10”.




Kate Dearden

Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State

19th March 2026

Department for Business and Trade




Explanatory Note

(This note is not part of the Regulations)
 
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
  
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(4) increases the accommodation offset amount which is applicable where any employer provides a worker with living accommodation from £10.66 to £11.10 for each day that accommodation is provided (regulation 16(1) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
A full regulatory impact assessment of the effect that this instrument will have on the costs of business and the voluntary sector is available from the Employment Rights Directorate, Department for Business and Trade, Old Admiralty Building, London SW1A 2AY and is annexed to the Explanatory Memorandum which is available alongside the instrument on www.legislation.gov.uk.

quotes.whole:
A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.
NOTES FOR EDITORS
The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.

verdict.summary:
UK statutory minimum wage rates from 1 April 2026 — answers

1. National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
2. National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21): £10.85 per hour.

Both apply from 1 April 2026 and remain in force until 31 March 2027. Both are UK-wide (England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland).

These are legislated rates, not proposals or recommendations. They were given effect by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/357), made 19 March 2026 and coming into force 1 April 2026, which amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621).

Statutory basis, provision by provision

| Rate | Amended provision (SI 2015/621) | Old | New | SI 2026/357 provision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage, 21 and over | reg. 4 | £12.21 | £12.71 | reg. 2(2) |
| NMW, 18–20 (18 or over, not yet 21) | reg. 4A(1)(b) | £10.00 | £10.85 | reg. 2(3)(a) |
| NMW, under 18 | reg. 4A(1)(c) | £7.55 | £8.00 | reg. 2(3)(b) |
| Apprentice rate | reg. 4A(1)(d) | £7.55 | £8.00 | reg. 2(3)(c) |
| Accommodation offset (per day) | reg. 16(1) | £10.66 | £11.10 | reg. 2(4) |

Full rate table effective 1 April 2026 (for payroll and policy use)

| Band | Hourly rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Change (£) | Change (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | +£0.50 | +4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | +£0.85 | +8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | +£0.45 | +6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | +£0.45 | +6.0% |
| Accommodation offset (max per day) | £11.10 | +£0.44 | +4.1% |

(The last three rows are outside the two asks; they are included so the table is complete and so the age bands are unambiguous. Arithmetic check: 12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85; 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00; 10.66 + 0.44 = 11.10.)

Sources and currency

- Primary (law): The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, in force 1 April 2026 — legislation.gov.uk, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made. Reg. 2(2) and reg. 2(3)(a); Explanatory Note.
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' (the operational rates page): April 2026 row shows 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85 — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates.
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', published 1 April 2026 — confirms £12.71 (21+) and £10.85 (18–20), and records that the increases follow LPC recommendations made in October 2025, accepted by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
- Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026', published 26 November 2025 — the Government accepted the LPC's recommendations in full.
- GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026.

Chain of authority: LPC recommended (27 October 2025) → Government accepted in full (announced 26 November 2025) → SI 2026/357 made (19 March 2026) → in force (1 April 2026). The figure to rely on is the one in the statutory instrument; the gov.uk pages agree with it.

Points of confusion to avoid

- Statutory National Living Wage vs the 'Real Living Wage'. £12.71 is the statutory NLW, enforced by HMRC and payable by all employers. The Real Living Wage is a separate voluntary benchmark set by the Living Wage Foundation on a different methodology and different annual timetable. It is not the answer to this question and the two must not be conflated in payroll or communications.
- 'National Living Wage' vs 'National Minimum Wage'. The NLW is simply the top band of the NMW, for workers aged 21 and over. The 18–20 rate is an NMW rate and is sometimes loosely called 'the minimum wage for young workers' — it is £10.85, not £12.71, and not the apprentice rate.
- Age threshold history: the NLW age threshold was 25 before April 2021, 23 from April 2021, and 21 from April 2024. It is 21 for the April 2026 rates.
- Apprentices aged 21+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, or aged under 19, are on the apprentice rate (£8.00), not the NLW; apprentices aged 19+ who have completed the first year move to the rate for their age (£12.71 if 21+).
- Accommodation offset: £11.10 per day is the maximum an employer may deduct (or count) for providing living accommodation; it is a daily figure, not hourly.

Forward look (outside the scope of this answer, given only to prevent mis-dating): the GOV.UK rates page also lists rates for April 2027 — 21 and over £13.21, 18 to 20 £11.27, under 18 £8.31, apprentice £8.31. Those are not the April 2026 rates and must not be used for the 2026–27 tax year.

Scope and caveats

- This covers the headline hourly rates only. It does not address apprentice/under-18 entitlements in detail, salary sacrifice and deductions, uniform and tool allowances, time-recording and 'time work' rules, or employer eligibility — all of which can change what must actually be paid.
- Rates are set annually with effect from 1 April. Anyone relying on these figures for a pay run after 31 March 2027 should re-check the then-current statutory instrument.

quotes.whole:
Air Miles and Statute Miles
In the short-haul exceptions to the hours-of-service regulations, you will see the term “air miles.”
This is a different measurement of a mile than what is used for statute miles on a roadmap.
An air mile is longer than a statute mile. There are 6,076 feet in an air mile and 5,280 feet in a statute
mile. One-hundred air miles is equal to 115.08 statute miles.
Therefore, a 100 air-mile radius from your work reporting location can be figured as 115.08 statute,
or “roadmap,” miles (185.2 km) from your work reporting location. A 150 air-mile radius from your
work reporting location can be figured as 172.6 statute miles (277.8 km).
What Are the Hours-of-Service Limits?
The hours-of-service regulations focus on when and how long you are allowed to drive by placing
specific limits on the amount of time you drive your truck and how many total hours you can work
before you are no longer permitted to drive a c ommercial motor vehicle. You must follow three
maximum duty limits at all times. They are the 14-hour “driving window” limit, 11-hour driving
limit, and 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day duty limits.
14-Hour Driving Window

verdict.summary:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Operational Limits

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius within which the driver must operate, measured from the normal work reporting location | **150 air miles** (the regulation's own equivalent: 172.6 statute miles / 277.8 km) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must return and be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** |

Both figures are from the exception that relieves the driver of the record-of-duty-status requirement, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), as currently in force.

## 2. Controlling regulatory text

> **§ 395.1(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver.** A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a **150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)** of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, **returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours**;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

Corroborated by FMCSA's Summary of Hours of Service Regulations and the FMCSA HOS Visor Card: "A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours... must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours."

## 3. How each figure is measured

**Radius (150 air miles).**
- The unit is **air miles**, not road/statute miles: 1 air mile = 6,076 ft vs 5,280 ft for a statute mile (factor 1.15076). 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles = 277.8 km. This is the regulation's own conversion and must be used verbatim; do not substitute a road-mile or drive-distance ring.
- The center point is the **normal work reporting location** — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not the carrier's terminal generically and not the driver's home.
- The constraint applies to the **whole operation for the day**, not merely to driving: the vehicle and driver must remain inside the 150 air-mile ring at all times during the duty tour (the text is "the driver operates within," not "the driver drives within").
- Air miles are straight-line (great-circle) distance; a routing/geofence implementation should compute geodesic distance from the geocoded reporting location and compare against 150 air miles, not against accumulated odometer miles.

**Release limit (14 consecutive hours).**
- The clock is **consecutive hours**, running from the moment the driver comes on duty. It is the same 14-hour construct as the 395.3(a)(2) driving window: off-duty time taken inside the tour does **not** pause or extend it.
- Two events must both occur inside the 14 hours: the driver must **return to the work reporting location** and be **released from work** there. A driver who returns at hour 13 but is not released until hour 15 fails the condition; so does a driver released at hour 13 at a location other than the reporting location.
- The exception is a **RODS exception only** (it exempts from §§ 395.8 and 395.11). It does **not** exempt the driver from the underlying limits in § 395.3: the 11-hour driving limit, the 14-hour driving window, the 60/70-hour limit, and the 10-consecutive-hour off-duty requirement (property-carrying) all still apply, and the 10 hours off duty must separate each 14 hours on duty.
- Passenger-carrying drivers under (e)(1) need **8** consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty, not 10.
- A **driver-salesperson** is carved out of the (e)(1)(ii) release condition by the words "except a driver-salesperson" and is addressed by a separate provision in § 395.1. The 150 air-mile radius condition still reads on its face without that carve-out.
- Qualifying drivers under (e)(1) or (e)(2) are also not subject to the 30-minute break requirement of § 395.3(a)(3)(ii), per FMCSA guidance.

## 4. Distinguishing the neighboring provisions (do not cross-apply)

| Provision | Who / what | Radius | Time limit | Exempts from RODS? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **§ 395.1(e)(1)** — 150 air-mile radius driver | Any CDL or non-CDL driver of a property- or passenger-carrying CMV | **150 air miles** | **Released within 14 consecutive hours** | **Yes** (§§ 395.8, 395.11) |
| § 395.1(e)(2) — non-CDL property-carrying | Only property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL; driver must return to the reporting location at the end of each duty tour | 150 air miles | No driving after the **14th** hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, and after the **16th** hour on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days | Yes (§§ 395.3(a)(2), 395.8, 395.11) |
| § 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception | Property-carrying; requires return to and release at the reporting location for the previous 5 duty tours, and no use in the previous 6 consecutive days | n/a | Released within **16** hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty | No — extends the window only |
| § 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites | Property or passenger transport to/from a theatrical or TV production site | **100 air miles** | Separate driving limits | No — exempts from § 395.3(a) only |

**Superseded values — flagged for anyone working from an older FMCSA PDF.** The 2015 and 2016 editions of FMCSA's *Interstate Truck Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* and FMCSA's New Entrant pages still print the pre-2020 figures for this exception: **100 air miles and 12 consecutive hours**. The 2020 hours-of-service final rule (published June 2020, effective September 29, 2020) amended § 395.1(e)(1) to 150 air miles and 14 hours. Any compliance document, geofence, or dispatch rule built on 100/12 is stale. The correct current pair is **150 / 14**; a mixed pair (150 with 12, or 100 with 14) matches no version of the rule and should be rejected on sight.

## 5. Correction to a common assumption

The short-haul exception at **(e)(1) has no day-count cap**. There is no rule limiting how many days in a rolling period a driver may use (e)(1), provided the 150 air-mile radius, the 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release, the applicable 10- or 8-hour off-duty separation, and the carrier's 6-month time records are all satisfied, and provided the driver still respects the 60/70-hour limit (with the 34-hour restart available under § 395.3(c)). The "5 days at 14 / 2 days at 16" day-count structure belongs to **(e)(2)**, and the "once every 7 consecutive days" structure belongs to **(o)**. Applying a day-count cap to (e)(1) would over-restrict lawful operations.

## 6. Conditions checklist for a carrier asserting (e)(1)

1. Driver operates entirely within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location. [ ]
2. Driver returns to that location and is released from work there within 14 consecutive hours of coming on duty (driver-salespersons excepted). [ ]
3. Property-carrying: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty. Passenger-carrying: at least 8. [ ]
4. Carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records of: report-for-duty time each day, total hours on duty each day, release-from-duty time each day, and — for drivers used for the first time or intermittently — the total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2). [ ]
5. Driver still complies with § 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 60/70-hour). [ ]

## 7. Failure handling

If on a given day the driver exceeds 150 air miles or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception simply does not apply for that day — the driver is not thereby in violation of the hours-of-service rules, but must complete a record of duty status for that day (FMCSA guidance, § 395.1(e) Q&A). The carrier should treat any excursion as a signal to switch that day to full RODS/ELD, not as an automatic violation.

## 8. Scope of this answer

This states the **federal interstate** rule in 49 CFR 395.1(e) as currently in force. It does not address state intrastate hours-of-service rules, which may set different radii or release periods, nor Canadian or Mexican rules. It also does not address the separate (e)(2), (o), or (p) provisions except to distinguish them above.

**Sources:** 49 CFR 395.1(e), eCFR (current) and govinfo CFR 2024/2025 editions; FMCSA *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations*; FMCSA HOS Visor Card (FMCSA-MCE-20-009); FMCSA *Interstate Truck Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* (2022 revision, and the superseded 2015/2016 editions cited only to identify the stale 100/12 figures).

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

Section 2307(a)(8) of FESSA established limitations for operations

quotes.whole:
3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT AND OCCUPANT LIMITS (14 CFR 61.113(i), as amended)

Governing authority. BasicMed is the alternate qualification under 14 CFR 61.113(i), enacted by section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA) and codified in the note to 49 U.S.C. 44703. Section 828(a)(4) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63) amended FESSA 2307(j) to enlarge the 'covered aircraft' envelope and amended 2307(a)(8)(A) to enlarge the passenger limit. Those statutory changes were self-implementing on 12 November 2024; the FAA conformed the regulation in the final rule published at 89 FR (doc. FAA-2024-26935, 18 November 2024) and issued Notice N 8000.386 dated 14 November 2024. All three answers below reflect the post-12-November-2024 rule, which is the rule in force.

THE THREE ANSWERS

1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb (maximum takeoff weight; for a type-certificated aircraft, the maximum certificated takeoff weight shown on the type certificate data sheet / design approval). Preamble: 'a covered aircraft ... has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; FAA BasicMed page, Aircraft Requirements: 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.' Note the regulation itself omits the word 'certificated' (deliberately, so that experimental aircraft — which are not type certificated — can qualify); the metric is the aircraft's approved maximum takeoff weight, not the actual weight on a given flight. Up from 6,000 lb.

2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7. The test is the aircraft's authorized capacity under Federal law (its design approval — TC, STC, or ATC; for experimental aircraft, the operator's stated maximum per 14 CFR 91.319(j)), not the number of seats installed. Preamble: 'a covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers)'; FAA BasicMed page: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants.' Up from 6.

3. Passengers on board: 6. Preamble: 'and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board'; FAA BasicMed page, Operating Requirements: 'Carries not more than six passengers.' Up from 5.

HOW THE THREE FIT TOGETHER
- The occupant figure (7) is a property of the aircraft; the passenger figure (6) is a limit on the flight. An aircraft authorized for 8 occupants does not become a covered aircraft merely because two seats are removed — the authorized count must be reduced by a new design approval (STC or amended TC). Conversely an aircraft authorized for 7 may fly with any mix of crew and passengers, but the non-crew count may not exceed 6.
- The passenger limit is derived by subtracting required flight crew from the occupant limit: 7 occupants − 1 required pilot = 6 passengers. In an aircraft type certificated for two flight crewmembers, the practical passenger maximum is 7 − 2 = 5.
- The weight and occupant tests are applied independently; both must be satisfied on the same aircraft.

EXCLUSION ADDED IN 2024. Transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29 are excluded from the covered-aircraft definition regardless of weight or seat count (preamble: section 828(a)(4) 'added a third provision ... to exclude transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under part 29').

COMPANION OPERATING LIMITS (stated so the answer is not misleadingly partial; 14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)–(3))
- At or below 18,000 ft MSL.
- Indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots.
- Within the United States, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized.
- Not for compensation or hire.
- VFR or IFR both permitted.
- The limits apply to the whole flight: a pilot operating under BasicMed may not act as PIC at any point in a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot aboard holds a medical certificate and acts as PIC for part of it.

SUPERSEDED VALUES — DO NOT USE (shown only so stale sources are recognizable)
| Item | Pre-12-Nov-2024 | Current |
| Maximum takeoff weight | 6,000 lb | 12,500 lb |
| Occupants authorized | 6 | 7 |
| Passengers on board | 5 | 6 |
Sources still carrying the old numbers: AC 68-1A (3.2, 5.1.2, 5.2.1) and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing. Notice N 8000.386 states both sets explicitly, applying the new set 'on or after November 12, 2024'.

CITATIONS FOR VERIFICATION
- FAA, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program' (15 Nov 2024): passenger limit 6 (from 5), occupants 7 (from 6), takeoff weight 12,500 lb (from 6,000 lb), excluding transport category helicopters.
- 89 FR, doc. 2024-26935 (18 Nov 2024), section B (Covered Aircraft Requirements) and section C (Passengers in Covered Aircraft).
- FAA BasicMed program page, 'Aircraft Requirements' and 'Operating Requirements'.
- FAA Notice N 8000.386 (14 Nov 2024), para. 5a (aircraft requirements, both before and on/after 12 Nov 2024) and 5b (flight requirements).

SCOPE NOTE (compliance). This is a restatement of the Federal aviation-medical operating limits; it is not a determination for a specific pilot, aircraft, or flight. State-law, insurer, employer, or club/rental restrictions can be more restrictive and are outside the scope of what was asked. Whether a particular aircraft meets the occupant test requires its type certificate data sheet or other design approval, which must be checked aircraft by aircraft.

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

quotes.whole:
On-Duty Time – § 395.2
On-duty time means all time from the time a driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until the time the driver is relieved from work and all responsibilities for performing work. Performing other compensated work for a person who is not a motor
carrier is also on-duty time. The complete deﬁnition of on-duty time can be found in § 395.2.
Travel Time – § 395.1(j)
When a driver at the direction of a motor carrier is traveling, but not driving any vehicle or assuming any other responsibility to the carrier (“cushioning”), such time shall be counted as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty when arriving at destination, in which case he/she shall be
considered off duty for the entire period.
Relief Drivers
On long-distance trips requiring straight-through driving, motorcoach companies may send a relief driver ahead.
In cases when the driver is driven or uses public transportation to get to a layover location, and the driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty after arriving, travel time may be recorded as off duty.

verdict.summary:
# Hours of service for a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) — US federal rules

## Scope and authority

Governing rule: **49 CFR § 395.5, "Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles"** (Subpart A of Part 395, FMCSA), promulgated at 70 FR 50073 (Aug. 25, 2005) and unchanged in the current eCFR text. It applies "[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1."

Basis of scope: the request specifies a *passenger-carrying* commercial motor vehicle (motorcoach). Passenger-carrying and property-carrying CMVs are governed by different limits — § 395.5 (passenger) versus § 395.3 (property) — so the property-carrying figures (11-hour driving / 10-hour off-duty reset / 14-hour on-duty window) are **not** the answers here and should not be substituted. The figures below assume a driver subject to the standard rule set, with no § 395.1 exception invoked.

## The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Regulatory text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, "[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty does the limit reset? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2), both of which run "following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(2): no driving "[f]or any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |

Short form: **10 hours driving / 8 consecutive hours off duty to reset / 15 hours on duty.**

## How the three limits interact

- Driving time is a subset of on-duty time. The 10 driving hours must be consumed **within** the 15-hour on-duty window that opens after the 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour clock is elapsed on-duty time, not driving time, so non-driving on-duty work (loading, inspections, paperwork, waiting in readiness for work, compensated work for a non-motor carrier) burns the window without adding driving hours.
- The two prongs are independent stop conditions: driving must cease at whichever comes first — 10 hours of driving accumulated, or the 15th hour on duty.
- The 8-hour reset restarts both clocks together. There is no separate reset for the driving limit versus the on-duty limit.
- **Worked example.** Driver comes on duty at 06:00 after 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour window closes at 21:00; no driving is permitted at or after 21:00 regardless of how few driving hours were used. Within that window, driving may not exceed 10 hours. If the driver accumulates 10 driving hours at 19:00, driving stops at 19:00 even though 2 hours of the on-duty window remain. The driver may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.
- **Additional cumulative gate (context, not the answer to ask 3).** § 395.5(b) separately bars driving after the driver has been on duty **60 hours in any 7 consecutive days** (carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week) or **70 hours in any 8 consecutive days** (carrier operates CMVs every day of the week), regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services. A compliant schedule must satisfy the 10-hour, 15-hour, and 60/70-hour limits simultaneously; the 15-hour answer above is the per-shift on-duty bar, and the 60/70-hour limits are a rolling multi-day bar that can stop driving earlier.

## Definitions that drive the calculation

- **On-duty time (§ 395.2)** — "all time from the time a driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until the time the driver is relieved from work and all responsibilities for performing work." Compensated work for a person who is not a motor carrier also counts as on-duty time. A driver working more than one job of any kind must count that time as on-duty.
- **Off-duty time** — not separately defined in the regulations; in effect it is any time that is not on-duty time.
- **Travel time / "cushioning" (§ 395.1(j))** — travel at the carrier's direction while not driving and not assuming any other responsibility for the carrier counts as on-duty time **unless** the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival at destination, in which case the entire period may be treated as off duty. For relief drivers: if the driver is driven or uses public transportation to a layover point and then takes 8 consecutive hours off duty, the travel time may be recorded as off duty; if the driver drives him/herself in a non-CMV to the layover point, that time is on duty (not driving).

## Exceptions to check before relying on the base numbers

§ 395.5 is expressly "[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1." The base figures above are correct for the standard case; the following can change them or change how the reset is accumulated:

- **Sleeper berth (§ 395.1(g)(3))** — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth as defined in § 393.76 may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. This is a substitute method of accumulating the 8-hour reset, not a relaxation of the 10- or 15-hour limits.
- **Adverse driving conditions and other § 395.1 relief** — the FMCSA passenger-carrier guidance identifies further exceptions under § 395.1 (its passenger brochure references an exception at § 395.1(e)); any claimed exception should be verified against the current § 395.1 text and its conditions before it is relied on. None is assumed in the answers above.
- **Non-business private motor carriers of passengers** are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements (logbook / ELD), though the driving limits themselves are stated without that carve-out.

## Records (adjacent obligation, not asked)

Drivers required to keep a record of duty status must do so, and most motor carriers of passengers and their drivers are subject to the ELD rule, including drivers domiciled in Canada or Mexico operating in the United States absent an exception. ELD exceptions include drivers required to prepare a record of duty status no more than 8 days in any 30-day period, driveaway-towaway operations where the vehicle is part of the shipment, and vehicles manufactured before model year 2000. Motor carriers of passengers must use only ELDs self-certified and registered on FMCSA's website.

## Answer as it would be stated to the driver

> You may drive **10 hours** after taking **8 consecutive hours off duty**. You may not drive **after you have been on duty 15 hours** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty. You also may not drive after **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** (carrier not operating every day) or **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** (carrier operating every day).

## Currency note

Text confirmed against the current eCFR § 395.5 and corroborated by the FMCSA "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers" guidance and the FMCSA Motor Carrier Safety Planner § 6.4.3 as of 2026-11-16. The three figures have been stable since the 2005 rulemaking; verify against eCFR before relying on them for enforcement-sensitive work.

(a) No certificate holder may schedule any flight crewmember, and no flight crewmember may accept an assignment, for flight time in scheduled operations or in other commercial flying if that crewmember's total flight time in all commercial flying will exceed—

What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?
In most cases, if you have a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after your duty period before you have another duty period. However, under certain circumstances, our regulations allow a rest period of only eight consecutive hours. If your employer schedules you for an eight hour rest period, your next rest period must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the eight hour rest period.
You can find additional guidance on our Cabin Safety Legal Interpretations website.

verdict.summary:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Requirement | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum scheduled rest period owed to a flight attendant after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | That rest period may be scheduled or reduced to | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Applies to a Part 135 certificate holder that uses flight attendants, in on-demand (unscheduled) charter as well as scheduled operations — 135.273 is not limited to scheduled operations.

## 2. Controlling rule text (14 CFR 135.273)

> (b)(1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> (b)(2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (b)(3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (b)(10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> (b)(11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

FAA public guidance states the same rule in plain language: "if you have a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after your duty period before you have another duty period. However, under certain circumstances, our regulations allow a rest period of only eight consecutive hours. If your employer schedules you for an eight hour rest period, your next rest period must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the eight hour rest period." (FAA, "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?")

## 3. The 8-hour reduction is conditional — all four elements must hold

A reduced rest is lawful only if every one of the following is satisfied:

1. **Floor of 8, never lower.** The rest may be "scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours." Eight is the absolute floor for a duty period of 14 hours or less; 7 hours 59 minutes is not authorized by this section under any condition.
2. **A subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** must actually be provided (not merely planned as a possibility).
3. **That subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.** The clock starts at the *beginning of the reduced rest*, not at the end of the duty period and not at the end of the reduced rest.
4. **The subsequent rest must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period** — i.e., a genuine ground rest block, not time overlapping duty, deadhead, positioning, training, or administrative work.

Additional hard limits that travel with any reduced-rest schedule:

- **135.273(b)(10):** no duty period may be assigned at all unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section.
- **135.273(b)(11):** no duty of any kind — flight, deadhead, ground positioning, training, paperwork, phone contact that constitutes duty under the operator's manual — may be assigned during a required rest period. A "rest period" interrupted by duty is not rest.
- The rest must be **consecutive**; it cannot be assembled from fragments.

## 4. Worked example (shows the 24-hour trigger)

- **Base case:** Scheduled duty Day 1 ends 2100. Required rest = 9 consecutive hours, 2100 Day 1 → 0600 Day 2. Earliest subsequent duty start: 0600 Day 2.
- **Reduced case:** Scheduled duty Day 1 ends 2100. Operator schedules 8 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 → 0500 Day 2. Duty Day 2 may begin 0500 Day 2.
  - The subsequent rest must **begin no later than 2100 Day 2** (24 hours after 2100 Day 1, the start of the reduced rest) and must be **at least 10 consecutive hours**.
  - Compliant construction: Duty Day 2 runs 0500–2030 Day 2; subsequent rest 2030 Day 2 → 0630 Day 3 (10 hours, begins 30 minutes inside the 24-hour limit).
  - Non-compliant construction: Duty Day 2 runs 0500–2300 Day 2; the subsequent rest cannot begin until 2300 Day 2, which is 26 hours after the reduced rest began — the reduction was therefore never available, and the original 9-hour rest was owed.

## 5. Applicability checks before relying on these figures

1. **Does the operation actually use flight attendants?** 135.273 governs certificate holders conducting Part 135 operations who utilize flight attendants. If a given aircraft/configuration does not require and does not carry a flight attendant, there is no flight attendant to rest and this section generates no rest obligation for that leg.
2. **Has the operator made a 135.273(c) election?** Section 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder, under written procedures approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications, to apply the Part 135 subpart F **flight crewmember** flight time, duty, and rest requirements to its flight attendants instead. If such an election is in effect, the 9/8 figures above do **not** govern; the applicable crew-member scheme (135.265 for scheduled operations, 135.267 for unscheduled operations) does. Confirm against the operator's ops specs and manual before applying this memo.
3. **Any exemption, deviation, or special authorization?** None is assumed here. An FAA-granted exemption or ops-spec authorization could alter the requirement and must be checked.
4. **"Scheduled" vs. actual.** Section 135.273(b)(2)-(3) constrain what the certificate holder may *schedule/assign*. If actual duty runs beyond the scheduled duty period and exceeds 14 hours, the analysis moves to 135.273(b)(4)-(7), which carry different rest figures and are outside the scope of this memo. The 9/8 answer is correct only for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

## 6. Common errors this memo is written to prevent

- Treating 8 hours as freely available rest. It is available **only** with the paired 10-hour compensatory rest, correctly timed.
- Measuring the 24-hour window from the end of duty or the end of the reduced rest instead of from the **start** of the reduced rest.
- Scheduling the 10-hour compensatory rest to begin after the 24-hour deadline, which retroactively invalidates the 8-hour rest.
- Assigning any duty (deadhead, training, calls) inside a required rest period, contrary to 135.273(b)(11).
- Importing Part 121 flight attendant figures (121.467) or Part 135 flight crewmember figures (135.265/135.267) without confirming whether a 135.273(c) election is in force.

## 7. Self-verification of the stated values

- 9 consecutive hours is the base requirement for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 135.273(b)(2). ✔
- 8 consecutive hours is the permitted reduction, and 8 < 9, so it is a genuine reduction and not a mislabeled base figure — 135.273(b)(3). ✔
- The compensatory rest is 10 consecutive hours, which is greater than the 9-hour base, consistent with the rule's structure. ✔
- The 24-hour trigger is stated as running from the beginning of the reduced rest period, matching the rule text, and the worked example places the subsequent rest inside that window. ✔
- No figure is stated for duty periods exceeding 14 hours, so no value in this memo conflicts with an unverified threshold. ✔

## 8. Bottom line for the operator

Schedule **at least 9 consecutive hours** of rest between the end of any scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less and the start of the next duty period. You may schedule or reduce that to **8 consecutive hours** only if you also give the flight attendant a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** that begins **no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest** — and no duty of any kind may be assigned during either rest period.

Ensuring that processing time is not dependent on the value of a secret is the best defense against any form of timing attack.
11. IANA Considerations
This revision of HTTP/2 marks the HTTP2-Settings header field and the h2c upgrade token, both defined in [RFC7540], as obsolete.
Section 11 of [RFC7540] registered the h2 and h2c ALPN identifiers along with the PRI HTTP method. RFC 7540 also established a registry for frame types, settings, and error codes. These registrations and registries apply to HTTP/2, but are not redefined in this document.
IANA has updated references to RFC 7540 in the following registries to refer to this document: "TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs", "HTTP/2 Frame Type", "HTTP/2 Settings", "HTTP/2 Error Code", and "HTTP Method Registry". The registration of the PRI method has been updated to refer to Section 3.4; all other section numbers have not changed.
IANA has changed the policy on those portions of the "HTTP/2 Frame Type" and "HTTP/2 Settings" registries that were reserved for Experimental Use in RFC 7540. These portions of the registries shall operate on the same policy as the remainder of each registry.

This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext
Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). HTTP/2 enables a more
efficient use of network resources and a
reduced perception of latency by introducing header field compression and allowing multiple
concurrent exchanges on the same connection.¶
This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax.
HTTP's existing semantics remain unchanged.  This document obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.¶
Discussion Venues
This note is to be removed before publishing as an RFC.¶
Discussion of this document takes place on the HTTPBIS Working Group mailing list
(ietf-http-wg@w3.org), which is archived at https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/.¶
Source for this draft and an issue tracker can be found at
https://github.com/httpwg/http2-spec.¶
Status of This Memo

TECHNICAL NOTE — CURRENT HTTP/2 SPECIFICATION AND ITS OBSOLESCENCE SET

1. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113.
  Title:      Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)
  Editors:    M. Thomson (Ed.), Mozilla; C. Benfield (Ed.), Apple Inc.
  Date:       June 2022
  Category:   Standards Track (Proposed Standard; not yet an Internet Standard)
  Stream:     IETF
  ISSN:       2070-1721
  Canonical:  https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113
  Also at:    https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113 (HTML)
              https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html (HTTPWG copy)

Ask 2 — RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113: exactly two — RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.
  RFC 7540 — Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2), R. Peon and M. Belshe (Eds.), May 2015, Standards Track. This was the original HTTP/2 specification.
  RFC 8740 — Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2, D. Benjamin, February 2020, Standards Track. This was a narrow update to RFC 7540 adding TLS 1.3 guidance; its content is folded into RFC 9113 (Section 9.2), so the standalone document is retired.

Both facts come from a single authoritative field: the RFC 9113 header block, which reads "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" and whose Abstract states "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." The same header block supplies the answer to Ask 1 (RFC 9113 is the document bearing that header). There is no inference step between the two answers.

2. OBSOLESCENCE CHAIN

  RFC 7540 (May 2015, HTTP/2)
      |  updated by (not obsoleted by)
  RFC 8740 (Feb 2020, TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2)
      |
      |  both obsoleted together by
      v
  RFC 9113 (Jun 2022, HTTP/2)   <-- current specification

Note the direction of the RFC 8740 relationship: RFC 8740 *updated* RFC 7540; it did not obsolete it. RFC 9113 then obsoletes both at once, because it merges the TLS 1.3 requirements into the main text and reissues the whole specification. Anyone who answers Ask 2 as "only RFC 7540" (the 'HTTP/2 predecessor' reading) is wrong against the header; anyone who answers "RFC 7540 and everything that referenced it" is also wrong, because obsolescence is not transitive through references.

3. WHAT RFC 9113 DOES *NOT* OBSOLETE (guard against over-broad answers)

  - RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2, May 2015): NOT obsoleted. RFC 9113 cites it normatively as [COMPRESSION]; HPACK remains the header-compression scheme for HTTP/2.
  - RFC 7301 (TLS ALPN): NOT obsoleted; still the negotiation mechanism HTTP/2 uses.
  - RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1): siblings published in the same June 2022 revision cycle, not obsoleted by 9113.
  - RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (requirement keywords): referenced, not obsoleted.
  - HTTP/1.1 message syntax: RFC 9113 explicitly states HTTP/2 is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, HTTP/1.1.

4. SUBSTANTIVE CHANGES THAT MOTIVATE THE OBSOLESCENCE (for reviewers who need the 'why')

  - TLS 1.3 support: defined per RFC 8740, which this document obsoletes (Appendix B).
  - Priority: the RFC 7540 priority scheme (PRIORITY frame, HEADERS priority fields) is deprecated. Frame formats and mandatory handling are retained for interoperability; the semantics remain described only in RFC 7540 Section 5.3. The successor scheme is RFC 9218 (Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP).
  - HTTP/1.1 Upgrade to h2c: removed from the specification; the h2c upgrade token and the HTTP2-Settings header field are registered as obsolete (Sections 3.1 and 11). Prior-knowledge h2c remains.
  - Experimental-use codepoint ranges for frame types and settings are opened to normal registration policy.

5. SCOPE, PROVENANCE AND CAVEATS

  - Definition of 'current' used here: the most recent Standards Track RFC specifying HTTP/2 as of the sources consulted (fetched 2026-11-16). This is not a project-pinned version; if a consumer pins an older revision, RFC 7540 remains the governing text for that pin.
  - 'Obsoletes' is read strictly as the explicit obsoletes-list in the RFC 9113 header, not as transitive obsolescence and not as 'documents superseded in practice'.
  - Errata: verified errata exist against HTTP/2 RFCs and should be consulted at https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=9113 before treating the text as normative for implementation. Errata correct text; they do not change the RFC number or the obsoletes-list.
  - Drafts: draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-* is the pre-publication draft of RFC 9113 (e.g., -02, June 2021, header "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 (if approved)"). It is superseded by RFC 9113 and must not be cited as the current specification.
  - Successor check: no RFC obsoleting or replacing RFC 9113 appears in any consulted source; the HTTPWG copy at httpwg.org still serves RFC 9113 as the current HTTP/2 spec. A later revision would surface as a new 'Obsoletes: 9113' header — re-verify against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 before relying on this answer far from the 2026-11-16 retrieval date.

6. ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

  "HTTP/2 is specified by RFC 9113 (June 2022, Standards Track), which obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740."

quotes.whole:
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.
Different minimum wage rates continue to apply to 18-20 year olds, 16-17 year olds and apprentices aged under 19 or in the first year of an apprenticeship. The Government has stated its ambition to reduce the NLW age threshold from 21 to 18; this follows the LPC’s own stated ambition and advice, as set out in the publication The National Minimum Wage Beyond 2024.
Rates for workers aged under 21, and apprentices, are currently lower than the NLW to reflect lower average earnings and higher unemployment rates. International evidence also suggests that younger workers are more exposed to employment risks arising from the pay floor than older workers. Unlike the NLW (where the possibility of some consequences for employment have been accepted by the Government), the LPC’s remit requires us to set the rates for 16-17 year olds and apprentices as high as possible without causing damage to jobs and hours.

The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.
The Low Pay Commission is an independent body made up of employers, trade unions and experts whose role is to advise the Government on the minimum wage. The rate recommendations introduced today were agreed unanimously by the Commission. The current Low Pay Commissioners are: Baroness Philippa Stroud (Chair), Nigel Cotgrove, Matthew Fell, Andrew Goodacre, Louise Fisher, Professor Patricia Rice, Simon Sapper, Professor Jonathan Wadsworth and Janet Williamson.
Baroness Philippa Stroud can be contacted via the Low Pay Commission’s press office (07341 098734).

verdict.summary:
# UK National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage — rates effective from April 2026

## Direct answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Annual increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage, workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85 per hour** | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both figures are **confirmed, announced rates** — not forecasts or projections. They take effect on **1 April 2026** and apply until 31 March 2027.

## Full April 2026 rate table (for context and to prevent band confusion)

| NMW rate | From 1 April 2026 | Increase (£) | Increase (%) | Previous (April 2025 – March 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 | 4.1 | £12.21 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 | 8.5 | £10.00 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 | £7.55 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 | £7.55 |
| Accommodation Offset (daily limit) | £11.10 | £0.44 | 4.1 | £10.66 |

**Out of scope — do not confuse:** the same GOV.UK rates page also lists indicative **April 2027** rates (21+ £13.21; 18–20 £11.27; under-18 £8.31; apprentice £8.31). Those are not the answer to this question and are shown here only so the two years are not mixed up.

## Status and provenance

- **Announced:** 26 November 2025 by the Government, accepting in full the Low Pay Commission's recommendations (LPC advice submitted October 2025).
- **In force:** from 1 April 2026; the LPC's impact report *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* was published 1 April 2026.
- **Authority:** GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission. The same two numbers (£12.71 and £10.85) appear identically in four separate GOV.UK locations, so there is no source conflict to reconcile:
  1. LPC press release, *LPC recommendations take the National Living Wage to £12.71*, 26 Nov 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/lpc-recommendations-take-the-national-living-wage-to-1271
  2. LPC, *Minimum wage rates for 2026* (advice to Government), 26 Nov 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
  3. LPC, *The National Minimum Wage in 2026*, 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
  4. GOV.UK, *National Minimum Wage rates* (live rates table) — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates

## Applicability notes

- **Age band structure is unchanged for April 2026.** The NLW applies to workers aged **21 and over** (the threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and 23 to 21 in April 2024). Workers aged 20 and under remain on the age-related NMW rates. A separate 18–20 Year Old Rate therefore still exists for the whole of 2026/27.
- **Forward look (not part of the answer):** the LPC has set out a path to extend the NLW to 20-year-olds in **2027** and to 18- and 19-year-olds in **2028 or 2029**, subject to economic conditions and government policy. Anyone using these figures for multi-year planning should treat the 18–20 band as time-limited, but it is fully in force for April 2026.
- **Gap between the two rates:** £10.85 is **85.4%** of £12.71 — the gap narrowed from 81.9% in April 2025 (£10.00 / £12.21) but the rates are not aligned.
- **Regional scope:** these are UK-wide statutory rates; no regional or devolved variation applies.
- **Gross headline rates:** the figures are the statutory hourly minimums before tax, NI and pension deductions. The only permitted offset relevant here is the **accommodation offset** (£11.10 per day maximum for April 2026), which is a separate limit, not an adjustment to the hourly rates above.
- **Apprentice carve-out:** apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, are entitled to the Apprentice Rate (£8.00), not the NLW/age rate — even if they are 21 or over. Once they are 19+ and have completed the first year, the full rate for their age applies.

## Verification procedure (how to re-confirm before relying on this)

1. Open https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates and locate the row labelled **April 2026** in the 'Current rates' table; read the '21 and over' and '18 to 20' columns. Expect **£12.71** and **£10.85**.
2. Cross-check against the statutory instrument commenced 1 April 2026 (the annual National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations for that uprating) if a legal citation is needed rather than a guidance citation.
3. Confirm the page has not been superseded: from 1 April 2027 the current-rates row rolls forward to April 2027 (£13.21 / £11.27), at which point the April 2026 figures move into the 'Previous rates' section — they remain correct for the 2026/27 year but would no longer be the live rate.
4. If any source disagrees with £12.71 / £10.85 for the 1 April 2026 uprating, treat GOV.UK and the LPC publications as authoritative over press summaries and re-check for a correction notice.

**Bottom line: £12.71/hour for workers aged 21 and over, and £10.85/hour for 18–20 year olds, both effective 1 April 2026.**

The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.
Different minimum wage rates continue to apply to 18-20 year olds, 16-17 year olds and apprentices aged under 19 or in the first year of an apprenticeship. The Government has stated its ambition to reduce the NLW age threshold from 21 to 18; this follows the LPC’s own stated ambition and advice, as set out in the publication The National Minimum Wage Beyond 2024.
Rates for workers aged under 21, and appren

This year, the 16-17 Year Old Rate and the Apprentice Rate will increase by 6 per cent to £8.00.
The recommendation for 16-17 year olds balances the weaker labour market for this age group with the need to ensure their rate does not become unmoored from the adult rate, particularly as Government policy is to remove the 18-20 Year Old Rate.
Having increased significantly in 2025, we expect coverage for 16-17 year olds to increase again this year, from 22 to 23 per cent. Coverage for apprentices is also expected to increase from 17 to 18 per cent.

PROPERTY-CARRYING DRIVERS
PASSENGER-CARRYING DRIVERS
11-Hour Driving Limit
May drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
10-Hour Driving Limit
May drive a maximum of 10 hours after 8 consecutive hours off duty.
14-Hour Limit
May not drive beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty, following 10 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time does not extend the 14-hour period.
15-Hour Limit
May not drive after having been on duty for 15 hours, following 8 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period.
30-Minute Driving Break
Drivers must take a 30-minute break when they have driven for a period of 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption. The break may be satisfied by any non-driving period of 30 consecutive minutes (i.e., on-duty not driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of these taken consecutively).
60/70-Hour Limit
May not drive after 60/70 hours on duty in 7/8 consecutive days. A driver may restart a 7/8 consecutive day period after taking 34 or more consecutive hours off duty.

May not drive after 60/70 hours on duty in 7/8 consecutive days.

Drivers are allowed to extend the 10-hour maximum driving time and 15-hour on-duty limit by up to 2 hours when adverse driving conditions are encountered.
Short-Haul Exception
A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in §395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location.
Short-Haul Exception
A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in §395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location.

verdict.summary:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — THE TWO QUALIFYING THRESHOLDS
Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), '150 air-mile radius driver' (current eCFR text, verified against the FMCSA Hours-of-Service summary page and FMCSA short-haul training materials).

ANSWERS
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation parenthetically equates this to 172.6 statute miles. This is an air-mile (great-circle) measure, not road miles; a route that stays under 172.6 statute miles of driving distance but exceeds 150 air miles point-to-point from the reporting location is outside the exception.
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The clock runs from the time the driver comes on duty; the driver must both physically return to the reporting location and be released there inside that 14-hour window. There is no averaging across days and no extension of the 14-hour release requirement.

VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))
'(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.'

SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY NOTES (needed to apply the two figures correctly)
- Carrier type: the 150 air-mile / 14-hour pair applies to both property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. Carrier type changes only the required off-duty period separating duty periods — 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying — not the 150-mile radius or the 14-hour release window.
- Driver-salesperson: the release-within-14-hours condition in (e)(1)(ii) is expressly inapplicable to a driver-salesperson; the radius condition still governs.
- Effect of the exception: it exempts the driver from the record-of-duty-status requirement in 395.8 and the supporting-documents requirement in 395.11. It does not exempt the carrier from the 6-month time-record obligation in (e)(1)(iv), which must capture report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and (for new or intermittent drivers) the preceding 7 days' totals.
- Exceeding a threshold: if on a given day the driver goes outside the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must record duty status for that day (paper log or ELD). FMCSA guidance applies the ELD rule by frequency: 8 or fewer days in the last 30 may be logged on a paper graph grid; more than 8 days in the last 30 requires an ELD for that day.
- Adverse driving conditions do not enlarge the 14-hour release threshold. The adverse-driving-conditions provision extends the driving window and driving time by up to 2 hours, but FMCSA's published short-haul Q&A states that a short-haul driver who cannot return to the reporting location within 14 hours because of an adverse driving condition must record duty status for that day. The 14-hour figure above therefore stands as the operative release threshold.
- Measurement of the reporting location: the location must be the same at the start and end of the shift, but it need not be the same location from shift to shift (FMCSA short-haul Q&A). The radius is measured from that day's normal work reporting location.

PROVISIONS THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (flagged to prevent misapplication)
- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2), property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL: also a 150 air-mile radius and a return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, but it has no single 'released within X consecutive hours' figure; instead the driver may not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, or after the 16th hour on 2 of those days. The 14/16-hour driving cutoffs in that provision are not the release threshold asked about here.
- 49 CFR 395.1(o), the 16-hour window for certain property-carrying drivers: a separate exception with its own five-duty-tour precondition; its 16-hour figure is not the short-haul release threshold.
- 49 CFR 395.1(p), motion picture production sites: a 100 air-mile radius provision; not applicable to the short-haul exception.

BOTTOM LINE
A driver qualifies for the RODS-free short-haul exception only if the driver operates within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location and returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours, while also meeting the applicable consecutive-off-duty requirement and the carrier's 6-month time-record obligation.

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.
