verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — 14 CFR 61.113(i) (current text, as amended November 2024)

1. ANSWERS

  Ask 1 — Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds (maximum certificated takeoff weight, inclusive ceiling).
  Ask 2 — Occupents the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 (inclusive ceiling).
  Ask 3 — Passengers on board: 6 (inclusive ceiling).

  Source text (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), eCFR current / GPO CFR 2025 title 14 vol 2):
  'The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupents, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter.'

2. WHAT EACH NUMBER MEANS (the definitions matter for compliance)

  - Maximum takeoff weight = the aircraft's MAXIMUM CERTIFICATED TAKEOFF WEIGHT under its design approval (TC, STC, or ATC), NOT the actual weight of a given flight. The FAA's BasicMed page states it as 'maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.' An aircraft whose certificated MTOW is 12,500 lb is inside the rule; 12,501 lb is outside it. A light aircraft flown heavy is a weight-and-balance problem, not a BasicMed eligibility problem.
  - Occupents authorizated = the number the aircraft's design approval permits it to carry, including required flightcrew. It is a property of the aircraft, not of the flight.
  - Passengers on board = the actual count on a given flight, excluding the PIC (and excluding other required flightcrew, who are occupents but not passengers).
  - Arithmetic check: 6 passengers + 1 PIC = 7 occupents — exactly at the ceiling, permitted. The two limits are deliberately set so that a 7-seat aircraft flown by a single PIC can be filled with 6 passengers.
  - Additional, separate disqualifier: a transport-category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 is prohibited regardless of its weight or seat count. This is an independent condition, not a numeric threshold.

3. FULL AIRCRAFT/OPERATING CONDITION SET (§ 61.113(i)(1)–(3)) — for context, the three asked items are items 1–3

  1. Aircraft authorized to carry not more than 7 occupents.
  2. Maximum certificated takeoff weight not more than 12,500 lb.
  3. No more than 6 passengers on board.
  4. Not a transport-category rotorcraft certificated under part 29.
  5. Flight, including each portion, not above 18,000 ft MSL.
  6. Not outside the United States unless authorized by the country concerned.
  7. Not above 250 knots indicated airspeed.
  8. No compensation or hire.
  9. Pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets § 61.23(c)(3), and carries in the logbook the completed § 68.7 CMEC and the § 61.23(c)(3) course-completion certificate.

  Experimental aircraft: § 91.319(j) separately caps BasicMed operation of experimental aircraft at the same occupent ceiling; it should be read consistently with the amended § 61.113(i)(1) figure of 7.

4. VERSION CONTROL — DO NOT APPLY THE OLD NUMBERS

  The FAA's Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17), quoted in the research fetches, still carries the pre-amendment limits: 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, 6 occupents, 5 passengers. Those figures were superseded by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and the FAA's 15 November 2024 update (FAA newsroom, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program'), which state: passengers increased to six from five, occupents to seven from six, and maximum takeoff weight to 12,500 lb from 6,000 lb, excluding transport-category helicopters. Any checklest, kneeboard card, or self-assessment built on AC 68-1A is out of date and must be corrected to 12,500 lb / 7 occupents / 6 passengers.

5. RESULTING COMPLIANCE STATEMENT

  A flight is within BasicMed aircraft limits if and only if: certificated MTOW ≤ 12,500 lb; design approval authorizes ≤ 7 occupents; actual passengers on board ≤ 6; and the aircraft is not a part 29 transport-category rotorcraft. The three requested values are therefore 12,500 lb, 7 occupents, and 6 passengers, current as of the November 2024 amendment.

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.





[70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

The driver must be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus or passenger-carrying CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight that it may be transporting.

verdict.summary:
# Hours of Service — Driver of a Passenger-Carrying CMV (e.g., Motorcoach), Interstate, US

**Governing rule:** 49 CFR § 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A), subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1. Current as published on eCFR and identical in the 2019 printed CFR edition and on FMCSA's own passenger-carrier guidance, so the numbers are stable across editions.

---

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** | § 395.5(a)(1) — no driving "more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may they drive again? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) — both limits are measured from "8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | § 395.5(a)(2) — no driving "for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |

### The rule in one sentence
After **8 consecutive hours off duty**, the driver may drive up to **10 hours**, and may not drive at all once **15 hours on duty** have elapsed — whichever comes first ends driving for that shift.

---

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text (§ 395.5)

> **§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.**
> Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
>
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
>
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
>
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
>
> (b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—
>
> (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
>
> (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.
>
> [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

---

## 3. How the three limits interlock

The 8-hour off-duty period is a single reset that starts two independent clocks:

- **Driving clock:** 10 hours of driving accumulated after the reset.
- **On-duty clock (the "window"):** 15 consecutive hours measured from coming on duty after the reset.

Both clocks run from the same 8-consecutive-hour off-duty reset. Driving stops at whichever is reached first:

- Driver drives 6 hours, then sits on duty (loading, paperwork, waiting) for 9 hours → **15-hour window expires; no further driving**, even though only 6 of the 10 driving hours were used.
- Driver drives 10 hours within the first 12 hours of the shift → **10-hour driving limit reached; no further driving**, even though 3 hours of the 15-hour window remain.

Neither limit may be exceeded by borrowing from the other. On-duty time that is not driving still consumes the 15-hour window. The regulation does not prescribe a minimum off-duty break *within* the shift for passenger carriers (unlike the 30-minute break in the property-carrying rule at § 395.3(a)(3)(ii)); the only mandatory rest is the 8 consecutive hours between shifts.

---

## 4. Weekly (cumulative) limits — context, not the answer to ask 3

§ 395.5(b) adds a separate cumulative ceiling. These are **not** the 15-hour daily window and should not be conflated with ask 3:

| Carrier operates CMVs… | On-duty ceiling | Rolling period |
|---|---|---|
| Not every day of the week | **60 hours** | any 7 consecutive days |
| Every day of the week | **70 hours** | any 8 consecutive days |

Driving is prohibited after the ceiling is reached, regardless of how much daily driving time remains. The 60/70-hour limits are on-duty hours, not driving hours, and include on-duty-not-driving time.

---

## 5. Common errors this answer is written to prevent

1. **Property-carrying rules substituted for passenger rules.** The property rule, § 395.3, is **11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off duty / 14-hour window**, plus a 30-minute break after 8 hours and a 34-hour restart. **None of those apply here.** For passenger-carrying CMVs the figures are **10 / 8 / 15**. The 2019 govinfo PDF snippet in the source set that shows "10 consecutive hours off duty" and "14 consecutive hours" is § 395.3, the *property* rule, and must not be used.
2. **The 34-hour restart.** The 34-hour restart provision in § 395.3(c) belongs to the property-carrying rule; the passenger rule at § 395.5 contains no restart provision. A passenger carrier driver recovers weekly capacity only by the passage of the 7- or 8-day window, not by a 34-hour reset.
3. **The 14 in the short-haul exception.** § 395.1(e) exempts drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released within **14** consecutive hours from the record-of-duty-status requirement. That 14 is a recordkeeping threshold, **not** a driving window. The 15-hour driving prohibition still applies.
4. **Confusing "8 hours off" with "8 hours sleeper berth."** § 395.1(g)(3) permits a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth to accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods meeting § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv). This is a way to *satisfy* the 8-hour reset, not a reduction of it.
5. **Treating off-duty as any non-driving time.** Off-duty time requires the driver to be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the vehicle, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage, and freight. A driver who remains responsible for the coach or passengers during a meal stop is not off duty.

---

## 6. Exceptions that can move the numbers (§ 395.1)

The base answers above are the general limits. The following are the only common variations; each is stated with its effect on the 10 / 8 / 15 figures:

| Provision | Effect on the three figures |
|---|---|
| § 395.1(b)(1) — adverse driving conditions | The **10-hour driving** and **15-hour on-duty** limits may each be extended by up to **2 hours** (to 12 and 17) when the driver encounters unusually adverse conditions that could not reasonably have been known. It does **not** extend the 60/70-hour limits, and the 8-hour off-duty reset is unchanged. |
| § 395.1(e) — short-haul / 150 air-mile | Recordkeeping exemption only. **10 / 8 / 15 unchanged.** |
| § 395.1(g)(3) — sleeper berth (passenger) | Two rest periods may accumulate the equivalent of the **8 consecutive hours off duty**. The 8-hour figure itself is unchanged. |
| § 395.1(k) — State of Alaska | Allows alternate 20-hour driving/off-duty cycles under specified conditions. Not applicable outside Alaska. |
| § 395.1(h) — State of Hawaii | Special rules; not applicable outside Hawaii. |

**Scope caveat.** These are the **federal interstate** limits. A driver operating **intrastate only** is governed by the state's own rules (many states adopt the federal passenger limits by reference, but some do not), and non-business private motor carriers of passengers are exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirement (though not from the driving limits). If the operation is intrastate, the state authority must be checked before relying on 10 / 8 / 15.

---

## 7. One-line compliance check a carrier or dispatcher can apply

For each driver, each shift:

1. Confirm **≥ 8 consecutive hours off duty** immediately before the shift. If not, no driving.
2. Track driving hours; at **10.0 hours of driving**, stop driving.
3. Track elapsed time since coming on duty; at **15.0 hours on duty**, stop driving regardless of driving hours remaining.
4. Track the cumulative on-duty total; at **60 hours in 7 days** (carrier not operating every day) or **70 hours in 8 days** (carrier operating every day), stop driving regardless of 1–3.

Whichever of steps 2, 3, or 4 triggers first ends driving until the applicable reset is satisfied.

(a) For purposes of this section—
Calendar day means the period of elapsed time, using Coordinated Universal Time or local time, that begins at midnight and ends 24 hours later at the next midnight.
Duty period means the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time.
Flight attendant means an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — 14 CFR Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

1. SHORT ANSWER

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | At least 9 consecutive hours | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| To what that rest may be reduced | To 8 consecutive hours, but only with a compensatory subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are regulatory minimums for a required flight attendant. The 8-hour figure is a hard floor; there is no provision allowing less.

2. WHY THIS RULE GOVERNS

14 CFR 135.261(e) (the applicability section of Part 135 Subpart F) states: "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." Section 135.273 is therefore not limited to scheduled passenger operations, nor to the 135.265/135.267/135.269 flight-crewmember framework. An on-demand (unscheduled) Part 135 charter operator is squarely within it. The flight-crewmember rest rules in 135.263-135.271 do not supply the answer for cabin crew; 135.273 does.

The rule applies to a "flight attendant," defined in 135.273(a) as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under its operations specifications, or in addition to that minimum, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include cabin-safety responsibilities. If the person is carried but is neither part of the required complement nor assigned cabin-safety duties, 135.273 does not apply — but in that case there is no regulatory rest minimum at all, only company policy.

Part 121 flight attendant rest rules (121.467) do not apply to a Part 135 certificate holder and were not used here.

3. THE TWO PARAGRAPHS, VERBATIM

135.273(b)(1): "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

135.273(b)(2): "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

135.273(b)(3): "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

4. CONDITIONS ATTACHING TO THE 8-HOUR REDUCTION — ALL FOUR MUST BE MET

A reduction from 9 to 8 hours is lawful only if every element below is satisfied. Miss any one and the rest owed is 9 hours.

(a) Floor: the reduced rest is at least 8 consecutive hours. Eight is the minimum; 7 hours 59 minutes is non-compliant.
(b) Compensatory rest: the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours.
(c) Timing: that subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the BEGINNING (not the end) of the reduced rest period.
(d) Placement: the subsequent rest period occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period — i.e., it is a real, scheduled, logged rest period in the sequence, not a notional credit.

Additional operative constraints in the same section:
- 135.273(b)(10): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section.
- 135.273(b)(11): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period.
- 135.273(a): "Rest period means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." Deadhead travel, positioning, training, phone availability, or any assigned task inside the rest window destroys the rest period.
- Duty period means the elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder.

5. WHAT THE REDUCTION IS NOT (common scheduling errors)

- 135.273(b)(9) does NOT attach to the (b)(3) reduction. Paragraph (b)(9)'s bar on scheduling a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of a reduced rest period is expressly limited to an election to reduce rest to 10 hours "as authorized by paragraph (b)(8)." No equivalent next-day 14-hour cap is imposed by (b)(3). Do not import it into the 8-hour case, and do not drop it from the (b)(8) case.
- The 9-hour and 8-hour figures are for scheduled duty periods of 14 hours or less only. For scheduled duty periods exceeding 14 hours, 135.273(b)(4) through (b)(9) contain a separate regime. Those paragraphs are outside the scope of this question and their figures must not be conflated with 9/8; a scheduler must branch on the duty-period length before applying a rest value.
- "Scheduled" is the trigger. Under 135.273(b)(14), a flight attendant is not considered scheduled for duty in excess of the limitations if the flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limitations but, due to circumstances beyond the certificate holder's control (e.g., adverse weather), were not at departure expected to reach destination within the scheduled time. That relieves the duty-period-limit exposure; it does not relieve the rest obligation. The 9-hour (or properly reduced 8-hour) rest is still owed before the next assignment.
- 135.273(c) alternative: a certificate holder may elect, by written procedures applying to all its flight attendants, to apply the Part 135 flight-crewmember flight time and duty/rest requirements to flight attendants (rest facilities on board not required). If such an election is in place, the rest values change to the flight-crewmember scheme (135.265: rest tied to scheduled flight time, reducible under 135.265(c) with compensatory rest). This memo assumes no such election, no OpsSpec deviation, no exemption, and no collective bargaining agreement more restrictive than the regulation. Any of those would have to be checked against the specific certificate.

6. WORKED EXAMPLE

Scheduled duty period ends 2100 local on Day 1.

- Baseline (no reduction): 9 consecutive hours → next duty period may not commence before 0600 Day 2.
- Reduced: rest 2100 Day 1 to 0500 Day 2 (8 consecutive hours). Next duty period 0500-1500 Day 2. The compensatory subsequent rest must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must BEGIN no later than 2100 Day 2 (24 hours after 2100 Day 1, the start of the reduced rest). A rest from 1500 to 0100 Day 3 satisfies both tests: it begins 6 hours inside the deadline and runs exactly 10 consecutive hours.
- Non-compliant variant: next duty 0500-1700 Day 2, rest 1700 Day 2 to 0300 Day 3. The rest is 10 hours but begins at 1700, which is still within the 24-hour window (2100 Day 2 deadline), so this one is actually compliant on timing — the failure mode to watch is a rest that begins after 2100 Day 2, or one that runs only 9 hours.

7. SCHEDULING AND RECORDS PROCEDURE

1) Identify each person as a 135.273 flight attendant (OpsSpecs complement or assigned cabin-safety duties) before applying any rest value.
2) Compute the scheduled duty period (report to release) and branch: 14 hours or less → apply 9 hours; more than 14 hours → apply the separate (b)(4)-(b)(9) regime, not this memo.
3) Default to 9 consecutive hours. Use 8 only as an affirmative, documented election with the 10-hour compensatory rest already placed on the schedule inside the 24-hour window measured from the start of the reduced rest.
4) Verify the rest window contains no duty, no deadhead, no training, no on-call availability, and no required contact — rest means free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.
5) Record, per pairing: scheduled duty start/end, rest start/end, whether reduced, the compensatory rest start/end and the elapsed time from reduced-rest start to compensatory-rest start (must be 24 hours or less). Retain with the crew schedule and duty logs.
6) Re-check after any irregular operation: a delay that pushes the actual duty period past 14 hours does not retroactively authorize the 8-hour rest, and a delay that eats into a scheduled rest requires recomputing from the actual rest obtained.

8. SCOPE AND CAVEATS

This answer assumes the current published text of 14 CFR Part 135 as reflected in the eCFR and the 2025 govinfo compilation, a required flight attendant, no 135.273(c) election, no applicable exemption or OpsSpec relief, and no more-restrictive CBA. Confirm the currency of the regulation and check the specific certificate's operations specifications and any exemptions before relying on it operationally. State, local, or foreign jurisdiction rest requirements are not addressed.

Abstract
This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics
of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP
version 2 (HTTP/2).  HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network
resources and a reduced perception of latency by introducing header
field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the
same connection.  It also introduces unsolicited push of
representations from servers to clients.
This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the
HTTP/1.1 message syntax.  HTTP's existing semantics remain unchanged.

Notes:
It's unclear from the text whether PRIORITY frames affect stream states (as shown in the state machine in Section 5.1).  The original intent was that prioritization of streams was independent of the mechanics of opening and closing streams, but this was not consistently captured.
Two small additions to the document would help considerably.
In Section 5.3 (Stream Priority) add a new paragraph:
> The information that an endpoint maintains for stream priority is separate from other state. Importantly, this includes stream states (Section 5.1).  A stream in any state can have its priority changed with a PRIORITY frame. The state of a stream is not changed as a result of changing its priority.  The number of streams for which state is remembered is at the discretion of an endpoint, see Section 5.3.4 for details.
In Section 6.4 (PRIORITY) a new sentence at the end of the first paragraph:
> Sending or receiving a PRIORITY frame does not affect the state of any stream (Section 5.1), only the priority of streams is altered.

# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, M. Thomson, Ed. and C. Benfield, Ed., Proposed Standard |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

**As of:** the source pages below were retrieved 2026-11-16 (UTC). RFC status can change; re-check the RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 before relying on this in a dated document.

## 1. The current specification: RFC 9113

Evidence (primary, RFC Editor):

- `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/` — header block reads: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 … June 2022. M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed. Proposed Standard".
- `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` — banner: "This RFC is now obsoleted, see RFC 9113."
- The RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject page (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/`) lists 9113 as the HTTP/2 core document, with 7540 shown only in its historical role.

So the replacement chain for the core document is **RFC 7540 (May 2015) → RFC 9113 (June 2022)**, and 9113 is the current one. Note the maturity level: 9113 is a **Proposed Standard**, not a full Internet Standard — do not describe it as "the HTTP/2 standard (STD)" in downstream text.

Also worth recording: 9113 is a *revision* of 7540, not a from-scratch design; it keeps the frame layout and HPACK (RFC 7541) and changes TSL 1.3 handling, deprocates the priority scheme, deprocates the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade / h2c path, and tightens field validation (Appendix B of RFC 9113).

## 2. What RFC 9113 obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740

Direct quote, appearing verbatim in both the info page and the XML source (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml`):

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Expanded:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Publication | Why it is in the Obsoletes list |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 7540 | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | May 2015, Belshe, Peon, Thomson (Ed.) | The original HTTP/2 core specification, wholly repleaced by 9113. |
| RFC 8740 | *Using TSL 1.3 with HTTP/2* | February 2020, D. Benjamin | It was a patch on 7540 (forbidding TSL 1.3 post-handshake auth); its content is folded into 9113. Confirmed by RFC 9113 Appendix B: "Use of TSL 1.3 was defined based on [RFC 8740], which this document obsoletes." |

That is the complete list. The Obsoletes header names exactly those two documents; no others.

## 3. Relations that are frequently conflated — keep them apart

- **Obsoleted vs. updated.** RFC 7540 was *updated* by RFC 8740 **and** *obsoleted* by RFC 9113. The errata listing for 7540 shows both lines side by side: "Obsoleted by: RFC9113 / Updated by: RFC8740". These are distinct relations; 8740 never obsoleted 7540.
- **Obsoletes vs. updated-by, for 9113 itself.** In the pages retrieved, RFC 9113 carries **no** "Updated by" and **no** "Obsoleted by" notice. Report it as current *as of the retrieval date*, not as current forever.
- **Transitive obsoletion is not in scope** (and would add nothing here anyway): 9113's Obsoletes list is read literally, as the two documents named above. Nothing named in that list itself obsoleted a further RFC that would need to be carried forward.
- **Companion documents are not obsoleted.** RFC 7541 (HPACK) is still the current header-compression spec and is cited normatively by 9113; RFC 8441 (WebSockets over HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (the ORIGIN frame) and RFC 8164 (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2, Historic) are separate documents in the HTTP/2 subject area and are **not** in 9113's Obsoletes header. Do not list them as obsoleted. (Their own Updates/Updated-by relations are a different question and are not asserted here.)

## 4. How to re-verify in under a minute

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/`. Check two things: (a) no "Obsoleted by" banner at the top (if one appears, the answer to ask 1 has changed — follow it); (b) the sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." in the abstract.
2. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` and confirm the banner "This RFC is now obsoleted, see RFC 9113."
3. For the authoritative header rather than the HTML rendering, use the XML (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml`) and read `<obsoletes>` in the front matter; it should contain exactly two entries, 7540 and 8740.
4. If citing in a document that must be stable, write the as-of date next to the claim.

## 5. Citation-ready form

> RFC 9113, *HTTP/2*, M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed., June 2022, Proosed Standard. Obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740. (Verified against the RFC Editor, 2026-11-16.)

Out of scope by the stated assumptions, and therefore not answered here: which RFCs *update* HTTP/2 without obsoleting it, and any transitive-obsoletion chain.

quotes.whole:
Kate Dearden
Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State
19th March 2026
Department for Business and Trade
Explanatory Note
(This note is not part of the Regulations)
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).

Impact Assessments generally accompany all UK Government interventions of a regulatory nature that affect the private sector, civil society organisations and public services. They apply regardless of whether the regulation originates from a domestic or international source and can accompany primary (Acts etc) and secondary legislation (SIs). An Impact Assessment allows those with an interest in the policy area to understand:
Why the government is proposing to intervene;
The main options the government is considering, and which one is preferred;
How and to what extent new policies may impact on them; and,
The estimated costs and benefits of proposed measures.

quotes.whole:
A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.
NOTES FOR EDITORS
The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.

verdict.summary:
UK NATIONAL MINIMUM WAGE / NATIONAL LIVING WAGE — RATES EFFECTIVE 1 APRIL 2026

1. HEADLINE ANSWERS

1.1 National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
    Previous rate (1 April 2025 – 31 March 2026): £12.21. Increase: 50p, 4.1%.

1.2 National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21): £10.85 per hour.
    Previous rate: £10.00. Increase: 85p, 8.5%.

Both rates take effect on 1 April 2026 and apply throughout England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (SI 2026/357, reg. 1(3)).

2. LEGAL BASIS

The rates are set by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026 and coming into force 1 April 2026. The instrument amends the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621):

  - reg. 2(2): in regulation 4 (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
  - reg. 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) (18 or over but not yet 21), for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'.
  - reg. 2(3)(b): in regulation 4A(1)(c) (under 18), for '£7.55' substitute '£8.00'.
  - reg. 2(3)(c): in regulation 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate), for '£7.55' substitute '£8.00'.

The figures implement in full the Low Pay Commission's recommendations submitted to Government on 27 October 2025 and accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025. These are final, in-force statutory rates — not projections or draft recommendations.

3. FULL TABLE FOR CONTEXT (all effective 1 April 2026)

  Band                              | Rate    | Cash increase | % increase
  ----------------------------------|---------|---------------|-----------
  National Living Wage (21 and over)| £12.71  | £0.50         | 4.1
  18–20 Year Old Rate               | £10.85  | £0.85         | 8.5
  16–17 Year Old Rate               | £8.00   | £0.45         | 6.0
  Apprentice Rate                   | £8.00   | £0.45         | 6.0
  Accommodation Offset             | £11.10 | £0.44         | 4.1

(Only the first two rows are responsive to the request; the remainder are supplied so the two headline figures are not misapplied in payroll or contract drafting.)

4. WHO EACH RATE APPLIES TO

4.1 NLW at £12.71: workers aged 21 and over. The NLW age threshold has been 21 since April 2024 (it was 25 before April 2021 and 23 from April 2021 to March 2024). 'National Living Wage' in this answer means the statutory NLW only.

4.2 18–20 Year Old Rate at £10.85: workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21. Age is determined by the worker's age on the relevant pay reference period, not by length of service.

4.3 Apprentice interaction (frequent compliance error): an apprentice is entitled to the £8.00 apprentice rate only if aged under 19, or aged 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to the full £12.71 NLW. An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to £8.00.

5. CAVEATS AND COMMON CONFUSIONS

5.1 The statutory National Living Wage is not the 'Real Living Wage' published by the Living Wage Foundation (a voluntary rate, separately calculated and higher). Any figure attributed to the Living Wage Foundation should not be used for HMRC national minimum wage compliance.

5.2 Rates are statutory hourly minimums. They are not annual salaries; any annualised figure (e.g. 'worth £X a year') depends on assumed hours and should not be presented as a statutory amount.

5.3 The rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. Workers whose pay reference period straddles 1 April are dealt with under the usual pay reference period rules in the 2015 Regulations; the April 2026 rate applies from the first pay reference period beginning on or after that date.

5.4 For forward planning only: the same GOV.UK rates page lists indicative April 2027 figures of £13.21 (21 and over), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (under 18), £8.31 (apprentice). These are not the answer to this request and are subject to the 2027 uprating cycle.

6. SOURCES

  - The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made
  - Low Pay Commission / GOV.UK, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
  - GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour
  - Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
  - GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates

Air Miles and Statute Miles
In the short-haul exceptions to the hours-of-service regulations, you will see the term “air miles.”
This is a different measurement of a mile than what is used for statute miles on a roadmap.
An air mile is longer than a statute mile. There are 6,076 feet in an air mile and 5,280 feet in a statute
mile. One-hundred air miles is equal to 115.08 statute miles.
Therefore, a 100 air-mile radius from your work reporting location can be figured as 115.08 statute,
or “roadmap,” miles (185.2 km) from your work reporting location. A 150 air-mile radius from your
work reporting location can be figured as 172.6 statute miles (277.8 km).
What Are the Hours-of-Service Limits?
The hours-of-service regulations focus on when and how long you are allowed to drive by placing
specific limits on the amount of time you drive your truck and how many total hours you can work
before you are no longer permitted to drive a commercial motor vehicle. You must follow three
maximum duty limits at all times. They are the 14-hour “driving window” limit, 11-hour driving
limit, and 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day duty limits.

verdict.summary:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — THE TWO REQUESTED CONDITIONS

CURRENT, IN-FORCE ANSWER (applicable to duty tours on or after September 29, 2020; verified against 49 CFR 395.1 as published in the 2024 edition of the CFR and on eCFR 'current'):

1. RADIUS — 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. (150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles, the conversion FMCSA states parenthetically in the rule itself.)

2. RELEASE TIME — 14 consecutive hours. The driver (other than a driver-salesperson) must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

CONTROLLING TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), quoted):

"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
 (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
 (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
 (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
 (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
 (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

§ 395.8 is the records-of-duty-status (RODS) requirement and § 395.11 is the supporting-documents requirement; the exemption from those two sections is what the question describes as 'frees a driver from keeping records of duty status.'

WHY THESE AND NOT OTHER FIGURES — THREE CONFLATIONS TO AVOID

(a) Superseded pre-2020 figures. Before the June 1, 2020 final rule (compliance date September 29, 2020), § 395.1(e)(1) read 100 air miles and 12 consecutive hours. FMCSA's own summary of that rule states it 'extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours' and 'extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from 100 to 150 air-miles.' Older guidance still in circulation (e.g., the 2015 Driver's Guide to HOS, which lists '100 air-mile radius driver ... report and return to work reporting location within 12 consecutive hours' at § 395.1(e)(1)) is out of date on both numbers. For current operations the answers are 150 and 14. If a specific historical duty tour is being adjudicated, the date of the tour controls: tours before September 29, 2020 → 100 air miles / 12 hours; tours on or after → 150 air miles / 14 hours.

(b) The non-CDL variant, § 395.1(e)(2). Operators of property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL under Part 383 also get a 150 air-mile radius, but the time condition is written differently: the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and must not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, nor after the 16th hour on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days. The 16-hour figure there is a two-days-per-week outer driving limit, not a general release time, and it does not convert the short-haul release condition into 16 hours. The 14-hour release answer above is from (e)(1).

(c) Other 100 air-mile provisions. § 395.1(o) (16-hour driving window, five duty tours, once per 7 consecutive days) and § 395.1(p) (motion picture production sites) each use a 100 air-mile radius for different relief and are not the general short-haul RODS exception. State, port, and drayage rules may impose different limits and do not alter the federal figures.

ADDITIONAL CONDITIONS THAT QUALIFY THE TWO NUMBERS (stated so the two figures are not read as the whole exception)

Meeting 150 air miles and 14 hours is necessary but not sufficient. A driver also needs: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty (property-carrying) or at least 8 consecutive hours (passenger-carrying); and the motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate and true time records of report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and — for drivers used for the first time or intermittently — total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2). The return-and-release condition does not apply to a driver-salesperson. Note also that § 395.1(e)(1) contains no 8-consecutive-days-in-30-days usage cap; that kind of frequency limit belongs to other exceptions, not this one.

PRACTICAL MEASUREMENT NOTES

Radius is measured in air miles, not road miles: 6,076 feet per air mile versus 5,280 feet per statute mile. FMCSA states 100 air miles = 115.08 statute miles and 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles (277.8 km). The radius is measured from the normal work reporting location, and the 14-hour clock runs from coming on duty, with the driver both returning to that location and being released from work by hour 14.

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

What is it?
BasicMed is an alternative pathway from traditional medical certification. Instead of seeing an aviation medical examiner, pilots who elect to fly with BasicMed work with a state licensed physician to go through a medical checklist every four years, and then take an online course covering various aeromedical topics every two years.  Every medical certificate has various privileges and limitations, and so does BasicMed. By flying with a BasicMed qualification, a pilot is limited to a six-place airplane, and five passengers, with a maximum takeoff weight of 6,000 pounds, and can fly up to 250 knots and up to 18,000 feet msl, day or night.

What are the limitations?
To fly with BasicMed, the aircraft must be certificated for six or fewer occupants with a maximum takeoff weight of 6,000 pounds or less. You can’t carry more than five passengers, fly higher than 18,000 feet, or exceed 250 knots, and it should go without saying that you can’t fly for compensation or hire. (Flight instruction is allowed and the CFI may be compensated for the instruction.) That’s it!
Personal responsibility
To date, more than 64,000 pilots have completed the online education course to qualify to fly under BasicMed. The course is available on AOPA online (aopa.org/basicmed), and covers various aeromedical topics. The Mayo Clinic also offers an online course.
The process to qualify under BasicMed isn’t difficult, but there are enough differences between it and traditional medical certification that pilots need to spend just a few minutes familiarizing themselves with the steps.
Gary Crump runs AOPA’s medical certification support team, and his staff fields thousands of calls a year from pilots with questions and concerns about all types of medical certification.

# BasicMed (United States) — aircraft limits

**Scope of this note:** the three aircraft-related eligibility limits in the FAA BasicMed rule, as currently in force. Other BasicMed operating limits are included only as context. This is a statement of the regulatory limits, not a determination that any particular pilot or aircraft qualifies.

---

## 1. Bottom line (current, effective 12 November 2024)

| # | Limit | Current value | Governing text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum **certificated takeoff weight** of the aircraft | **12,500 lb** (not more than) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as expanded by PL 118-63 §828 |
| 2 | **Occupants** the aircraft may be **authorized to carry** | **7** (not more than) | same |
| 3 | **Passengers on board** during the flight | **6** (not more than) | same |

All three are upper bounds stated as "not more than"; an aircraft certificated at exactly 12,500 lb, or at exactly 7 occupants, is within the rule. There is no lower bound in the rule other than what the aircraft's own airworthiness documents permit.

---

## 2. Authority and why these are the current numbers

**Statute.** BasicMed was created by §2307 of the 21st Century Cures Act (PL 114-255) and implemented by the FAA at 14 CFR 61.113(i), 61.23(c)(3), 14 CFR part 68, and 14 CFR 91.319(j).

**Expansion.** §828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63) raised all three aircraft limits, effective 12 November 2024. The FAA's implementing notice, **Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24)**, sets out both sets of numbers and states verbatim:

> "(2) Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024:
> • The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,
> • The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and
> • The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."

**Agency confirmation.** FAA newsroom release, Friday 15 November 2024, *FAA Updates BasicMed Program*:

> "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."

**Current FAA BasicMed page** (licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med), under "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements":

> "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers."

Three independent FAA sources — one dated after the effective date and one current web page — agree on 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers. That is the answer.

---

## 3. Superseded figures — DO NOT USE

For the period 1 May 2017 through 11 November 2024 the limits were:

| Limit | Old value | New value |
|---|---|---|
| MTOW | 6,000 lb | 12,500 lb |
| Occupants | 6 | 7 |
| Passengers | 5 | 6 |

These old numbers are **still printed** in FAA documents that have not been revised:

- **AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17)** — §3.2 ("no more than five passengers", "6,000 lbs", "no more than 6 occupants"), §5.1.2, §5.2.1 ("up to six occupants ... up to five passengers on board").
- **FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017, "The BasicMed Issue"** — "6,000 pounds or less ... not more than six occupants ... Max Passengers (five)".
- **AOPA, July 2021** — "six-place airplane, and five passengers ... 6,000 pounds".

Anyone citing AC 68-1A or the 2017 briefing as the current limit will get the pre-2024 numbers. If your compliance documentation, SOP, or training material cites the AC, it needs a revision note.

---

## 4. How each limit is measured

**Limit 1 — "maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds."**
It is the *certificated* MTOW in the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC), or the equivalent figure in the operating limitations for a non-type-certificated aircraft. It is **not** the actual weight at brake release. A 12,500 lb airplane that happens to be light is fine; a 12,500 lb airplane that is overloaded is an airworthiness violation under part 91, not a BasicMed violation. 12,500 lb is also the traditional "small aircraft / large aircraft" dividing line in 14 CFR 1.1, so the expansion now admits essentially the whole small-airplane fleet (e.g., a Cessna 208 Caravan at ~8,000 lb MTOW, most turboprop singles and light twins).

**Limit 2 — "authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants."**
The count that matters is the **occupant capacity in the design approval**, not the number of seats actually installed. AC 68-1A §5.1.2 makes the principle explicit (quoting the pre-2024 version): "the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry." The 2017 briefing gives the classic trap: "Certain aircraft, such as variants of the Piper PA-32 and PA-34 ... do not qualify under BasicMed because they are certificated to carry more than six occupants, even if they only have six seats installed." Under the current rule those same aircraft are measured against 7 — a PA-32-300 certificated for 7 occupants (1 pilot + 6) now qualifies.

**Occupants vs. passengers — the distinction the rule turns on.**
"Occupants" includes the pilot flying under BasicMed and any other required flight crew. "Passengers" excludes required flight crew. The two limits are separate and both must be satisfied:

| Aircraft certificated for | Required flight crew | Max passengers permitted by limit 3 | Permitted by limit 2? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 occupants | 1 pilot | 6 | Yes — 7 − 1 = 6 |
| 7 occupants | 2 pilots | 5 | Yes — 7 − 2 = 5 |
| 7 occupants | 1 pilot | 7 | **No** — exceeds limit 3 |
| 8 occupants | 1 pilot | 6 | **No** — exceeds limit 2 |

So a 7-occupant, single-required-pilot aircraft is the case that uses both limits to their full extent; any aircraft requiring two pilots can carry at most 5 passengers even though 6 are allowed by limit 3.

**Aircraft altered to fit.** An aircraft certificated above the limits can be brought inside them by a new design approval (STC or amended TC). AC 68-1A §5.1.2 states the principle — "if an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of more than 6,000 pounds is altered to have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of less than 6,000 pounds, then that aircraft would likewise meet the requirements" — and the same logic now applies with 12,500 lb and 7 occupants substituted. The alteration must be reflected in the design approval; a logbook entry or a removed seat row is not enough.

**Experimental / non-type-certificated aircraft.** Occupancy is governed by 14 CFR 91.319(j) rather than §61.113(i)(1); AC 68-1A §5.1.3 states that §91.319(j) "prohibits a person from operating an experimental aircraft under BasicMed carrying more than six occupants." **Verify before relying on this one:** the 2024 expansion raised the §61.113(i)(1) figure to 7, and the FAA BasicMed web page now states the 7-occupant limit generically ("any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"), but I did not have the amended §91.319(j) text in front of me. Confirm the current eCFR text of §91.319(j) before operating an experimental aircraft with 7 occupants under BasicMed.

---

## 5. Exclusions and traps

1. **Transport category helicopters.** The FAA newsroom release states the MTOW increase to 12,500 lb is "excluding transport category helicopters." For those, the 6,000 lb limit continues to apply. Do not apply 12,500 lb to a transport category rotorcraft.
2. **The limit applies to the whole flight.** Per the 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, Congress made the limitations apply to the entire flight: "Even if the pilot you are flying with holds a valid medical certificate and has the ability to operate beyond the constraints of BasicMed, you cannot act as PIC at any time during that flight if those limitations are exceeded." You cannot split a flight to get around the weight/occupant/passenger caps.
3. **State law does not change these numbers.** These are federal aircraft-eligibility limits; no state varies the 12,500 lb / 7 / 6 figures. States differ only on recognition of BasicMed for state-law purposes, which is outside this question.
4. **BasicMed vs. a medical certificate.** These limits are conditions of the BasicMed privilege. A pilot operating on a valid FAA medical certificate is not bound by them.

---

## 6. Related BasicMed operating limits (context only — not the ask)

From §61.113(i)(2) and the FAA BasicMed page, a flight under BasicMed must be conducted:

- at or below **18,000 ft MSL**;
- at an indicated airspeed **not exceeding 250 knots**;
- **within the United States**, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized;
- **not for compensation or hire** (flight instruction is permitted and the CFI may be compensated for the instruction);
- day or night, VFR or IFR;
- not during a medical deficiency (14 CFR 61.53).

---

## 7. Pre-flight verification checklist for a specific aircraft

1. Pull the aircraft's **TCDS or other design approval (TC/STC/ATC)** from the FAA website — not the POH, not the seat count.
2. Read the **maximum certificated takeoff weight**; it must be ≤ **12,500 lb** (≤ 6,000 lb if a transport category helicopter).
3. Read the **occupant capacity** in the design approval; it must be ≤ **7**.
4. Count **required flight crew** for the planned operation; planned passengers must be ≤ **6** and ≤ (7 − required crew).
5. Confirm the flight will stay within 18,000 ft MSL, 250 KIAS, US airspace, and no compensation or hire.
6. For an experimental aircraft, check the current text of 14 CFR 91.319(j) (see §4 above).

---

## 8. Sources

- FAA, *BasicMed* — https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med ("not more than 7 occupants"; "not more than 12,500 pounds"; "not more than six passengers").
- FAA Newsroom, *FAA Updates BasicMed Program*, 15 Nov 2024 — https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-updates-basicmed-program.
- FAA Notice **N 8000.386**, 11/14/24 — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Notice/N_8000.386.pdf (the two-tier table and the 12 Nov 2024 effective date).
- FAA **AC 68-1A**, 5/3/17 — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_68-1A.pdf (**superseded figures**; still useful for the definitions in §5.1.2, §5.1.3, §5.2.1).
- FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017, *The BasicMed Issue* — https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med/JulAug2017.pdf (**superseded figures**; useful for the whole-flight rule and the "certificated for more occupants than seats installed" trap).
- 14 CFR 61.113(i), 61.23(c)(3), part 68, 91.319(j); PL 114-255 §2307; PL 118-63 §828.

Travel Time – § 395.1(j)
When a driver at the direction of a motor carrier is traveling, but not driving any vehicle or assuming any other responsibility to the carrier (“cushioning”), such time shall be counted as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty when arriving at destination, in which case he/she shall be
considered off duty for the entire period.
Relief Drivers
On long-distance trips requiring straight-through driving, motorcoach companies may send a relief driver ahead.
In cases when the driver is driven or uses public transportation to get to a layover location, and the driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty after arriving, travel time may be recorded as off duty.
If the CMV driver drives him/herself in a non-CMV, time spent driving the non-CMV to a layover location must be recorded as on duty, not driving.
Exception – § 395.1(e)
A driver is exempt from the logbook or record of duty status requirements if he/she operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and is released from duty within 14 consecutive hours or less.

verdict.summary:
# Hours of service — driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach), US interstate operation

**Authority: 49 CFR § 395.5(a)** (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles), issued under 49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A. Text as currently published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16) and repeated verbatim on FMCSA's 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' page.

## Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Basis (49 CFR § 395.5(a)) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** | (a)(1): no driver shall drive 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may they drive? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | (a)(1) and (a)(2): both limits are measured 'following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours** | (a)(2): no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |

Plain-language statement for the driver: *You get 10 hours of driving inside a 15-hour on-duty window, and both clocks restart only when you take 8 consecutive hours off duty.*

## How the three numbers fit together (and the traps to avoid)

1. **Two clocks, one reset.** The 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit both run from the end of the same 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period. Eight hours off duty is the only thing that restarts both.
2. **The 15-hour clock is a window, not a driving allowance.** It counts *all* on-duty time — pre-trip inspection, fueling, loading bags, waiting at terminals, paperwork, yard moves — not just wheels-turning time. A driver who drives only 6 hours but is on duty 15 hours and 1 minute may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty.
3. **'On duty' includes other employment.** § 395.5(b) applies 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services,' and FMCSA's passenger page states: 'All compensated work for a motor carrier or a non-motor carrier is on-duty time.' A second job counts.
4. **Do not use the property-carrying numbers.** Property-carrying CMVs run 11 driving / 10 off duty / 14 on-duty window under § 395.3. The passenger numbers are 10 / 8 / 15. The regulation itself draws this line in § 395.1 (short-haul time records): '(A) A property-carrying … driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; (B) A passenger-carrying … driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty.' Mixing the two sets is the single most common error on this question.
5. **The 10 is a maximum, not a target.** 10 driving hours and 15 on-duty hours are independent ceilings; whichever is reached first stops the driver. Because 10 < 15, a driver who drives the full 10 hours will typically still have window time left, but may not exceed 10 driving.

## Additional ceilings that also stop the driver (not asked, but binding)

Under **§ 395.5(b)**, no passenger-carrying CMV driver may drive after:
- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days**, if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days**, if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.

These are cumulative on-duty totals across all carriers, and they override the daily numbers: a driver with window and driving time remaining is still barred once the 60/70-hour total is reached.

## Scope conditions and caveats (compliance notes)

- **Assumed in scope:** US interstate (or otherwise federally regulated) for-hire or private motor carrier of passengers; no emergency declaration, waiver or exception in effect; current rule as published, not a historical or pending version.
- **Sleeper berth — affects the '8 hours' answer in form, not in substance.** Per § 395.1(g)(3), a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four conditions of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are met. The requirement remains '8 hours of off-duty-equivalent rest'; only the way it is accumulated changes. If the carrier uses split sleeper-berth rest, the compliance analysis must test the four conditions, not just add the two periods.
- **Short-haul / 150 air-mile provision — does not change 10/8/15.** § 395.1(e) exempts qualifying drivers (within 150 air miles of the normal work-reporting location, released within 14 consecutive hours) from the *record-of-duty-status/logbook* requirement. It is an paperwork relief, not a relief from the driving, off-duty or on-duty limits. The 14-hour figure in that provision is a condition of eligibility for the exemption — it is **not** the on-duty driving cutoff, which remains 15.
- **Adverse driving conditions — flagged, not quantified.** § 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1', and § 395.1(b) contains an adverse-driving-conditions exception. The text of § 395.1(b) was not among the passages retrieved for this answer, so no numeric extension is stated here; a carrier relying on that exception must read § 395.1(b) in the current eCFR before doing so. The 10/8/15 figures above are the base rule.
- **Alaska is a separate regime.** The 15-hours-following-8-off-duty / 20-hours-on-duty figures that appear in § 395.1 are the **Alaska** passenger-carrying rules, not the general rule. They do not apply to operations in the 48 contiguous states or DC.
- **State variations and cross-border operations.** This answer states the federal rule only. Canada (Sleeper berth / daily limits under the provincial and federal HOS regimes) and Mexico have different limits; a driver crossing a border is subject to the more restrictive applicable regime in practice. State-level intrastate passenger rules can also differ.
- **Record-keeping is a separate obligation.** A driver subject to Part 395 must keep a record of duty status (ELD for most carriers of passengers); non-business private motor carriers of passengers are relieved of the logbook/RDS requirement but **not** of the driving limits. Exceeding 10/8/15 is a violation whether or not a log is required.

## Worked illustration (for training or audit use)

Driver reports for duty 06:00, takes 8 hours off duty from 22:00 to 06:00 the previous night (restart satisfied). Drives 06:30-10:30 (4.0 h driving). On duty at terminal 10:30-13:00. Drives 13:00-19:00 (6.0 h driving; cumulative 10.0 h — **driving cap reached at 19:00**). On-duty clock at 19:00 stands at 13.0 h, so window time remains, but the driver may not drive further. Had the driver instead taken a 3-hour break at midday, the on-duty clock would still have hit 15 hours at 21:00, ending driving at that point even with driving hours unused. Either ceiling — 10 driving or 15 on duty — ends the shift; 8 consecutive hours off duty restarts both.

## Source record

- 49 CFR § 395.5 (eCFR, current) — subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), (b)(2).
- 49 CFR § 395.1 — sleeper-berth equivalence (g)(3); short-haul (e); Alaskа and adverse-conditions provisions distinguished.
- FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (carrier-safety guidance restating § 395.5 and the on-duty-includes-all-compensated-work point).
- FMCSA Safety Planner § 6.4.3 'Passenger-Carrying Operations (395.5)' (same three limits, plus the multiple-employer on-duty note).

§ 135.267 Flight time limitations and rest requirements: Unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews.




(a) No certificate holder may assign any flight crewmember, and no flight crewmember may accept an assignment, for flight time as a member of a one- or two-pilot crew if that crewmember's total flight time in all commercial flying will exceed—




(1) 500 hours in any calendar quarter.






(2) 800 hours in any two consecutive calendar quarters.






(3) 1,400 hours in any calendar year.








(b) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, during any 24 consecutive hours the total flight time of the assigned flight when added to any other commercial flying by that flight crewmember may not exceed—




(1) 8 hours for a flight crew consisting of one pilot; or






(2) 10 hours for a flight crew consisting of two pilots qualified under this part for the operation being conducted.








(c) A flight crewmember's flight time may exceed the flight time limits of paragraph (b) of this section if the assigned flight time occurs during a regularly assigned duty period of no more than 14 hours and—




(1) If this duty period is immediately preceded by and followed by a required rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours of rest;






(2) If flight time is assigned during this period, that total flight time when added to any other commercial flying by the flight crewmember may not exceed—




(i) 8 hours for a flight crew consisting of one pilot; or






(ii) 10 hours for a flight crew consisting of two pilots; and








(3) If the combined duty and rest periods equal 24 hours.








(d) Each assignment under paragraph (b) of this section must provide for at least 10 consecutive hours of rest during the 24-hour period that precedes the planned completion time of the assignment.






(e) When a flight crewmember has exceeded the daily flight time limitations in this section, because of circumstances beyond the control of the certificate holder or flight crewmember (such as adverse weather conditions), that flight crewmember must have a rest period before being assigned or accepting an assignment for flight time of at least—




(1) 11 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by not more than 30 minutes;






(2) 12 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by more than 30 minutes, but not more than 60 minutes; and






(3) 16 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by more than 60 minutes.







(f) The certificate holder must provide each flight crewmember at least 13 rest periods of at least 24 consecutive hours each in each calendar quarter.

verdict.summary:
# Flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 14 CFR Part 135

## Answers

| # | Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|-----|--------|-----------|
| 1 | Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | Floor to which that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are *consecutive* hours of rest, and the rest must fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

## Governing text

§ 135.273(b)(2):

> "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

§ 135.273(b)(3):

> "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

## Conditions attached to the reduction to 8 hours — all four must hold

1. **The reduced rest is still consecutive.** Eight consecutive hours; not eight hours split, not eight hours minus a phone call or a deadhead report.
2. **A subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.** This is compensatory rest, given after the duty period that follows the reduced rest.
3. **That subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the *beginning* of the reduced rest period.** The clock runs from the start of the reduced rest, not from its end and not from the end of the following duty.
4. **Both rest periods occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period** — i.e., they sit in the rest windows, not inside duty.

The reduction is a *scheduling election*. The regulation says the 9-hour period "may be scheduled or reduced to 8" — the operator may build an 8-hour rest into the pairing from the outset, or may reduce it in actuality. It is not conditioned on a delay, a mechanical, weather, or any other operational event.

## Worked timeline (verification of the 24-hour trigger)

- Day 1, 07:00 — report; scheduled duty period 14 hours; release 21:00.
- Baseline (no reduction): 9 consecutive hours of rest 21:00 D1 → 06:00 D2. Earliest next report 06:00 D2.
- Reduced: 8 consecutive hours of rest 21:00 D1 → 05:00 D2. Earliest next report 05:00 D2, **provided**:
  - the compensatory rest of ≥10 consecutive hours begins no later than **21:00 D2** (24 hours after 21:00 D1, the beginning of the reduced rest), and
  - that compensatory rest occurs after completion of the D2 duty period and before the next duty period.
- Practical consequence: the D2 duty period must be complete and the flight attendant released into the 10-hour rest by 21:00 D2. Any scheduling that pushes the second release past 21:00 D2 breaks the (b)(3) condition and the 8-hour rest becomes non-compliant retroactively.

## Related prohibitions the operator must also satisfy

- **§ 135.273(b)(10):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under the section.
- **§ 135.273(b)(11):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period — this forecloses using the flight attendant for positioning, training, phone contact, or administrative tasks inside the 9- or 8-hour window.
- **§ 135.273(b)(1):** no assignment to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours, except as permitted by (b)(4)–(b)(6) (additional flight attendants) — the 9/8 rest figures above are the ones keyed to the ≤14-hour case.

## What does NOT govern this answer — common traps

1. **Flight crewmember rest rules.** § 135.267 (unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews) requires, in substance, 10 consecutive hours of rest and permits reduction to a floor of 8 or 9 hours depending on scheduled flight time. Those numbers are for *flight crewmembers*, not flight attendants. Using § 135.267(c) here would wrongly produce "10 hours, reducible to 8." The correct flight-attendant baseline is 9, not 10.
2. **The over-14-hour flight attendant pair.** § 135.273(b)(7)/(b)(8) sets an 11-hour rest reducible to 10 consecutive hours for flight attendants assigned to duty periods exceeding 14 hours (up to 16 with an additional flight attendant). That pair is inapplicable to the ≤14-hour case asked about; do not answer 11/10.
3. **"Delays beyond the control of the certificate holder."** § 135.273(b)(14) provides that a flight attendant is not considered scheduled in excess of the duty period limitations where flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limits but, due to circumstances beyond the certificate holder's control (e.g., adverse weather), were not expected at departure to reach destination within the scheduled time. That provision relieves a *duty-period-limitation* exceedance; it is not the trigger for reducing rest. The reduction authority in (b)(3) is conditioned on compensatory rest, not on delay. An operator that reduces to 8 hours on the theory that a delay justifies it, without scheduling the 10-hour compensatory rest within 24 hours, is out of compliance.
4. **The election to use flight crewmember rules.** § 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder to apply the flight crewmember flight time/duty/rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all operations, but only if it establishes written procedures applying to all flight attendants used in the operation and includes the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), with the corresponding operations specification. If the operator has made that election, the numbers in this memo are displaced by the flight crewmember scheme. Confirm the election status before applying 9/8.
5. **Contractual overlays.** A collective bargaining agreement or company manual may impose more rest than the regulation; the regulatory figure is a floor. This answer states the regulatory minimum only.

## Applicability confirmation

§ 135.273 governs duty period limitations and rest for flight attendants of certificate holders operating under Part 135. "Flight attendant" is defined in § 135.273(a) as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or otherwise required by the regulations. The question presupposes a flight attendant is assigned to the crew, so the section applies to that individual. The scheduled-vs-unscheduled distinction that matters elsewhere in subpart F (§ 135.261 allocating §§ 135.265/135.267/135.269) does not change the flight attendant rest figures — § 135.273 applies to flight attendants independent of that allocation, subject only to the § 135.273(c) election described above.

## Compliance evidence the operator should retain

- Pairing/duty sheets showing scheduled duty period length and scheduled rest, by flight attendant and date.
- Actual release and report times (the (b)(3) conditions are measured against actual times: beginning of the reduced rest, beginning of the subsequent rest).
- Where 8-hour rest is used: a record pairing each reduced rest with the specific ≥10-hour compensatory rest and demonstrating that the compensatory rest began within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest.
- Evidence that no duty was assigned during required rest ((b)(11)) — no training, positioning, or administrative assignments logged inside the rest window.
- The written procedures and operations specification amendment, if the § 135.273(c) election is in effect.
- Records retention consistent with Part 135 recordkeeping requirements (verify the current text of § 135.63 for the applicable duty/rest record provisions and retention period before finalizing the record schedule).

## Bottom line

Nine consecutive hours, reducible to eight consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest of at least ten consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest. Eight is the floor; nothing in § 135.273 authorizes less for a duty period of 14 hours or less.
