Appendix B. Changes from RFC 7540
This revision includes the following substantive changes:¶
Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes.¶
The priority scheme defined in RFC 7540 is deprecated.  Definitions for the format of the
PRIORITY frame and the priority fields in the
HEADERS frame have been retained, plus the
rules governing when PRIORITY frames can be
sent and received, but the semantics of these fields are only described in RFC 7540.  The
priority signaling scheme from RFC 7540 was not successful.  Using the simpler signaling
in [HTTP-PRIORITY] is recommended.¶
The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is deprecated and no longer specified in this document. It
was never widely deployed, with plaintext HTTP/2 users choosing to use the prior-knowledge
implementation instead.¶
Validation for field names and values has been narrowed.  The validation that is mandatory
for intermediaries is precisely defined, and error reporting for requests has been amended
to encourage sending 400-series status codes.¶

Notes:
It's unclear from the text whether PRIORITY frames affect stream states (as shown in the state machine in Section 5.1).  The original intent was that prioritization of streams was independent of the mechanics of opening and closing streams, but this was not consistently captured.
Two small additions to the document would help considerably.
In Section 5.3 (Stream Priority) add a new paragraph:
> The information that an endpoint maintains for stream priority is separate from other state. Importantly, this includes stream states (Section 5.1).  A stream in any state can have its priority changed with a PRIORITY frame. The state of a stream is not changed as a result of changing its priority.  The number of streams for which state is remembered is at the discretion of an endpoint, see Section 5.3.4 for details.
In Section 6.4 (PRIORITY) a new sentence at the end of the first paragraph:
> Sending or receiving a PRIORITY frame does not affect the state of any stream (Section 5.1), only the priority of streams is altered.

verdict.summary:
# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answers

1. **The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track, edited by M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.).
2. **RFC 9113 obsoletes two RFCs: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.**

## Evidence (primary sources)

### RFC 9113 header block

Quoted from the RFC Editor's info page and the IETF Datatracker's HTML rendering of RFC 9113:

```
Stream:  Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
RFC:     9113
Obsoletes:  7540, 8740
Category:  Standards Track
Published:  June 2022
ISSN:     2070-1721
Authors:   M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla)
           C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
```

The abstract states it explicitly: *"This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."*

Appendix B (*Changes from RFC 7540*) repeats the relationship for the TLS 1.3 content: *"Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."*

### Independent corroboration from the other direction

The RFC Editor errata search for RFC 7540 displays, on every errata record:

```
⚠ This RFC has been obsoleted!
Obsoleted by: RFC9113
Updated by:   RFC8740
```

This confirms both directions of the graph: 7540 → obsoleted by 9113, and 8740 → had *updated* 7540 (a different relation, see below).

## Documentation notes and edge cases

- **Obsoletes ≠ updates.** RFC 8740 (*Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*) *updated* RFC 7540; RFC 9113 then *obsoleted* both 7540 and 8740, folding the TLS 1.3 rules into the base specification. So 8740 belongs in the obsoletes list even though its own relationship to 7540 was an update. Do not conflate the two header fields.
- **Obsoletes ≠ obsoleted by.** RFC 9113 obsoletes 7540 and 8740. RFC 9113 is not itself obsoleted by anything in the groundling; it is the leaf of the chain 7540 → 9113.
- **Not in scope: HTTP semantics RFCs.** RFC 9113 does **not** obselete RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), or RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1). The same caution appears in RFC 7540's own abstract: *"This specification is an alternative to, but does not obselete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax."* HTTP/2 is an alternative expression of HTTP semantics, not a replacement for the semantics documents.
- **Not in scope: extensions.** RFC 7541 (HTTP/2 *Negotiation* / Upgrade Token) is a distinct document and is not named in RFC 9113's Obsoletes header. Only the two RFCs in the header count.
- **Errata do not change the obsoletes relationship.** The errata records for RFC 7540 (e.g. Errata-ID 5031 Verified, 4535 Held for Document Update, 4645/5249 Rejected) are editorial/technical corrigenda to the obsoleted text; none alters which RFC is current, and RFC 9113 carries its own errata process via its info page.
- **Meaning of "current".** "Current" here is asserted as of the source-fetch date (2026-11-16) using the RFC Editor and IETF Datatracker as the authoritative index. No successor RFC to 9113 appears in the groundling. If a later revision is published, it would appear as an `Obsoletes: 9113` entry in that new RFC's header; the answer should then be re-derived by the same procedure below, not patched by hand.
- **Status nuance.** The RFC Editor info page lists RFC 9113 as **Proposed Standard**; the document's own Status of This Memo calls it an *Internet Standards Track document*. Both are consistent — Standards Track is the stream, Proosed Standard the current maturity level. Neither affects the obsoletes answer.

## Reproducible verification procedure

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113` (or `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113`).
2. Read the header block. Confirm `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
3. Confirm the abstract sentence *"This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."*
4. Cross-check by opening the errata search for RFC 7540 (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=7540`) and confirming the banner `Obsoleted by: RFC9113`.
5. Optional negative check: confirm RFC 9113's header does **not** list 9110/9111/9112 or 7541, which would indicate scope creep beyond the two obsoleted RFCs reported here.

## One-line answer

> RFC **9113** is the current specification of HTTP/2; it obsoletes RFC **7540** (the original HTTP/2 specification, May 2015) and RFC **8740** (Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2).

These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).

quotes.whole:
Our remit from Government for this year was published on 16 March 2026. It says that two-thirds of median hourly earnings should continue to be the key reference point for future NLW rates, so here we provide indicative estimates of the increases required to achieve this for the 2027 National Living Wage uprating.
Alongside this report, we have published our consultation on minimum wage rates for 2026 and beyond. We welcome submissions from all interested parties. We are also holding regional visits across the UK and invite meetings with any and all other interested parties. If you have something to contribute, please get in touch with us via lpc@lowpay.gov.uk.

quotes.whole:
A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.
NOTES FOR EDITORS
The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.

quotes.whole:
1. The National Living Wage
Our remit from the Government asks us to do the following when recommending the National Living Wage rate for 2026:
Ensure that the rate does not drop below two-thirds of median earnings for workers in the National Living Wage population.
Take account of the cost of living, including inflation forecasts between April 2026 and April 2027.
Take account of the impact on business, competitiveness, the labour market and the wider economy.
It is our responsibility to balance these considerations. In talking to both workers and businesses over the year, it is clear that both are under pressure.
GDP growth has been mixed over the last 18 months or so, following the downturn at the end of 2023. Forecasts are for GDP growth in 2025 and 2026 (around 1.4 and 1.2 per cent respectively) to improve on what we saw in 2023 and 2024 – but remain below the norms of the 2010s and the 2000s. Productivity growth has remained sluggish. Stakeholders tell us that growth has been constrained by general economic uncertainty, restrictive monetary policy and low consumer demand, particularly in the consumer-facing services where many low-paid workers work.

The Low Pay Commission (LPC) is the independent body which advises the Government on the levels of the National Minimum Wage (NMW), including the National Living Wage (NLW). New rates of the NMW come into force on 1 April 2026, based on recommendations we made in October 2025. This report considers some of the potential impacts of these increases, looks at our remit for the year ahead and sets out our evidence-gathering plans for the rest of the year. We are keen to hear from workers and employers affected by the rates; more details can be found on page 14.

verdict.summary:
UK statutory minimum wage rates in force from 1 April 2026

HEADLINE ANSWER

| Age band | Statutory rate name | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21 and over | National Living Wage (NLW) | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 18 to 20 | National Minimum Wage (18–20 Year Old Rate) | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |

So: NLW for workers aged 21 and over = £12.71 per hour; NMW for 18–20 year olds = £10.85 per hour. Both effective 1 April 2026.

LEGAL BASIS

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357. Made 19 March 2026; coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621) (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations, for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'. The Explanatory Note confirms regulation 4A(1)(b) is 'the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21)'.
- Because the instrument was made on 19 March 2026 and commenced on 1 April 2026, these are the rates actually in force from that date, not projections or recommendations awaiting implementation.

CORROBORATION (all four agree with the instrument)

1. Low Pay Commission advice to Government on 2026 minimum wage rates, published 26 November 2025: recommends NLW (21 and over) £12.71 and 18–20 Year Old Rate £10.85 from 1 April 2026. Government accepted the recommendations at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
2. Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', published 1 April 2026: NLW (for those aged 21 and over) £12.71; 18–20 Year Old Rate £10.85; 16–17 Year Old Rate £8.00; Apprentice Rate £8.00; Accommodation Offset £11.10.
3. GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates': April 2026 row — 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; Under 18 £8; Apprentice £8.
4. GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026: same table of rates.

SCOPE AND APPLICATION NOTES (needed to apply the figures correctly)

- Geographic extent: UK-wide. The rates are set by UK secondary legislation and extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland; there is no separate national rate for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
- Effective date: the rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. 'April 2026' in the question is read as rates in force from 1 April 2026, the standard annual uprating date.
- Age determination: the worker's age on the first day of the pay reference period determines the band. A worker aged 21 or over on that date is entitled to the NLW (£12.71); a worker aged 18, 19 or 20 is entitled to the 18–20 Year Old Rate (£10.85).
- Apprentice override: the apprentice rate (£8.00 from 1 April 2026) applies instead of the age-band rate where the worker is aged under 19, or is aged 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship is therefore entitled to £8.00, not £12.71; an apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to £12.71. The figures above assume a non-apprentice worker, as the question's age-band framing implies.
- Accommodation offset: where an employer provides living accommodation, the maximum daily offset from 1 April 2026 is £11.10 (up from £10.66), which reduces the amount of pay that counts towards the minimum wage but does not change the hourly rate itself.
- Statutory vs 'Real Living Wage': these are the statutory rates enforceable under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998. They are not the voluntary Real Living Wage promoted by the Living Wage Foundation, which is set independently, is higher, and is not a legal minimum. The two are commonly confused; the values above are the statutory ones.
- Completeness for the same date (not requested, supplied for context only): 16–17 Year Old Rate £8.00; Apprentice Rate £8.00; Accommodation Offset £11.10. Rates already announced for 1 April 2027 are NLW £13.21 and 18–20 rate £11.27 — these do not apply in the 2026/27 year.

CONFIDENCE

High. The values are taken from the operative statutory instrument and independently confirmed by the Low Pay Commission's recommendation, its post-implementation report, the GOV.UK rates page and a GOV.UK press release. Arithmetic cross-checks against the published cash and percentage increases are exact (12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85). No ask is blocked.

Improves safety and flexibility 
for drivers by increasing on-

30 minutes—allowing drivers 
to reach their destination 
easier.  
 
Split-Sleeper 
Berth 
 
A driver can use the 
sleeper berth for an 8/2 split 
–8 hours of rest that does

Modifies the sleeper-

quotes.whole:
The Agency will increase safety and flexibility for the 30-minute break rule by tying the break requirement to 8 hours of driving time without an interruption for at least 30 minutes, and allowing the break to be satisfied by a driver using on duty, not driving status, rather than off duty.
The Agency will modify the sleeper-berth exception to allow drivers to split their required 10 hours off duty into two periods: an 8/2 split, and a 7/3 split—with neither period counting against the driver’s 14‑hour driving window.
The Agency will modify the adverse driving conditions exception by extending by 2 hours the maximum window during which driving is permitted.
The Agency will change the short-haul exception available to certain commercial drivers by lengthening the drivers’ maximum on‑duty period from 12 to 14 hours and extending the distance limit within which the driver may operate from 100 air miles to 150 air miles.
The new rule would not increase driving time and would continue to prevent CMV operators from driving for more than 8 consecutive hours without at least a 30-minute change in duty status.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))

1. THE TWO VALUES

Ask 1 — Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The rule states the statute-mile equivalent in the same sentence: 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. Air miles are straight-line (great-circle) distance, not highway/road miles; a route that is 180 road miles but 140 air miles from the reporting location is inside the radius.

Ask 2 — Release from work: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (quoted verbatim; eCFR current 49 CFR 395.1 and govinfo CFR-2025-title49-vol5 sec. 395-1 agree word for word)

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
(A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
(B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
(C) The time the driver is released from duty each day;
(D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

Corroborating restatements in the record: FMCSA "Summary of Hours of Service Regulations" — "the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours... must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours." FMCSA HOS Final Rule page and "Get To Know The New Rule" — the exception was lengthened "from 12 to 14 hours" and "from 100 air miles to 150 air miles."

3. SCOPE OF THE RELIEF GRANTED

Satisfying (e)(1) exempts the driver from 49 CFR 395.8 (records of duty status) and 395.11 (supporting documents). It does NOT exempt the driver from the underlying hours-of-service limits in 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 60/70-hour), from 395.5 for passenger carriers where applicable, or from 395.13 (out-of-service). The exemption is from the paperwork, not from the driving limits.

4. CONDITIONS THAT MUST ALL HOLD — radius and release time alone do not create the exemption

(a) Radius: every point of operation on the tour within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location. Ask 1.
(b) Return and release: returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours. Ask 2. Carve-out: a driver-salesperson is not required to meet the return/release condition in (e)(1)(ii), but must still meet the radius and the other conditions.
(c) Off-duty separation: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for a property-carrying CMV driver; 8 consecutive hours for a passenger-carrying CMV driver.
(d) Records: the employing motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records of (i) time the driver reports for duty each day, (ii) total hours on duty each day, (iii) time released from duty each day, and (iv) total time for the preceding 7 days per 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

If any day fails (a), (b) or (c), the driver must complete a RODS for that day (395.8) and is subject to the standard 395.3 limits, including the 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving without a 30-minute interruption.

5. HOW THE 14 CONSECUTIVE HOURS ARE COUNTED (the usual point of dispute)

Clock starts when the driver comes on duty / reports for duty at the normal work reporting location; clock stops when the carrier releases the driver from duty at that same location. It is a single continuous 14-hour span: off-duty time taken inside the span does not stop or extend the clock. Being released at hour 14:01 at the yard is a failure of the exception for that day, even if total driving was small. The measurement is from the start of the duty tour, not from the start of driving, and not from the end of the previous tour.

6. MEASUREMENT OF THE RADIUS / WHAT IS THE 'NORMAL WORK REPORTING LOCATION'

- The rule defines the point as 'the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, i.e., the normal work reporting location.' It is a fixed, carrier-designated location, not wherever the driver happens to start a given day.
- Measure straight-line air miles from that point to the furthest point actually reached during the tour (including the return leg). Do not measure by odometer.
- A driver with multiple terminals: each terminal can serve as a normal work reporting location only if the carrier designates it and the driver in fact reports to and is released from it; a driver who rotates reporting points must satisfy the 150-mile radius measured from the applicable designated location on each tour, and the carrier should document the designation. Shifting the designation day-to-day to capture a wider route is not a defense; the designation must reflect the driver's actual normal reporting point.

7. NEIGHBORING PROVISIONS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH (e)(1)

- 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMVs for which no CDL is required: also a 150 air-mile radius, but a different structure: return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour; no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7; 6-month time records. A driver using (e)(2) is expressly ineligible to use (e)(1), (g) or (o).
- 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception: requires return to and release at the normal work reporting location for the previous five duty tours, release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, and no use of the exception in the previous 6 consecutive days (unless a new 7/8-day period began with 34+ consecutive hours off duty).
- 395.1(p) — motion picture production site transportation: 100 air-mile radius; a different, narrower provision.
- Superseded thresholds: 100 air miles and 12 hours are the pre-2020 short-haul values quoted in the older fact-sheet comparison table. They are not the current answer and should not be used in a compliance document.

8. SCOPE NOTE

This answer states the federal interstate rule (49 CFR Part 395). A state intrastate analog may set different radius or duty-period thresholds, and a driver operating intrastate under state rules should be checked against that state's adoption. The request asks for the federal short-haul thresholds, which are the values given above.

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

quotes.whole:
BasicMed is an alternative to the FAA’s medical certification requirements for noncommercial flyers who have previously held an airman medical certificate. The FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 set the stage and required the FAA to adopt regulations implementing BasicMed. Since then, several key changes have been made: allowing pilots to act as safety pilots without being pilot in command, expanding the allowed maximum certificated takeoff weight, increasing the number of allowed occupants, and allowing pilot examiners to use BasicMed, among others.
In its current form, BasicMed has several eligibility requirements for airmen. First, the airman must possess a valid U.S. driver’s license and comply with all associated medical requirements or restrictions. Second, the pilot must have held an airman medical certificate that was valid at any point after July 14, 2006. Paragraph 4.3 of Advisory Circular AC 68-1A provides guidance to help determine if a medical was valid after that date. Importantly, this medical may be expired and may have been a special issuance medical certificate.

There are also some eligibility requirements for the aircraft, which were recently increased in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024. The aircraft cannot have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of more than 12,500 pounds. Additionally, the aircraft cannot be certified to carry more than seven occupants. Finally, there are operational limitations to adhere to. There can be no more than six passengers on board. The entirety of the flight must be at or below 18,000 feet msl. verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT FEDERAL RULE (effective 12 November 2024)

Governing authority: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended to implement Section 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Public Law 118-63. The FAA's implementing guidance is Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24) and the BasicMed pages at faa.gov; AC 68-1A (5/3/17) remains the structural advisory circular but its numeric limits are superseded.

=== THE THREE LIMITS ===

1) MAXIMUM CERTIFICATED TAKEOFF WEIGHT: 12,500 pounds.
   The aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) of not more than 12,500 lb. (Was 6,000 lb before 12 Nov 2024.)
   Caveat: the FAA's 15 Nov 2024 announcement states the increase to 12,500 lb applies "excluding transport category helicopters" — i.e., transport-category helicopters remain subject to the 6,000 lb ceiling. For every other aircraft category the figure is 12,500 lb.

2) OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY: 7 occupants.
   The aircraft must be "authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants." (Was 6 before 12 Nov 2024.)
   "Authorized to carry" is a design-approval quantity, not a seat count: it is set by the aircraft's type certificate (TC), supplemental type certificate (STC) or amended TC (ATC), as read from the Type Certificate Data Sheet. An aircraft certificated for more than 7 occupants does not qualify even if fewer seats are installed (the classic example being certain Piper PA-32/PA-34 variants under the old 6-occupant rule). Conversely, an aircraft altered by STC/ATC to a certificated capacity of 7 or fewer does qualify.

3) PASSENGERS ON BOARD: 6 passengers.
   The flight must be conducted carrying not more than 6 passengers. (Was 5 before 12 Nov 2024.)

=== WHY 7 OCCUPANTS AND 6 PASSENGERS ARE DIFFERENT NUMBERS ===
"Occupants" includes the pilot in command and any other required flightcrew member; "passengers" excludes them. The two limits therefore interact as follows (arithmetic checked against both limits):
 - Aircraft type certificated for one required pilot: 1 pilot + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants. Both limits satisfied exactly.
 - Aircraft type certificated for two required flightcrew: 2 crew + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants. Occupant limit satisfied exactly; passenger count (5) is within the 6 limit. Note that 2 crew + 6 passengers = 8 occupants would breach the 7-occupant limit, so 6 passengers is NOT available in a two-crew aircraft.
 - In every case the binding passenger figure is 6, and the aircraft's certificated occupant capacity is 7.

=== SCOPE / CHARACTER OF THE LIMITS ===
These are operational limits on the pilot exercising BasicMed privileges, not limits on the aircraft's own certification or airworthiness. The same aircraft flown by a pilot using an FAA medical certificate is not subject to them.

Experimental (amateur-built/experimental) aircraft: occupant carriage is separately addressed by 14 CFR 91.319(j), which cross-references the BasicMed occupant limit; read the current codified text of 91.319(j) rather than the 2017 AC, whose "six occupants" phrasing predates the 2024 amendment.

=== ADJACENT BASICMED OPERATING LIMITS (context, not part of the three answers) ===
Entire flight within the United States (or another country that authorizes BasicMed); at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; not operated for compensation or hire. Limitations apply to the whole flight from takeoff to touchdown — a BasicMed pilot may not act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot on board holds a medical certificate and acts as PIC for the rest of the flight.

=== EFFECTIVE-DATE WARNING (the usual source of error) ===
Any source dated before 12 November 2024 — including AC 68-1A, the FAA Safety Briefing July/August 2017 article, and older third-party summaries — will state 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers. Those figures are superseded. Use 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers for any flight conducted on or after 12 November 2024.

=== HOW TO VERIFY ===
Check the current text of 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) on eCFR (paragraph (i)(1) for the aircraft/occupancy limits, (i)(2) for the altitude/airspeed/geographic limits, (i)(3) for logbook carriage), cross-check the FAA BasicMed page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med, "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements" bullets), and for a specific airframe read the occupant capacity and MTOW from its Type Certificate Data Sheet.

=== ONE-LINE ANSWER ===
Under BasicMed (on or after 12 November 2024) a pilot may fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 lb, authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, with not more than 6 passengers on board (transport category helicopters remain limited to 6,000 lb).

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

Travel Time – § 395.1(j)
When a driver at the direction of a motor carrier is traveling, but not driving any vehicle or assuming any other responsibility to the carrier (“cushioning”), such time shall be counted as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty when arriving at destination, in which case he/she shall be
considered off duty for the entire period.
Relief Drivers
On long-distance trips requiring straight-through driving, motorcoach companies may send a relief driver ahead.
In cases when the driver is driven or uses public transportation to get to a layover location, and the driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty after arriving, travel time may be recorded as off duty.
If the CMV driver drives him/herself in a non-CMV, time spent driving the non-CMV to a layover location must be recorded as on duty, not driving.

quotes.whole:
are allowed to drive by placing specific limits on the amount of time
you drive your commercial motor vehicle and how many total hours

follow three maximum duty limits at all times. They are the 15-hour
on-duty limit, 10-hour driving limit, and 60/70-hour duty limit.
15-Hour On-Duty Limit
The first limit is the 15-hour on-duty limit. Following 8 consecu-
tive hours off duty, you must not drive a commercial motor vehicle
after being on duty 15 hours. You may do other work after being on
duty 15 hours, but you may not drive.
Off-duty time taken during the day, such as a lunch break or nap,
does not count toward this 15-hour limit. Also, if  you have a sleeper berth in your vehicle, you
may be able to use it to get the required rest and to extend the 15-hour limit. Sleeper berth provi-
sions will be discussed later in this section.
Example: You have had 8 continuous hours off and you come to work at 6:00 a.m. You work
for 7 hours, take one hour off for lunch, and work another 8 hours until 10:00 p.m., for a total of
15 on-duty hours. You must not drive a commercial motor vehicle after 10:00 p.m. that evening.

verdict.summary:
HOURS OF SERVICE — DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (MOTORCOACH), UNITED STATES

GOVERNING AUTHORITY
49 CFR 395.5 (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles), made subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1. This is the passenger-carrying rule set; it is NOT the property-carrying rule set in 49 CFR 395.3 (which is 11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off duty / 14-hour window and must not be substituted). Assumes interstate operation, no waiver or exemption in force, and a driver required to keep a record of duty status.

THE THREE ANSWERS

1. Maximum driving time — 10 HOURS.
   Sec. 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV "more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."
   The 10 hours is accumulated driving time within the duty period, not necessarily consecutive; it may be taken in one block or split into many blocks.

2. Consecutive hours off duty required before a new driving period — 8 CONSECUTIVE HOURS.
   Same provision. The 8 hours may be off-duty time, sleeper-berth time, or any combination of the two, but there must be no on-duty time and no driving time at any point inside those 8 hours. Only a full 8-consecutive-hour break restarts both the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock.

3. On-duty hours after which driving is no longer permitted — 15 HOURS ON DUTY.
   Sec. 395.5(a)(2): no driving "for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."
   This is a driving cutoff, not a work cutoff. After the 15th on-duty hour the driver may continue non-driving work, but may not drive again until another 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.

HOW THE 15-HOUR LIMIT IS MEASURED (passenger rule — differs from property rule)
The passenger rule is written as "having been on duty 15 hours," i.e. 15 accumulated hours of on-duty time (driving time plus on-duty-not-driving time) counted from the end of the last 8-consecutive-hour break. Off-duty time taken during the day (meal break, nap) does NOT count toward the 15 hours. FMCSA's own worked example in the Interstate Passenger-Carrying Driver's Guide: on duty at 06:00, work 7 hours, 1 hour off for lunch, work 8 more hours until 22:00 = 15 on-duty hours; the driver must not drive after 22:00 but may do other work. Do not describe this using the property-carrier 14-hour "elapsed window" semantics, where an off-duty break does not pause the clock — the passenger provision is drafted and administered as an on-duty accumulation.

ADDITIONAL CAPS THAT CAN BIND EARLIER (weekly limits — 49 CFR 395.5(b))
A driver may not drive after having been on duty:
  - 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days, if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
  - 70 hours in any 8 consecutive days, if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
These are on-duty (not driving-only) totals and include work for any other motor carrier or non-motor-carrier employer. The 10-hour daily driving maximum is therefore an upper bound per duty period, not an entitlement on every duty day: the 60/70-hour cap can stop driving sooner. There is NO 34-hour restart in the passenger rule set — the 34-hour restart lives in 49 CFR 395.3(c), which applies to property-carrying CMVs. A passenger driver gets back under 60/70 by letting on-duty hours age out of the rolling 7- or 8-day window.

DEFINITIONS THAT DRIVE THE COUNT (49 CFR 395.2)
- Driving time: time spent at the controls of a CMV in operation.
- On-duty time: all time from coming on duty until going off duty, including driving, waiting to be dispatched, inspecting/ servicing the vehicle, loading/unloading, remaining in readiness to operate, and all compensated work for a motor carrier or non-motor-carrier employer.
- Off-duty time: not separately defined; in effect any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper-berth time. FMCSA guidance: a meal or routine stop counts as off duty only if the driver is relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight being carried.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (how to apply the three numbers to a duty day)
Step 1 — Start the clocks. At the end of 8 consecutive hours off duty (off duty, sleeper berth, or combination, with no work inside the 8), the driver comes on duty. Two clocks start: DRIVE (10 h) and ON-DUTY (15 h).
Step 2 — Add every on-duty minute (driving + on-duty not driving) to the ON-DUTY clock. Do not add off-duty breaks to it.
Step 3 — Add driving minutes only to the DRIVE clock.
Step 4 — Stop driving when EITHER clock is exhausted: DRIVE reaches 10:00, or ON-DUTY reaches 15:00. Whichever happens first controls.
Step 5 — Also track the rolling 60-in-7 or 70-in-8 on-duty total; stop driving when that total is reached even if both daily clocks have room.
Step 6 — Restart only with 8 consecutive hours off duty (or a qualifying equivalent under Step 7). Nothing else resets the clocks; a short break does not.

WORKED EXAMPLE
Off duty 22:00–06:00 (8 consecutive hours) -> clocks start 06:00.
06:00–11:00 drive (5:00 drive / 5:00 on duty)
11:00–11:30 on-duty not driving, pre-trip/inspection (5:00 / 5:30)
11:30–12:00 off duty, lunch (5:00 / 5:30 — off duty does not advance the 15-hour clock)
12:00–17:00 drive (10:00 / 10:30)
Result: DRIVE clock exhausted at 10:00 -> no further driving, even though only 10:30 of the 15 on-duty hours are used. The driver may perform non-driving work until the ON-DUTY clock reaches 15:00, and may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty.

EXCEPTIONS AND HOW THEY INTERACT (49 CFR 395.1) — none changes the three numbers unless it is actually invoked
- 150 air-mile short-haul (395.1(e)): a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours or less is exempt from the record-of-duty-status (logbook/ELD) requirement. This is a paperwork exemption only; it does not raise the 10-hour driving limit or the 15-hour on-duty cutoff. Do not treat it as a change to the three answers.
- Passenger sleeper berth (395.1(g)(3)): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two qualifying sleeper-berth periods. Where this is relied on, the split-rest conditions in 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) must all be met and the current eCFR text should be read before use; absent a qualifying split, the plain 8-consecutive-hour rule applies.
- Adverse driving conditions: relief under 395.1(b) extends the time needed to complete the run; it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving maximum. After an adverse-conditions run, a passenger-carrying driver must be off duty at least 8 consecutive hours before driving again.
- Travel/cushioning time (395.1(j)) and relief drivers: travel to a layover counts as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case it may be recorded as off duty. Time driving oneself in a non-CMV to a layover is on duty, not driving.
- Multiple-employer drivers (395.8(j)): all compensated work for any employer is on-duty time; obtain the signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty before using the driver.

COMMON MISAPPLICATIONS TO AVOID
- Using 11 / 10 / 14 (property-carrying, 395.3) instead of 10 / 8 / 15 (passenger-carrying, 395.5). This is the single most likely error.
- Confusing the 8-consecutive-hour reset with the 34-hour restart. The 34-hour restart does not exist for passenger-carrying drivers; weekly limits are satisfied by hours aging out of the rolling window.
- Treating the 15-hour limit as a limit on all work. It is a limit on driving only; non-driving work may continue.
- Counting off-duty breaks toward the 15-hour on-duty total, or assuming a mid-day break extends the 15 hours (it does not — it simply is not counted as on-duty time).
- Assuming the 10 driving hours are available every day regardless of the 60/70-hour weekly total.

VERIFICATION SOURCES
49 CFR 395.5 (eCFR and Cornell LII text, both quoted identically above); 49 CFR 395.1 (exceptions, incl. (e), (g)(3), (j)); 49 CFR 395.2 (definitions); FMCSA brochure FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022, "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers"; FMCSA "Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service."

SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
Applies to US interstate operations under FMCSA rules for passenger-carrying CMVs. Intrastate drivers may be subject to a state rule set that differs (some states adopt the federal passenger rules, some do not); a specific state's requirements are outside this answer. School bus, transit, and other statutory exemptions under 395.1 were not evaluated and could change the applicable limits if one applies.

quotes.whole:
§ 135.265 Flight time limitations and rest requirements: Scheduled operations.




(a) No certificate holder may schedule any flight crewmember, and no flight crewmember may accept an assignment, for flight time in scheduled operations or in other commercial flying if that crewmember's total flight time in all commercial flying will exceed—




(1) 1,200 hours in any calendar year.






(2) 120 hours in any calendar month.






(3) 34 hours in any 7 consecutive days.






(4) 8 hours during any 24 consecutive hours for a flight crew consisting of one pilot.






(5) 8 hours between required rest periods for a flight crew consisting of two pilots qualified under this part for the operation being conducted.








(b) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, no certificate holder may schedule a flight crewmember, and no flight crewmember may accept an assignment, for flight time during the 24 consecutive hours preceding the scheduled completion of any flight segment without a scheduled rest period during that 24 hours of at least the following:




(1) 9 consecutive hours of rest for less than 8 hours of scheduled flight time.






(2) 10 consecutive hours of rest for 8 or more but less than 9 hours of scheduled flight time.






(3) 11 consecutive hours of rest for 9 or more hours of scheduled flight time.








(c) A certificate holder may schedule a flight crewmember for less than the rest required in paragraph (b) of this section or may reduce a scheduled rest under the following conditions:




(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest period.






(2) A rest required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 11 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest period.






(3) A rest required under paragraph (b)(3) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 9 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 12 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest period.







(d) Each certificate holder shall relieve each flight crewmember engaged in scheduled air transportation from all further duty for at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive days.

verdict.summary:
PART 135 FLIGHT ATTENDANT REST AFTER A SCHEDULED DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS

1. CONTROLLING RULE
§135.273 (Duty period limitations and rest requirements: flight attendants). Applicability is set by §135.261(e): 'Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part.' It therefore applies to an on-demand charter operator under §135.267 just as it applies to a §135.265 scheduled operator. The §135.265(b) rest table (9/10/11 consecutive hours keyed to scheduled FLIGHT TIME) is a flight CREWMEMBER table and does not govern a flight attendant unless the operator makes the §135.273(c) election described in item 6.

2. ASK 1 — REST AFTER A SCHEDULED DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS
Value: 9 consecutive hours, scheduled.
Basis: §135.273(b)(2) — 'a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'
The 14-hour figure is the band ceiling in §135.273(b)(1) ('no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours', except the extended-duty paragraphs (b)(4)-(b)(6)). A duty period of exactly 14 hours sits inside the band, so 9 hours is the base rest.

3. ASK 2 — TO WHAT IT MAY BE REDUCED
Value: 8 consecutive hours (the floor; no lower figure exists in the rule).
Conditions, all of which must hold (§135.273(b)(3)):
  (a) the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours;
  (b) that subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the BEGINNING of the reduced rest period (the 24-hour clock runs from the start of the reduced rest, not its end);
  (c) that subsequent rest period occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
Supporting prohibitions: §135.273(b)(10) — no duty period may be assigned unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section; §135.273(b)(11) — no duty may be assigned during any required rest period.

4. VALLEY TABLE (every figure cross-checked)
| Item | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Base scheduled rest, duty ≤14 h | 9 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(2) |
| Floor to which that rest may be reducible | 8 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Compensatory subsequent rest required if reducible to 8 | at least 10 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Deadline for compesatory rest to begin | no later than 24 h after beginning of reduced rest | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Base scheduled duty period ceiling | 14 h | §135.273(b)(1) |
Checks: 9 > 8 (a reduction, not an increase); 8 meets but does not breach the 8-hour floor; 10 meets but does not breach the 10-hour compesatory minimum; 24 h is a deadline measured from the beginning of the reduced rest.

5. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE FOR THE OPERATOR
Step 1 — Determine the SCHEDULED duty period (the published/assigned schedule), not the actual duty period. The band and the rest trigger are keyed to the scheduled figure. If the scheduled duty period exceeds 14 h, paragraphs (b)(4)-(b)(6) and the 12-hour rest of (b)(7) apply instead, and this answer does not cover it.
Step 2 — If the scheduled duty period is 14 h or less, build the pairing with at least 9 consecutive hours of rest between completion of that duty period and commencement of the next one.
Step 3 — If 8 hours is used, the schedule must show, in the same pairing or the immediately adjacent one, a compesatory rest block of at least 10 consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest began and falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.
Step 4 — Before publishing, chek that no duty is assinged during either rest period (§135.273(b)(10), (b)(11)).
Step 5 — Record the reduced rest and the compesatory rest in the crew scheduling system so the 24-hour deadline can be audited; the deadline is a hard scheduling constraint, not a crew-room discretion.

6. WORK ED EXAMPLE (arithmetic chek)
Scheduled duty period ends 21:00 Day 1. Reduced rest begins 22:00 Day 1 and runs 8 hours to 06:00 Day 2 (8 h = the floor, not fewer). The compesatory rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must be scheduled to begin no later than 22:00 Day 2 (22:00 Day 1 + 24 h = 22:00 Day 2) and must sit between the completion of the Day 1 duty period and the commencement of the next duty period. A 10-hour block beginning 22:00 Day 2 satisfies (a) 10 ≥ 10 and (b) start exactly at the 24-hour deadline, not past it. A 10-hour block beginning 23:00 Day 2 would breach the deadline even though it is long enough.

7. TRAPS / COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Applying §135.265(b)'s 9/10/11-hour table (keyed to scheduled flight time) to a flight attendant. Wrong section; the flight attendant table is keyed to scheduled DUTY period.
- Reducing to 8 h without the at-least-10-hour compesatory rest, or without the 24-hour deadline. Both are conditions of the reduction, not suggestions.
- Measuring the 24 hours from the end of the reduced rest rather than its beginning. That overstates the available window by the length of the reduced rest.
- Treating 14 h as the actual duty period. The trigger is the scheduled duty period; a late-running flight that pushes actual duty past 14 h does not by itself move the crew into paragraph (b)(7), but it must be tracked against the schedule.
- Assuming any discretion below 8 h, or a 'ad hoc' reduction for unforeseen circumstances. The rule contains no such provision for flight attendants; 8 h is the absolute floor.
- Confusing §135.273(b)(9) (the 14-hour cap that follows a 10-hour reduction under (b)(8), which belongs to the over-14-hour band) with the 8-hour reduction in (b)(3). (b)(9) does not attach to a ≤14-hour duty period.

8. ELECTION CAVEAT (§135.273(c)) — VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME
An operator may apply the flight crewmember flight time/duty/rest rules of Part 135 to its flight attendants if it establishes written procedures that apply to all its flight attendants, include the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant per excess flight crewmember, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its ops specs. If — and only if — this operator holds that election, the applicable rest becomes §135.265(b)'s table keyed to scheduled flight time (9 h for less than 8 h scheduled flight time; 10 h for 8 to less than 9 h; 11 h for 9 h or more), reducible under §135.265(c) to 8/8/9 h with compesatory rests of 10/11/12 h beginning no later than 24 h after the beginning of the reduced rest. Absent that election, the answer stated in items 2 and 3 governs. Chek the ops specs and the approved procedures before applying either table; do not blend them.

9. SCOPE NOTES
This is the regulatory minimum. A collective bargaining agreement or company policy may be more restrictive and would control as a matter of employment/contract, but it does not change the Part 135 floor. The answer covers a flight attendant serving as cabin crew only; a crewmember who also serves as a flight crewmember is governed by the flight crewmember rest rules for that function, and augmented-crew, deadhead transportation and rest-facility questions are outside this ask.

verdict.summary:
## Answers

**1. Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113** — "HTTP/2", Standards Track, published June 2022, editors M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.), ISSN 2070-1721.

**2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740** — exactly two documents.

- **RFC 7540** — "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", the original HTTP/2 specification (May 2015).
- **RFC 8740** — "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", Proposed Standard (D. Benjamin, February 2020), which had itself updated RFC 7540 by forbidding TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication. RFC 9113 folds that rule in and obsoletes the standalone document.

## Evidence (verbatim from the fetched pages)

RFC 9113 header block (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html):

```
RFC:            9113
Obsoletes:      7540, 8740
Category:       Standards Track
Published:      June 2022
ISSN:           2070-1721
Authors:        M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla)
                C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
```

Abstract, final sentence: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Appendix B (Changes from RFC 7540): "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

Corroboration from the RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject index: RFC 8740 is listed with "Obsoleted by RFC 9113", and RFC 7540 is listed with "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". The pre-publication draft (draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-04) carried the header "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 (if approved)", which the published RFC 9113 confirms by dropping the conditional.

## Precision notes a downstream user should carry forward

1. **"Obsoletes" is not "updates".** The obsoletes relationship is a full replacement of the listed documents. An *updates* relationship is a targeted amendment and is a different header field. The fetched RFC 9113 header excerpt shows an `Obsoletes:` line and no `Updates:` line, so this answer asserts no updates relationship. (It is widely repeated that RFC 9113 also updates RFC 9110 and RFC 9111; that claim is not visible in the grounding available here, is not part of either ask, and is therefore deliberately excluded rather than stated as fact.)

2. **RFC 9113 does not obsolete the rest of the HTTP/2 document family.** Still current alongside it, per the subject index: RFC 7541 (HPACK header compression), RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame). These are companion specifications, not superseded ones. Do not list them in answer 2.

3. **RFC 7540's own obsoletes list is irrelevant to this question.** Ask 2 asks what RFC 9113 obsoletes, not what RFC 7540 obsoleted. The chain is one hop: RFC 9113 → {RFC 7540, RFC 8740}.

4. **RFC 7541 is unaffected.** HPACK survives the 7540→9113 transition unchanged; only RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 were retired.

## Verification procedure (reproducible)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html and read the document header.
2. Confirm the `RFC:` field reads 9113 and the title is "HTTP/2" with Category "Standards Track".
3. Read the `Obsoletes:` field verbatim — this, not the abstract prose, is the normative obsoletion list.
4. Cross-check the abstract sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." against the header; both must agree, and they do.
5. Optionally confirm from the reverse direction at https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/ that RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 each show "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".

## Staleness condition

This answer is valid as of the retrieval date (2026-11-16) and remains valid until a successor document with `Obsoletes: 9113` is published. Re-run the verification procedure if the RFC Editor index shows a later HTTP/2 specification.

quotes.whole:
The 16-17 Year Old Rate and the Apprentice Rate will increase by 6 per cent to £8.00 in April. These increases ensure that pay for these workers does not become too detached from the rates for older workers.
As a result of these increases we expect youth coverage to rise. However, the impacts on effective coverage (the number of jobs paid below the NLW) are more uncertain.
Our remit for 2026
Our 2026 remit asks us to recommend an NLW that takes into account the condition of the labour market, the cost of living, the impact on businesses and competitiveness, and wider macroeconomic conditions. The remit also states that two-thirds of median hourly earnings should continue to be “the key reference point for future rates”. We project that two-thirds of median earnings for those aged 21 and over in October 2027 will fall somewhere in the range of £13.02 to £13.34, with a central estimate of £13.18.
Our remit for 2026 restates the Government’s commitment to lower the NLW age to 18 but gives the Commission “full flexibility to determine the pace and ultimate timing of that alignment, with priority being given to the employment prospects of younger workers.”

The Secretary of State makes these Regulations in exercise of the powers conferred by sections 1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 (“the 1998 Act”)(1).

A draft of these Regulations was laid before Parliament in accordance with section 51(5) of the 1998 Act and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.



Citation, commencement and extent

1.—(1) These Regulations may be cited as the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026.

(2) These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.

(3) These Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Amendments to the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015

2.—(1) The National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015(2) are amended as follows.

(2) In regulation 4 (the national living wage) for “£12.21” substitute “£12.71”.

(3) In regulation 4A(1) (workers who qualify for the national minimum wage at a different rate)—

(a)in sub-paragraph (b) for “£10.00” substitute “£10.85”;

(b)in sub-paragraph (c) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”;

(c)in sub-paragraph (d) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”.

(4) In regulation 16(1) (amount for provision of living accommodation) for “£10.66” substitute “£11.10”.




Name

Title

Explanatory Note

(This note is not part of the Regulations)
 
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
  
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(4) increases the accommodation offset amount which is applicable where any employer provides a worker with living accommodation from £10.66 to £11.10 for each day that accommodation is provided (regulation 16(1) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
A full regulatory impact assessment of the effect that this instrument will have on the costs of business and the voluntary sector is available from the Employment Rights Directorate, Department for Business and Trade, Old Admiralty Building, London SW1A 2AY and is annexed to the Explanatory Memorandum which is available alongside the instrument on www.legislation.gov.uk.

By law, the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage are the minimum hourly rates you must pay your workers, regardless of how many people you employ.

verdict.summary:
UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026 — HR/Payroll answer

1. HEADLINE ANSWER

| Ask | Band | Gross hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Change on prior year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over) | £12.71 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) from £12.21 |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) from £10.00 |

Both figures are the statutory rates legislated for the 2026 uprating — not forecasts, projections or voluntary-benchmark figures.

2. LEGAL BASIS (why these are facts, not projections)

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI 2026 No. 357), coming into force 1 April 2026, amend the 2015 Regulations:
  - reg. 2(2): in regulation 4 (the national living wage) for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
  - reg. 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21) for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'.
- Explanatory Note to the same SI: 'increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour' and 'increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour'.
- Low Pay Commission advice to Government, published 26 November 2025: recommends £12.71 (21+) and £10.85 (18–20) to apply from 1 April 2026. Government accepted the recommendations at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; rates came into force 1 April 2026 (LPC press release, 1 April 2026).
- GOV.UK 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' page, April 2026 row: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85.

All five sources agree; there is no conflict to resolve.

3. EFFECTIVE DATE AND PAYROLL APPLICATION

- The rates apply from 1 April 2026 and replace the April 2025–March 2026 rates (£12.21 and £10.00).
- Employer rule (GOV.UK employer bulletin, April 2026): use the new rates from the first pay period starting on or after 1 April 2026. A pay period that straddles 1 April (e.g. a 26 March–8 April fortnightly payroll) is not split — the old rate applies to that whole period and the new rate from the next one. Check the pay reference period definition in the 2015 Regulations before splitting any period manually.
- The rates extend to England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (SI reg. 1(3)) — there is no regional variation in the statutory rate.

4. SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS (HR traps)

- 'National Living Wage' here means the STATUTORY rate in the 2015 Regulations. It is not the Living Wage Foundation's voluntary 'Real Living Wage', which is set on a different cycle, is higher, and has a separate London figure. If a contract, tender or accreditation refers to 'the Living Wage', establish which one is meant before quoting £12.71.
- The NLW has covered workers aged 21 and over only since April 2024 (23+ from April 2021; 25+ before that). Historic payslips and backpay calculations must use the threshold in force for the period concerned, not today's.
- The 18–20 band is a National Minimum Wage rate, not an NLW rate — it applies to workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21.
- Rates are gross per hour, before tax, NI and pension deductions. They are not adjusted for region, seniority or length of service.
- Age is the determining factor, not job title, grade or apprentice status alone. Where a worker's age changes mid-employment, the higher rate takes effect from the start of the next pay reference period after the birthday under the 2015 Regulations — do not switch mid-period without checking the pay reference period rules.

5. CONTEXT BANDS (not asked for, but needed for a coherent pay structure)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 |
| Accomodation offset (per day) | £11.10 |

Apprentice rule: the apprentice rate applies if the apprentice is under 19, or is 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to £12.71.

6. HR COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST FOR THE APRIL 2026 UPRAATING

1. Re-band every worker by date of birth as at the pay period start; flag anyone turning 18 or 21 in the next 12 months.
2. Update payroll rates, and check salaried staff on 'salaried hours' calculations — a salary that looked compliant at £12.21 can fall below £12.71 once hours are modelled.
3. Re-check deductions: uniform, tools, training costs, salary sacrifice and over-deducted accommodation can all pull effective pay below the minimum. Accommodation offset is capped at £11.10 per day from 1 April 2026.
4. Confirm unpaid working time (opening/closing, handovers, travel between assignments) is counted in working time.
5. Update agency, umbrella and zero-hours worker rates and any contract or tender that references 'the National Living Wage' by name rather than by figure.
6. Record the uprating decision and the source used — inspectors and tribunals ask for the basis of the rate applied.

7. FORWARD LOOK (planning only, not the answer)

GOV.UK already lists April 2027 rates: £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (16–17 and apprentice). The LPC's 2026 remit restates the Government commitment to lower the NLW age to 18, with the Commission given flexibility over pace and timing. HR should plan for the 18–20 band eventually being absorbed into the NLW, and should not build long-term pay structures that depend on the youth differential persisting.

8. SOURCES

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI 2026 No. 357), legislation.gov.uk.
- LPC, 'National Minimum Wage in 2026' report, published 26 November 2025, gov.uk.
- LPC advice to Government on 2026 minimum wage rates, published 26 November 2025, gov.uk.
- GOU.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates'.
- GOU.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', 1 April 2026.
- GOU.UK Employer Bulletin, April 2026.

9. LIMITATIONS

- Figures verified against the sources above as at the research date. Rates are annual and can be amended; confirm against gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates before applying to a live payroll or quoting in a contract.
- This note covers the statutory headline rates and the interactions named above. It does not constitute legal advice on a specific underpayment, which should be taken from ACAS or a qualified adviser.

quotes.whole:
What has changed?
Short-haul Exception
Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception.
Adverse Driving Conditions Exception
Expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours.
30-Minute Break Requirement
Requires break of at least 30 consecutive minutes after 8 cumulative hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break.
Sleeper Berth Provision
Modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7 hours of that period in the berth combined with a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours. When used together as specified, neither qualify period counts against the 14-hour driving window.
Educational Tool for Hours of Service (ETHOS)
FMCSA launched a new online tool that allows users to enter driver records of duty status to see if there are potential violations with the new hours of service regulations.

verdict.summary:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — REGULATORY LIMITS

ANSWERS
1. Radius: 150 air miles from the driver's normal work reporting location. (The rule states this as '150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles).' The regulatory unit of measure is air miles, i.e., straight-line distance, not road/statute miles; the 172.6 figure is the rule's own parenthetical conversion of the 150 air miles, not a separate 172.6-mile limit.)
2. Release from work: within 14 consecutive hours — the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

CONTROLLING TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR / 2025 CFR compilation)
'(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
 (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
 (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
 (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
 (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.'

HOW THE TWO LIMITS OPERATE
- Both are conditions precedent. The exception from preparing a record of duty status (395.8) and from the ELD requirement (395.11) applies only if the driver satisfies the radius condition AND the 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release condition AND the off-duty separation AND the carrier's time-record condition. Failing any one forfeits the exception.
- The radius is measured as air (straight-line) miles from the normal work reporting location — the fixed location where the driver reports to and is released from work. Every point the driver operates to must lie within that 150-air-mile circle; the return leg does not get separate treatment.
- The 14-hour clock runs from the beginning of the work/duty period, not from the first driving hour. On-duty-not-driving time and any break time count against the 14 consecutive hours. There is no adverse-driving or other extension available inside this exception; the adverse driving conditions provision in 395.1(b) extends the driving window under 395.3, not the 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release test of (e)(1)(ii).
- The driver must physically return to the work reporting location and be released there within the 14 hours; merely ceasing driving within 14 hours is not sufficient.
- The driver-salesperson is carved out of the (ii) return-and-release condition by the text ('except a driver-salesperson').

CONSEQUENCE OF EXCEEDING EITHER LIMIT
If on a given day the driver exceeds the 150-air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception does not apply for that day and the driver must prepare a record of duty status for that day (paper log if required to keep RODS 8 or fewer days in the last 30; ELD if more than 8 days), per 395.8 and FMCSA ELD FAQ 17. The carrier's obligation to keep accurate time records (time in, total hours on duty, time released, plus the preceding-7-day total for new/intermittent drivers) for 6 months continues independently.

VARIANTS — NOT THE ANSWER TO THESE TWO ASKS, LISTED TO PREVENT MISAPPLICATION
- 395.1(e)(2) (property-carrying CMV driver not required to hold a CDL): also a 150 air-mile radius and a return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, but the time test is expressed as no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour on 2 of those days — not a single 'released within 14 consecutive hours' test. If the operation is non-CDL, this paragraph, not (e)(1)(ii), governs the hours condition.
- 395.1(o) 16-hour exception: a 16-hour return-and-release test with a 5-prior-duty-tour and 6-day-frequency precondition; separate from the short-haul exception and not a substitute for the 14-hour limit.
- 395.1(p) motion picture production: 100 air-mile radius; unrelated to short-haul.
- State or company rules may impose stricter limits; the federal figures above are ceilings, not entitlements.

CITATIONS
- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) and (ii), (iii), (iv) — eCFR and 2025 CFR compilation (govinfo, CFR-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1).
- FMCSA, Hours of Service regulations page (short-haul exception: 150 air miles, 14-hour duty period).
- FMCSA ELD FAQ 17 (drivers using short-haul/timecard exception not required to keep RODS or use ELDs).
- FMCSA HOS Q&A webinar materials (150 air-mile radius, start/end at same reporting location, maximum duty period 14 hours; loss of exception triggers a log/ELD for that day).

WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.

Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.
Pilots must meet specific conditions to operate under BasicMed. Among other things, they must have held a valid medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006; the most recent medical certificate cannot have been denied, revoked, or suspended; they must complete a medical exam by a state-licensed physician; they must complete an online medical education course; and they must hold a valid U.S. driver’s license.

Whether operating under BasicMed as a required pilot flightcrew member or PIC, pilots must meet the same BasicMed eligibility and qualification requirements.
Q: Can I fly under these rules as a CFI to instruct or as a DPE to administer checkrides?
Yes, the FAA final rule for BasicMed does apply to the person acting as PIC, including flight instructors or Designated Pilot Examiner (DPE). As an example, the FAA has noted that flight instructors meeting the requirements of the new rule may act as PIC while giving flight training without holding a medical certificate, regardless of whether the person receiving flight training holds a medical certificate. Remember though that only the CFI certificate (not commercial pilot privileges) can be used under BasicMed, even though ratings can be earned up to ATP.
Q: Do the new rules include twin-engine operations?
As long as the twin engine aircraft is not authorized under Federal law to carry more than 7 occupants and has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, you will be able to fly a twin-engine aircraft as long as you operate in accordance with the additional conditions in the new rule, listed above.
