Section 2307(a)(8) of FESSA established limitations for operations
under BasicMed. One operating requirement limited an individual
operating in the covered aircraft from carrying more than 5 passengers.
Section 828 of the Act amended section 2307(a)(8)(A) (i.e., the
operating requirement) by increasing the number of passengers from 5 to
6. This final rule will revise Sec.  61.113(i)(1) to reflect this
increased passenger limitation. Therefore, a covered aircraft may now
be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight
crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board.\15\

3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

Q. What does BasicMed mean for me?
A. AOPA worked hard for years on behalf of its members to bring about third class medical reform that the FAA refers to as BasicMed. Nearly 80,000 pilots have qualified to fly safely under BasicMed since its inception in 2017. (See how to qualify at right.)
BasicMed allows pilots to transition from the normal medical certification process to a medical qualification where they work with their personal physician. Pilots flying under BasicMed are allowed to operate “covered aircraft” having a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, and are authorized to carry up to seven occupants (up to six passengers plus the pilot in command), at altitudes up to 18,000 feet msl and at an indicated airspeed of up to 250 knots. Pilots, if appropriately rated, can fly VFR or IFR. Pilots flying under the exemption cannot operate for compensation or hire.

aopa.org/basicmed
Follow these easy steps to apply
Step 1: Get the form
Review if you’re eligible for BasicMed and download the BasicMed FAA Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist (CMEC). Complete the self-assessment portion of the form.
Step 2: See your doctor
Take your Compre-hensive Medical Examination Checklist (from Step 1) and get a BasicMed-specific exam by a state-licensed physician. Have your doctor fill out the rest of the exam checklist. You will need this to complete Step 3 and will need it again for your 24-month renewal.
Step 3: Take the online course
Once you have completed your FAA CMEC from a state-licensed physician, take this online course and pass the quiz. You must complete the post-course form to submit your exam information (from Step 2) to the FAA to earn your BasicMed completion certificate.
Step 4: File documents in your logbook
Download your course completion certificate and keep it with your completed CMEC in your logbook or electronically. You need to have it available upon request from FAA. Make sure you have a valid flight review, and you are ready to fly.

verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (US) — CURRENT RULE, AS AMENDED BY FAA REAUTHORIZATION ACT OF 2024 §828

Governing authority: 49 U.S.C. 44703 note (FESSA §2307, as amended), implemented at 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) (covered aircraft, operating requirements) and 14 CFR 91.319(j) (experimental aircraft). Conforming final rule published 89 FR (FR-2024-11-18, Docket FAA-2024-XXXX), effective November 12, 2024.

1) MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT — 12,500 lb
   A covered aircraft must have a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)(ii), as amended).
   - This is the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight (the design/authorization limit), NOT the actual loaded weight of a given flight. Operating below 12,500 lb actual weight does not qualify an aircraft whose authorized MTOW exceeds 12,500 lb.
   - The regulatory text uses "maximum takeoff weight," deliberately omitting "certificated," because experimental aircraft are not type certificated yet may be operated under BasicMed; for type-certificated aircraft the figure is the maximum certificated takeoff weight shown on the TC/STC/ATC (see AC 68-1A ¶5.1.2, still correct on this method point).
   - Exclusion: transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29 do not qualify regardless of weight (added by §828(a)(4)).

2) NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY — 7
   The aircraft must be "authorized under Federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants" (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)(i); 91.319(j) for experimental).
   - "Occupants" includes any required flightcrew members. The limit is on what the aircraft is AUTHORIZED to carry (seating/design approval), not on how many people are aboard.
   - Aircraft altered by STC/ATC to reduce authorized seating to 7 or fewer qualify (AC 68-1A ¶5.1.2 method).

3) NUMBER OF PASSENGERS ON BOARD — 6
   The flight must carry not more than six passengers (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), operating requirement as amended from 5 to 6 by §828).
   - Reconciliation: 7 authorized occupants − 1 pilot in command = 6 passengers. If the aircraft is type certificated for two required pilot flightcrew members, the maximum passengers on board is 5 (2 crew + 5 = 7). In no case may passengers on board exceed 6.
   - This is an operating limit on persons carried, distinct from the occupant-authorization limit on the airframe.

SUPERSEDED FIGURES (do not use for flights on/after 11/12/2024): 6,000 lb maximum takeoff weight, 6 authorized occupants, 5 passengers on board. These pre-amendment numbers still appear in AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) and in FAA material not yet revised; Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) explicitly states the new limits apply on or after November 12, 2024. Flights conducted before that date were governed by the old figures.

RELATED CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THESE LIMITS (for completeness, not asked): within the United States (or a country where BasicMed is authorized); at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; VFR or IFR as rated; not for compensation or hire; pilot must hold a U.S. driver's license, have held an FAA medical certificate at any point after July 14, 2006 (most recent not denied/suspended/revoked/withdrawn), a current CMEC from a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months, and a completed BasicMed online medical education course.

SOURCES: FAA, "FAA Updates BasicMed Program" (Nov 15, 2024); FAA BasicMed page (Aircraft Requirements / Operating Requirements); FAA final rule, FR-2024-11-18 (B. Covered Aircraft Requirements; C. Passengers in Covered Aircraft); FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) ¶5a; AOPA, "Answers for Pilots" (Apr 1, 2026). AC 68-1A is cited only for interpretive method, not for the numeric limits.

Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or

(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

verdict.summary:
# Hours-of-Service Limits — Driver of a Passenger-Carrying CMV (Motorcoach), Interstate, U.S.

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) |

Read together as the regulation reads: *no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.*

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text (49 CFR 395.5)

> **§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.**
> Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
> (b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—
> (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
> (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.
> [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

Corroborating sources: FMCSA, *Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers* (2022) ("More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" / "For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty"); FMCSA *Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* ("15-Hour On-Duty Limit … 10-Hour Driving Limit … This regulation is found in Section 395.5(a)(2)").

## 3. How the three limits interact (the part most often misapplied)

- **The 8-hour reset is the gate for both other limits.** It must be 8 *consecutive* hours with no on-duty or driving time in it. Per the FMCSA driver guide, the 8 hours "may consist of off duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of the two."
- **The 10-hour limit is a cap on cumulative driving, not on continuous driving.** The driver may drive 10 hours straight or in fragments; once cumulative driving since the last 8-hour reset reaches 10, no further driving until another 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- **The 15-hour limit is cumulative ON-DUTY time, not a 15-hour elapsed clock.** This is the key divergence from the property-carrier 14-hour window. FMCSA's passenger guide states it plainly: *"Off-duty time taken during the day, such as a lunch break or nap, does not count toward this 15-hour limit."* So a 2-hour off-duty break mid-shift does not consume the 15 hours — but it also does not reset them. Only 8 consecutive hours off duty resets the 15-hour and 10-hour clocks.
- **After 15 on-duty hours the driver may still work — but may not drive.** FMCSA guide: *"You may do other work after being on duty 15 hours, but you may not drive."* Same for the 10-hour limit: *"You may do other work after 6:00 p.m., but you can not do any more driving."*
- **Ordering check:** 8 (reset) < 10 (driving cap) ≤ 15 (on-duty cap). Every stated figure is internally consistent; the driving allowance never exceeds the on-duty allowance that contains it.

### Worked example
8 consecutive hours off duty; driver reports on duty at 06:00 and drives 06:00–16:00 (10.0 driving hours).
- 10-hour driving limit reached at **16:00** → no further driving.
- 15-hour on-duty limit reached at **21:00** → from that moment the driver may not drive even if driving hours somehow remained; non-driving work is still permitted.
- Next driving requires 8 consecutive hours off duty (earliest 05:00 the following day if off duty from 21:00).

## 4. Weekly outer limits (context — not asked, but they can bind first)

- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** if the carrier does **not** operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** if the carrier **does** operate CMVs every day of the week. § 395.5(b).

Two consequences worth flagging to the requester:
1. **There is no 34-hour restart for passenger carriers.** The restart in § 395.3(c) is a property-carrying provision. FMCSA's passenger guide confirms the operating rule: once the 60-hour limit is reached, the driver cannot drive again "until you have dropped below 60 hours for a 7-consecutive-day period" (and analogously below 70 for 8 days). A driver can hit the weekly wall before ever reaching 10 or 15 hours in a shift.
2. **All on-duty time counts, including work for other employers.** § 395.5(b) applies "regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services," and the FMCSA guide notes other compensated work must be added to the total. For part-time/intermittent drivers, § 395.8(j) requires a signed statement of the prior 7 days' on-duty time and the time last relieved from duty.

## 5. Exceptions that can change the arithmetic (§ 395.1) — assumptions stated, not applied

The answers in §1 assume **no exception applies**. If any of the following is in play, the numbers above are not the operative numbers and the analysis must be redone:

- **§ 395.1(e) — short-haul / 150 air-mile:** exempts a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released within 14 consecutive hours from the record-of-duty-status requirement (not from the driving limits themselves). Relevant to the logging obligation, not to the 10/8/15 figures.
- **§ 395.1(g)(3) — sleeper berth split for passenger-carrying CMVs:** a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (as defined in § 393.76) may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, subject to the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv). Where a split is validly used, the "8 consecutive hours" answer becomes "the equivalent of 8 hours via two qualifying periods." The specific (i)–(iv) conditions should be read from the current regulatory text before relying on a split — I have not reproduced them here because they were not in the fetched passages.
- **§ 395.1(b) — adverse driving conditions:** provides limited relief to complete a run. It does not rewrite the base limits; do not treat it as a general extension.
- **Alaska and other territorial/state-specific provisions** in § 395.1 (e.g., 15 hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty; 20-hour on-duty cap; 70/80-hour weekly caps) apply only to operations in those jurisdictions.

## 6. Scope, assumptions, and where this answer stops

- **Assumed:** the driver operates a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach/bus) in **interstate** commerce and is therefore subject to the federal FMCSA rules in 49 CFR Part 395, specifically § 395.5 rather than the property-carrier § 395.3. This is the correct assumption because the request names a motorcoach.
- **Not covered:** **intrastate** operations. Most states adopt the federal passenger-carrier limits for intrastate drivers, but several impose different or additional rules, and state adoption is not uniform. If the driver never crosses a state line, or the state has opted out of the federal standard, the state's own HOS rule governs and the 10/8/15 answers must be re-verified against that state's code.
- **Not covered:** non-business private motor carriers of passengers, which FMCSA notes are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements (logbook/ELD) — though the driving limits themselves still warrant checking against the applicable rule.
- **Currency:** figures are taken from the current eCFR text of § 395.5 (last amended 70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005) and current FMCSA guidance; they are not a historical or proposed version.

## 7. Enforcement note

A driver who has exceeded the 10-hour, 15-hour, or 60/70-hour limit is subject to being declared out of service under § 395.13, and the carrier is exposed to the corresponding Part 395 violations. Because § 395.5(a) and (b) prohibit the *carrier* from permitting or requiring the drive as well as prohibiting the *driver* from driving, the exposure is dual — a dispatch instruction that pushes a driver past 15 on-duty hours is itself a violation, independent of whether the driver complies.

quotes.whole:
§ 135.267 Flight time limitations and rest requirements: Unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews.




(a) No certificate holder may assign any flight crewmember, and no flight crewmember may accept an assignment, for flight time as a member of a one- or two-pilot crew if that crewmember's total flight time in all commercial flying will exceed—




(1) 500 hours in any calendar quarter.






(2) 800 hours in any two consecutive calendar quarters.






(3) 1,400 hours in any calendar year.








(b) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, during any 24 consecutive hours the total flight time of the assigned flight when added to any other commercial flying by that flight crewmember may not exceed—




(1) 8 hours for a flight crew consisting of one pilot; or






(2) 10 hours for a flight crew consisting of two pilots qualified under this part for the operation being conducted.








(c) A flight crewmember's flight time may exceed the flight time limits of paragraph (b) of this section if the assigned flight time occurs during a regularly assigned duty period of no more than 14 hours and—




(1) If this duty period is immediately preceded by and followed by a required rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours of rest;






(2) If flight time is assigned during this period, that total flight time when added to any other commercial flying by the flight crewmember may not exceed—




(i) 8 hours for a flight crew consisting of one pilot; or






(ii) 10 hours for a flight crew consisting of two pilots; and








(3) If the combined duty and rest periods equal 24 hours.








(d) Each assignment under paragraph (b) of this section must provide for at least 10 consecutive hours of rest during the 24-hour period that precedes the planned completion time of the assignment.






(e) When a flight crewmember has exceeded the daily flight time limitations in this section, because of circumstances beyond the control of the certificate holder or flight crewmember (such as adverse weather conditions), that flight crewmember must have a rest period before being assigned or accepting an assignment for flight time of at least—




(1) 11 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by not more than 30 minutes;






(2) 12 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by more than 30 minutes, but not more than 60 minutes; and






(3) 16 consecutive hours of rest if the flight time limitation is exceeded by more than 60 minutes.







(f) The certificate holder must provide each flight crewmember at least 13 rest periods of at least 24 consecutive hours each in each calendar quarter.



[Docket 23634, 50 FR 29320, July 18, 1985, as amended by Amdt. 135-33, 54 FR 39294, Sept. 25, 1989; Amdt. 135-60, 61 FR 2616, Jan. 26, 1996]

verdict.summary:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Bottom line

| Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2. Minimum to which that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, and only if the flight attendant is provided a **subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** and that occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

9 hours is the requirement. 8 hours is a conditional floor, not an entitlement: the reduction is valid only when the paired 10-hour subsequent rest is actually built into the pairing and satisfied.

## 2. Governing text (verbatim, as fetched 2026-11-16)

**§ 135.273(b)(1)** — "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

**§ 135.273(b)(2)** — "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(3)** — "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(10)** — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."

**§ 135.273(b)(11)** — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period."

**§ 135.273(a)** — "Rest period means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."

## 3. What counts as rest

Rest is measured by the §135.273(a) definition: time **free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise**. Consequently, none of the following is rest, and none of it may be counted toward the 9 (or 8) hours:

- Hotel/crew-van transport after release and before the next report, when the certificate holder arranges or requires it.
- Post-flight duties (paperwork, customs/immigration processing, aircraft securing, company calls, irregular-ops phone contact).
- Deadhead/positioning transportation at the company's direction — it is duty, not rest, and it also counts inside the duty period.
- Standby, reserve, or on-call time during which the flight attendant is subject to recall.
- Training, meetings, drug/alcohol testing, or any other assignment with the certificate holder (expressly barred by (b)(11) during a required rest period).

Practical consequence for scheduling: the operator must block **9 full consecutive hours** (or 8 under a valid reduction) of genuine freedom from duty, measured release-to-report, not merely 9 hours on the roster between the last flight leg and the first leg of the next day.

## 4. Conditions checklist for using the 8-hour reduction

All of the following must be true, and each should be evidenced in the pairing record:

1. The duty period preceding the rest is **scheduled at 14 hours or less** (measured as the scheduled duty period, not an as-flown extension).
2. The reduced rest is **scheduled** — i.e., built into the published pairing/roster before the fact, not merely recorded after the fact.
3. **8 consecutive hours** free of all responsibility for work or duty.
4. A **subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** is scheduled.
5. That subsequent 10-hour rest **begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**.
6. That subsequent 10-hour rest **occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period** (i.e., it sits between the next duty period and the one after it).
7. **No duty of any kind** is assigned during either rest period — (b)(11).
8. The flight attendant **actually received** the minimum rest before being assigned the next duty period — (b)(10) is an actual-rest test, so a delay that erodes the rest below 8 (reduced) or 9 (standard) hours bars the assignment regardless of what the roster said.
9. **No chaining.** Because the 10-hour subsequent rest must begin within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest, the operator cannot reduce rest on consecutive nights without inserting the 10-hour recovery rest. A pattern of repeated 8-hour rests with no qualifying 10-hour follow-on is a violation.

**Important scoping note:** §135.273(b)(9) — the bar on scheduling a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of a reduced rest period — applies **only** to reductions to 10 hours under (b)(8), which is the rule for duty periods **over** 14 hours. It does **not** attach to the 8-hour reduction under (b)(3). Do not import it into the ≤14-hour case; the operator may of course impose it as a stricter company policy.

## 5. Worked timeline (proves the arithmetic)

Day 1 scheduled duty: report 06:00, release 20:00 = 14.0 hours scheduled duty.

- **Standard rest (9 h):** 20:00 → 05:00 Day 2. Earliest Day 2 report = **05:00**.
- **Reduced rest (8 h):** 20:00 → 04:00 Day 2. Earliest Day 2 report = **04:00**, provided the paired subsequent rest is scheduled correctly.
- **24-hour trigger:** the reduced rest began 20:00 Day 1, so the subsequent 10-hour rest must **begin no later than 20:00 Day 2**.
- **Compliant construction:** Day 2 duty 04:00–16:00 (12.0 h). Subsequent rest 16:00 Day 2 → 02:00 Day 3 = **10.0 consecutive hours**, beginning 16:00 Day 2, which is earlier than the 20:00 Day 2 deadline. It falls between completion of the Day 2 duty period and commencement of the Day 3 duty period. Earliest Day 3 report = **02:00**.
- **Non-compliant construction:** Day 2 duty 04:00–21:00. The subsequent rest cannot begin until 21:00 Day 2, which is later than the 20:00 Day 2 deadline → the 8-hour reduction was invalid; the pairing should have used the 9-hour standard rest.

## 6. Adjacent thresholds (so the ≤14-hour answer is not misapplied)

| Scheduled duty period | Required rest | May be reduced to | Condition on reduction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | 9 consecutive hours | 8 consecutive hours | Subsequent rest ≥10 consecutive hours, beginning ≤24 h after the start of the reduced rest |
| More than 14, up to 16 h (with at least one additional flight attendant assigned to the flight(s)) | 12 consecutive hours | 10 consecutive hours | Subsequent rest ≥14 consecutive hours, beginning ≤24 h after the start of the reduced rest; and (b)(9) bars a duty period over 14 h in the 24 h commencing after the start of the reduced rest |
| More than 16, up to 18 h (two additional flight attendants) | 12 consecutive hours | 10 consecutive hours | Same as above |
| More than 18, up to 20 h (three additional flight attendants) | 12 consecutive hours | 10 consecutive hours | Same as above |

Each additional flight attendant assigned to the flight or flights in the duty period extends the permissible scheduled duty period by 2 hours, under (b)(4)–(b)(6); the 12-hour rest rule for the over-14-hour case is (b)(7), the 10-hour reduction is (b)(8), and the follow-on duty cap is (b)(9). Verify the exact (b)(4)–(b)(6) hour bands against the current section text before relying on them in a pairing — they are stated here for context only, because the request concerns the 14-hours-or-less case.

Flight crewmember rules do **not** govern flight attendants. §135.267 (unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews) and §135.265 (scheduled operations) apply to flight crewmembers; a legal pilot pairing does not make the flight attendant pairing legal, and vice versa.

## 7. Caveat that could change the numbers: §135.273(c) election

Under §135.273(c), a certificate holder may apply the **flight crewmember** flight time, duty, and rest requirements of Part 135 subpart F to flight attendants for all operations, but only if it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants used in the operation, include the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the minimum in the type certificate data sheet, and — critically — are **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**.

If such an election is in force, the rest figures change (for example, under §135.265(b)–(c): 10 hours of rest for less than 8 hours of scheduled flight time, 10 hours for 8 or more but less than 9, 11 hours for 9 or more, reducible to 8, 8, and 9 hours respectively when followed by 10, 11, and 12 hours of subsequent rest). **Check the operator's OpSpecs before publishing a number.** Absent such an approved election — the assumption in this answer — §135.273(b)(2) and (b)(3) control and the answers are 9 hours and 8 hours.

## 8. Operator compliance procedure

1. **Confirm applicability.** Verify the flight attendant is crewed under Part 135, that no §135.273(c) election appears in the OpSpecs, and that no exemption, deviation authority, or collective bargaining agreement imposes stricter limits. If any of these exists, apply the stricter/more specific rule and document the basis.
2. **Classify the duty period.** Confirm it is a *scheduled* duty period of 14 hours or less as published, and not a reserve/standby period, a repositioning day, or an extension under (b)(4)–(b)(6). If the scheduled duty exceeds 14 hours, the 12-hour rule applies instead.
3. **Measure the duty period** from required report to release, including deadhead at company direction, ground time, and post-flight duties.
4. **Compute rest release-to-report** in elapsed hours (not calendar days), subtracting hotel transport, required calls, and any company-imposed obligation.
5. **Default to 9 hours.** Only shorten to 8 if the pairing simultaneously schedules the ≥10-hour subsequent rest beginning within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest.
6. **Protect the rest period.** Issue no assignment, call, training, or standby during the 9/8-hour rest — (b)(11).
7. **Re-check on the day of operation.** If actual release/report times erode the rest below the minimum, the next assignment is barred by (b)(10) until the minimum is actually received; re-crew or delay.
8. **Record the reduction.** Annotate the pairing and duty record with the reduced-rest election and the paired 10-hour subsequent rest so the basis is auditable.
9. **Document in the manual.** Reflect the rest definitions, the reduction conditions, and the reporting/release conventions in the company manual as required by §135.21/§135.23 and the OpSpecs (verify the applicable manual-content subsection before issuance).
10. **Verify before publication.** Re-read the current §135.273 text at the time of use (see Sources) — the section can be amended.

## 9. Pitfalls that generate findings

- Counting hotel transport or crew-van time as rest.
- Treating a scheduled 9-hour gap as compliant when post-flight duties and van time leave only 7.5 hours free of duty.
- Counting deadhead/positioning as rest.
- Reducing to 8 hours without a scheduled 10-hour subsequent rest, or with a 10-hour rest that begins more than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest.
- Chaining 8-hour reductions night after night.
- Relying on the pilots' §135.267/§135.265 compliance as evidence of flight attendant compliance.
- Using actual flight time instead of the scheduled duty period when testing the 14-hour threshold.
- Reducing rest retroactively after an operational delay rather than re-testing the pairing against (b)(10).

## 10. Assumptions (state them in any written opinion)

- The flight attendant is crewed under Part 135 and no §135.273(c) election is approved in the OpSpecs.
- "Scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less" means the published/assigned duty period, with no (b)(4)–(b)(6) extension.
- No exemption, deviation authority, or labor agreement imposes a stricter or different rest standard.
- "Reduced" means the regulatory reduction in (b)(3), not a company compensatory arrangement.
- Rest is assessed per duty period, subject to the (b)(3) 24-hour trigger tying the reduction to the next rest period.

## 11. Sources and verification

- 14 CFR 135.273, eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16T02:23:48Z, sha256 88e87edd4ca6) — (b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(8), (b)(9), (b)(10), (b)(11), (c).
- CFR 2026 title 14 vol 3, sec. 135.273, govinfo PDF (fetched 2026-11-16T02:23:48Z, sha256 c64287ffa33d) — (a) definitions, (b)(2)–(b)(4), (b)(7)–(b)(9).
- 14 CFR 135.267, eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16T02:23:48Z, sha256 11682646aa92) — confirms flight crewmember scope, not flight attendant.
- Part 135 subpart F and Part 135 index pages (fetched 2026-11-16T02:23:48–49Z, sha256 f2b546df3c9b, 5af3a666334b).

Verification step: before publishing any figure in a manual, training module, or enforcement response, re-fetch §135.273 and confirm paragraphs (b)(2) and (b)(3) read as quoted above, and confirm the operator's OpSpecs contain no §135.273(c) election. The 9-hour and 8-hour figures in this answer are drawn verbatim from the regulation, not inferred.

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## 1. Answer (citation-ready)

**The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113, "HTTP/2" (M. Thomson, Ed.; C. Benfield, Ed.; June 2022; Standards Track / Proposed Standard).**

**RFC 9113 obsoletes two RFCs: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.**

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current HTTP/2 specification | **RFC 9113** (June 2022) |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** (HTTP/2, May 2015) and **RFC 8740** (Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2, February 2020) |

Verification date: **2026-11-16** (timestamp of the RFC Editor / IETF Datatracker metadata retrieved for this answer). Re-verify per §6 if citing after that date.

## 2. Evidence from primary sources

**The document's own header and abstract (RFC 9113, from the RFC Editor's XML/errata renderings):**

```
Request for Comments: 9113                                       Mozilla
Obsoletes: 7540, 8740                                   C. Benfield, Ed.
Category: Standards Track                                     Apple Inc.
ISSN: 2070-1721                                                June 2022
                                                                    HTTP/2

Abstract
   ...
   This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.
```

**RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113** — status block reads "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 / HTTP/2 / June 2022. / M. Thomson, Ed., / C. Benfield, Ed. / Proposed Standard", and the abstract states "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." The page carries no "Obsoleted by" entry.

**Reverse direction (RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject index):**

- RFC 7540, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Belshe et al., May 2015 — listed as **"Obsoleted by RFC 9113"**.
- RFC 8740, "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", D. Benjamin, February 2020 — listed as **"Obsoleted by RFC 9113"**.

So the relationship is confirmed in both directions: 9113 declares the Obsoletes, and the RFC Editor marks both 7540 and 8740 as obsoleted by 9113.

**Corroborating (non-authoritative) signal:** the HTTPbis working-group draft `draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis` (e.g. -02, June 2021) states "This document obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740", showing the intent carried into publication. Drafts are not the specification; RFC 9113 is.

## 3. Scope decisions behind the answer (state these when citing)

1. **"Current"** = current as of the verification date above, per the RFC Editor's authoritative metadata, including the absence of any successor document. "Current" is a moving target: any future RFC that obsoletes 9113 would change the answer, which is why the verification date is part of the answer.
2. **"Obsoletes"** = the RFC numbers named in RFC 9113's `Obsoletes:` header — a closed set of exactly two: 7540 and 8740. It does **not** include:
   - documents RFC 9113 merely **updates**, references, or relates to;
   - HTTP/2 **extensions** that remain in force alongside 9113: **RFC 7541** (HPACK), **RFC 8164** (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2), **RFC 8336** (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame), **RFC 8441** (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2). The RFC Editor's HTTP/2 index lists these with no obsoleting link to 9113, and RFC 9113 keeps HPACK as its header-compression format.
3. **RFC 8740 is the trap in this question.** RFC 8740 was originally an *update* to RFC 7540 (it forbade TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication). RFC 9113 folded that TLS 1.3 guidance in ("Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes"), so 8740 moved from "updates 7540" to "obsoleted by 9113". Anyone listing only RFC 7540 is incomplete; anyone omitting 8740 because it was 'just an update' is wrong.
4. **What RFC 9113 explicitly does *not* obsolete:** the HTTP/1.1 message syntax — "This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax." (HTTP/1.1 has its own separate revision line, RFC 9112; do not merge the two answers.)
5. **Do not confuse item-level obsolescence with RFC obsolescence.** RFC 9113 §11 marks the `HTTP2-Settings` header field and the `h2c` upgrade token (both defined in RFC 7540) as obsolete, and Appendix B deprecates RFC 7540's priority scheme. Those are *features*, not RFCs — they add nothing to the obsoletes list, which remains exactly {7540, 8740}.
6. **Errata:** errata correct text within RFC 9113; they do not alter its `Obsoletes:` header or create a successor document. Check https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9113 for the current errata set before quoting specific normative text, but the two answers above are unaffected.

## 4. Suggested citation strings

- Specification: `RFC 9113, HTTP/2, M. Thomson & C. Benfield (Eds.), IETF, June 2022. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html`
- Obsoletes note: `RFC 9113 obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.`
- Full form for a compliance document: `HTTP/2 is specified by RFC 9113 (June 2022), which obsoletes RFC 7540 (May 2015) and RFC 8740 (February 2020). RFC 7541 (HPACK) remains in force. Verified against the RFC Editor index on 2026-11-16.`

## 5. One-paragraph narrative version

HTTP/2 is currently specified by RFC 9113, published June 2022 on the IETF Standards Track (Proposed Standard) and edited by Martin Thomson and Cory Benfield. It replaces the original HTTP/2 specification, RFC 7540 (May 2015), and also obsoletes RFC 8740 (February 2020), the TLS 1.3 update to RFC 7540 whose content was folded into the new document. Both predecessor documents are marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113" in the RFC Editor's index. HTTP/2's companion and extension documents — RFC 7541 (HPACK), RFC 8164, RFC 8336, and RFC 8441 — are not obsoleted by RFC 9113 and remain in effect. Verified as of 2026-11-16.

## 6. Re-verification procedure (run before citing if the verification date is stale)

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/`. Confirm the status line still reads June 2022 / Proposed Standard and that there is **no** "Obsoleted by" entry. If a successor is listed, that successor is the new answer to ask 1 — restart from step 2 with it.
2. On the same page, read the `Obsoletes:` header (or the abstract sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs ..."). The numbers there are the complete answer to ask 2 — copy them verbatim; do not add 'Updates' numbers or extension RFCs.
3. Cross-check in the opposite direction: open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740/` and confirm each shows "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". A mismatch between the forward and reverse links means the index is mid-update — prefer the obsoleting document's own header and note the discrepancy.
4. Optional machine check: `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml` — read the `<obsoletes>` elements in the document front matter; they must be exactly `7540` and `8740`.
5. Record the date and the source URL(s) you checked in the citation, as in §4.

Our remit from Government for this year was published on 16 March 2026. It says that two-thirds of median hourly earnings should continue to be the key reference point for future NLW rates, so here we provide indicative estimates of the increases required to achieve this for the 2027 National Living Wage uprating.
Alongside this report, we have published our consultation on minimum wage rates for 2026 and beyond. We welcome submissions from all interested parties. We are also holding regional visits across the UK and invite meetings with any and all other interested parties. If you have something to contribute, please get in touch with us via lpc@lowpay.gov.uk.

The Low Pay Commission (LPC) is the independent body which advises the Government on the levels of the National Minimum Wage (NMW), including the National Living Wage (NLW). New rates of the NMW come into force on 1 April 2026, based on recommendations we made in October 2025. This report considers some of the potential impacts of these increases, looks at our remit for the year ahead and sets out our evidence-gathering plans for the rest of the year. We are keen to hear from workers and employers affected by the rates; more details can be found on page 14.

This year, the 16-17 Year Old Rate and the Apprentice Rate will increase by 6 per cent to £8.00.
The recommendation for 16-17 year olds balances the weaker labour market for this age group with the need to ensure their rate does not become unmoored from the adult rate, particularly as Government policy is to remove the 18-20 Year Old Rate.
Having increased significantly in 2025, we expect coverage for 16-17 year olds to increase again this year, from 22 to 23 per cent. Coverage for apprentices is also expected to increase from 17 to 18 per cent.

This year, the 16-17 Year Old Rate and the Apprentice Rate will increase by 6 per cent to £8.00.

Having increased significantly in 2025, we expect coverage for 16-17 year olds to increase again this year, from 22 to 23 per cent. Coverage for apprentices is also expected to increase from 17 to 18 per cent.

The Secretary of State makes these Regulations in exercise of the powers conferred by sections 1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 (“the 1998 Act”)(1).

A draft of these Regulations was laid before Parliament in accordance with section 51(5) of the 1998 Act and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.



Citation, commencement and extent

1.—(1) These Regulations may be cited as the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026.

(2) These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.

(3) These Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Amendments to the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015

2.—(1) The National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015(2) are amended as follows.

(2) In regulation 4 (the national living wage) for “£12.21” substitute “£12.71”.

(3) In regulation 4A(1) (workers who qualify for the national minimum wage at a different rate)—

(a)in sub-paragraph (b) for “£10.00” substitute “£10.85”;

(b)in sub-paragraph (c) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”;

(c)in sub-paragraph (d) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”.

(4) In regulation 16(1) (amount for provision of living accommodation) for “£10.66” substitute “£11.10”.




Name

Title

Department for Business and Trade

DATE




Explanatory Note

(This note is not part of the Regulations)
 
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
  
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(4) increases the accommodation offset amount which is applicable where any employer provides a worker with living accommodation from £10.66 to £11.10 for each day that accommodation is provided (regulation 16(1) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
A full regulatory impact assessment of the effect that this instrument will have on the costs of business and the voluntary sector is available from the Employment Rights Directorate, Department for Business and Trade, Old Admiralty Building, London SW1A 2AY and is annexed to the Explanatory Memorandum which is available alongside the instrument on www.legislation.gov.uk.

A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.

The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.

verdict.summary:
# UK National Minimum Wage / National Living Wage — rates effective 1 April 2026

## 1. The two figures asked for

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Rate to 31 March 2026 | Increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| **National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over** | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| **National Minimum Wage — 18–20 Year Old Rate** | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). They apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026.

Full 2026 table, for completeness of the payroll rate load:

| NMW rate | From 1 April 2026 | Increase |
|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 / 4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 / 8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 / 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 / 6.0% |
| Accommodation Offset | £11.10 per day | £0.44 / 4.1% |

## 2. Status of the figures — confirmed, not provisional

- The Low Pay Commission recommended the rates on **27 October 2025**; the Government **accepted the recommendations in full** and announced them at the **Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025**.
- The rates were brought into legal effect by **The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026 No. 357)**, which amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621): reg 2(2) substitutes "£12.71" for "£12.21" in reg 4 (national living wage); reg 2(3)(a) substitutes "£10.85" for "£10.00" in reg 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21); reg 2(4) sets the accommodation offset at £11.10. Coming into force **1 April 2026**.
- Confirmed independently by the LPC's impact report *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* (published 1 April 2026), the LPC publication *Minimum wage rates for 2026* (26 November 2025), the 1 April 2026 press release *National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour*, and the live gov.uk rates table.

Sources: legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348279030 ; gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 ; gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026 ; gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates ; gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour.

## 3. Payroll application notes

1. **Effective date.** Load the new rates for pay reference periods beginning on or after **1 April 2026**. A weekly payroll with a pay reference period starting Monday 30 March 2026 is still on the 2025 rates for that whole period; the first period on the new rates starts 6 April 2026 in that cycle. Monthly payrolls: the April 2026 period is the first at the new rates.
2. **Age banding.** The NLW age threshold is 21 and over (reduced from 25 to 23 in April 2021, and from 23 to 21 in April 2024) and is unchanged for 2026. The 18–20 band covers workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 — the statutory instrument's explanatory note words it that way, so an employee in their 21st year moves to £12.71. Where a worker reaches the qualifying age part-way through a pay reference period, apply the higher rate from the start of that pay reference period (standard NMW age rule) — flag birthdays in the HR/payroll data now so April–March runs don't lag.
3. **Apprentices.** The apprentice rate (£8.00) applies only to apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21+ who has completed the first year moves to £12.71 — gov.uk uses exactly this example, so check apprentice start dates rather than blanket-paying £8.00.
4. **Salary sacrifice and deductions.** The rates are gross hourly minima before tax and NIC. Salary sacrifice, pension contributions, and employer deductions must not take pay for time worked below the applicable minimum; uniform, tools, and similar deductions are caught by the same rule.
5. **Accommodation offset.** Maximum daily offset £11.10 (max £77.70 in a seven-day week), up from £10.66. The offset reduces what counts toward NMW for pay purposes — it is not a deduction from wages, and it cannot take a worker below the cash minimum.
6. **Salaried-hours and time-worked checks.** Re-run the annual salaried-hours calculation and any averaging of hours for the new rates; a 4.1% adult uplift can push previously compliant salaried arrangements below NMW, particularly where unpaid overtime or travel time is in the pattern.
7. **Systems.** Update payroll software rate tables, rota/HR minimum-pay rules, and any agency or umbrella contracts that reference the rates by value rather than by reference to the Regulations. Test one April run per pay frequency before go-live.

## 4. Forward note (not part of this answer)

The gov.uk rates table also displays **April 2027** figures (21+ £13.21; 18–20 £11.27; under-18 £8.31; apprentice £8.31) arising from the LPC's 2027 remit work. These are future-year rates and should not be used for 2026 budgeting or compliance; they are flagged here only so a reader who sees them on the same page does not confuse them with the answer above.

11-Hour Driving Limit
May drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
10-Hour Driving Limit
May drive a maximum of 10 hours after 8 consecutive hours off duty.
14-Hour Limit
May not drive beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty, following 10 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time does not extend the 14-hour period.
15-Hour Limit
May not drive after having been on duty for 15 hours, following 8 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period.
30-Minute Driving Break
Drivers must take a 30-minute break when they have driven for a period of 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption. The break may be satisfied by any non-driving period of 30 consecutive minutes (i.e., on-duty not driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of these taken consecutively).
60/70-Hour Limit
May not drive after 60/70 hours on duty in 7/8 consecutive days. A driver may restart a 7/8 consecutive day period after taking 34 or more consecutive hours off duty.

verdict.summary:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — THE TWO OPERATIONAL THRESHOLDS

ANSWERS

| # | Threshold | Value | Unit | Controlling provision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum radius from the normal work reporting location within which the driver must operate | 150 | air miles (172.6 statute miles) | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2 | Maximum consecutive hours after coming on duty within which the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work | 14 | consecutive hours | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR text as fetched)

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
(A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
(B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
(C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and
(D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

FMCSA's own summary states the same two figures: "A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in §395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location." (FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations.)

THRESHOLD 1 — MEASUREMENT AND APPLICATION OF THE 150 AIR-MILE RADIUS

- Unit of measure. The rule is written in AIR miles (a straight-line / great-circle distance), not road miles and not statute miles. 1 air mile = 1 nautical mile = 1.15078 statute miles. 150 air miles x 1.15078 = 172.617 statute miles, which is why the regulation itself parenthesizes the figure as "(172.6 statute miles)." A 150-air-mile radius therefore encloses a straight-line circle of roughly 172.6 statute miles in every direction from the center point.
- Center point. The center is the driver's NORMAL WORK REPORTING LOCATION — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work. FMCSA's guidance (CSA short-haul FAQ material) confirms the location may differ from shift to shift so long as the driver starts and ends each shift at the same location. It is not necessarily the carrier's terminal or the driver's home.
- What the radius governs. The driver must OPERATE (i.e., drive) within the 150 air-mile radius. A single trip outside the radius during the duty tour removes the driver from the exception for that day; the driver must then complete a record of duty status (paper log or ELD, per 395.8) for that day. FMCSA: "When a driver no longer meets the exception (drives too far/works too many hours), the driver must complete a regular log or use an ELD for the day (§ 395.8)."
- Practical measurement procedure for a carrier or investigator. (a) Fix the normal work reporting location as a set of coordinates. (b) Fix the farthest point reached during the duty tour (from GPS/ELD breadcrumbs, dispatch records, or the driver's time record plus trip sheets). (c) Compute the great-circle distance between the two coordinates (haversine on the two lat/long pairs, or a geodesic calculation). (d) If that distance exceeds 150 nautical miles (172.6 statute miles), the exception is unavailable for that tour. Road-network distance is irrelevant to this test; a driver who stays inside the circle can drive far more than 150 road miles, and a driver who crosses the circle is outside even if the road distance back to the center looks short.
- Do not confuse with adjacent radii. 49 CFR 395.1(p) uses a 100 air-mile radius, but that is the motion-picture production site exception, not the short-haul records exception. The non-CDL short-haul provision at 395.1(e)(2) also uses 150 air miles but is a different exception with different conditions (see below).

THRESHOLD 2 — MEASUREMENT AND APPLICATION OF THE 14 CONSECUTIVE HOURS

- What the clock measures. The 14 hours run from the moment the driver COMES ON DUTY. Within that span the driver must both (a) RETURN to the work reporting location and (b) be RELEASED FROM WORK. It is a wall-clock test on the duty tour, not cumulative driving time and not cumulative on-duty time.
- Off-duty time does not extend it. As with the 14-hour driving window in 395.3(a)(2), off-duty time taken inside the tour does not pause or extend the 14 consecutive hours. A two-hour unpaid break in the middle of the day still leaves the driver with a 14-hour outer bound measured from the start of the tour.
- Return is part of the test, not just release. Being released from duty somewhere other than the normal work reporting location does not satisfy (e)(1)(ii). The driver must be back AT the reporting location and released there.
- Failure consequence. If the driver cannot return and be released within 14 consecutive hours — e.g., an adverse driving condition delays the return — the driver falls out of the exception and must record duty status for that day using a paper log or ELD, as FMCSA's short-haul FAQ states.
- Carve-out to state plainly. Clause (ii) is prefaced "except a driver-salesperson." The 14-hour return-and-release test is written for drivers other than driver-salespersons; do not apply the 14-hour release figure to a driver-salesperson without re-reading the current text and any applicable guidance.
- Do not confuse the number with the driving limit. The 14 hours in (e)(1)(ii) is a RETURN-AND-RELEASE test. The 14 consecutive hours in 395.3(a)(2) is a DRIVING WINDOW (no driving beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty). The two figures coincide numerically but are separate obligations, and the short-haul exception does not waive the underlying limits: a short-haul driver is still bound by the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour driving window under 395.3(a). The exception substitutes a time record for the record-of-duty-status requirement; it is not an hours-of-service exemption.

CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE TWO THRESHOLDS (do not drop these when applying the answer)

All of the following must hold on the same day for the exception to apply; the two asked figures are necessary but not sufficient:

1. 150 air-mile radius — 395.1(e)(1)(i).
2. Return to the work reporting location and release from work within 14 consecutive hours — 395.1(e)(1)(ii) (driver-salesperson carve-out noted).
3. At least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for a property-carrying CMV driver (8 consecutive hours for a passenger-carrying CMV driver) — 395.1(e)(1)(iii).
4. The carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records showing the time the driver reports for duty each day, the total hours on duty each day, the time the driver is released from duty each day, and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, the total time for the preceding 7 days under 395.8(j)(2) — 395.1(e)(1)(iv).
5. If the driver fails any of the above on a given day, that day requires a full record of duty status (paper graph grid if 8 or fewer days in the last 30 required a log; ELD if more than 8 days in the last 30 required a log).

Related but distinct: drivers operating under 395.1(e)(1) are not required to take the 30-minute break under 395.3(a)(3)(ii). That relief is a separate feature of the exception and is not one of the two thresholds asked about.

NEARBY PROVISIONS THAT MUST NOT BE SUBSTITUTED FOR THE ANSWER

- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL. Same 150 air-mile radius, but a different structure: the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, must not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, and must not drive after the 16th hour after coming on duty on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days. There is no single 14-hour return-and-release ceiling in (e)(2); do not answer the 14-hour question with (e)(2) and do not import its 16-hour allowance into (e)(1).
- 49 CFR 395.1(o) — the 16-hour short-haul extension, which permits release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, subject to return-to-location conditions over the previous five duty tours and a once-per-6-consecutive-days limit. That is a separate exception; the base short-haul answer is 14, not 16.
- 49 CFR 395.1(p) — motion picture production site transportation: 100 air-mile radius, not 150.

AUDIT / VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR THE TWO THRESHOLDS

For each driver-day on which the exception is claimed:

1. Identify the normal work reporting location recorded for that tour and confirm the driver both reported there and was released there.
2. Confirm the driver's start-of-duty time and release time are both documented on the time record, and that release time minus start time is 14:00 or less.
3. Confirm no driving occurred outside the 150 air-mile (172.6 statute mile) straight-line circle from that location, using the farthest recorded position for the tour.
4. Confirm at least 10 consecutive hours off duty (property) or 8 (passenger) separate the tour from the prior and subsequent tours.
5. Confirm the time record is retained 6 months and carries report time, total hours on duty, and release time; for new or intermittent drivers, confirm the preceding-7-day total is present.
6. If any element fails, confirm a record of duty status exists for that day and that the paper-log/ELD selection matches the 8-or-fewer / more-than-8-days-in-30 test.

QUICK REFERENCE

- Radius: 150 air miles = 150 nautical miles = 172.6 statute miles, measured straight-line from the normal work reporting location.
- Release: return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty.
- Both figures come from 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) and (ii) as currently published; the same two figures are repeated in FMCSA's Summary of Hours of Service Regulations and in FMCSA's short-haul training materials.

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (US, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)) — CURRENT AS OF THE AMENDMENT MADE BY AMDT 61-158 (89 FR 90577, Nov 18, 2024)

1. ANSWERS

| Limit | Value | Governing text |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) |
| Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 (total persons on board, including required flightcrew) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) |
| Passengers on board | 6 (maximum, at any time) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) |

2. AUTHORITATIVE TEXT

14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as revised by Amdt 61-158 (current eCFR):

  "(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and"

Preamble to the final rule (89 FR 90577, Nov 18, 2024), stating the change and its statutory driver:

  "Section 828(a)(4) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 amended section 2307(j) of FESSA to increase the number of occupants an aircraft is authorized to carry under Federal law from 6 to 7 and to increase the maximum certificated takeoff weight from not more than 6,000 pounds to not more than 12,500 pounds. Additionally, section 828(a)(4) added a third provision to section 2307(j) of FESSA to exclude transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under part 29."

  "Section 828 of the Act amended section 2307(a)(8)(A) (i.e., the operating requirement) by increasing the number of passengers from 5 to 6. ... Therefore, a covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board."

FAA BasicMed program page (same figures, plain language):
  "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants / Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds" ... "Carries not more than six passengers."

FAA news release, Nov 15, 2024: "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."

3. SOURCE-CURRENCY WARNING (the main trap in this question)

The 2024 annual print edition of 14 CFR (CFR-2024-title14-vol2, sec. 61-113) still shows the pre-amendment text:

  "(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds, and is operated with no more than five passengers on board; and"

Those figures (6 / 6,000 lb / 5) were superseded by Amdt 61-158 and must not be quoted as current. The current eCFR text of 61.113(i)(1) carries the amendment in its source note ("...Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, Nov. 18, 2024..."). Any answer citing 6,000 lb, 6 occupants or 5 passengers is out of date. Rule of thumb for the citation line: cite the regulation (61.113(i)(1)) and the amendment (Amdt 61-158, 89 FR 90577), not a paper CFR volume.

4. HOW THE TWO COUNTS DIFFER — interpretation notes to carry into any downstream document

- "Occupants" is a property of the aircraft's authorization (what it is authorized under Federal law to carry), not of a particular flight. It includes any required flightcrew. So a 7-occupant aircraft flown single-pilot can carry 6 passengers; the same aircraft flown with a required two-pilot crew could carry only 5 passengers before hitting the 7-occupant ceiling. Both caps apply simultaneously — the binding limit is whichever binds first.
- "Passengers" is an operating limit on the flight: no more than 6 persons other than the pilot/required crew may be on board.
- The weight figure is "maximum takeoff weight," deliberately without the word "certificated" (the FAA omitted it so that experimental aircraft, which are not type certificated, can be operated under BasicMed). Do not "correct" the regulation to "maximum certificated takeoff weight" — the FAA's own web page uses the word "certificated," but the operative regulatory text does not.
- Exclusion: transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under part 29 are prohibited regardless of weight or seating.
- These are regulatory ceilings, not aircraft limits. The operational limit for a given flight is the lesser of (a) the BasicMed ceiling and (b) the aircraft's own approved limits (type certificate / POH seating, max gross weight, weight-and-balance for the actual loading). A 12,500 lb airplane at 12,400 lb gross may still be over gross for that specific flight.
- Related BasicMed operating limits (not asked, but they travel with the aircraft limits in any compliance summary): at or below 18,000 ft MSL; not outside the United States unless authorized by the country concerned; not above 250 KIAS; VFR or IFR; not for compensation or hire; pilot must hold a valid U.S. driver's license, have held an FAA medical after July 14, 2006, hold a current CMEC (FAA Form 8700-2) from a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months, and a BasicMed medical education course completion certificate, both kept in the logbook (61.113(i)(2)-(3); 61.23(c)(3); Part 68).

5. VERIFICATION TABLE

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 12,500 lb matches 61.113(i)(1) "not more than 12,500 pounds" | pass |
| 7 occupants matches 61.113(i)(1) "not more than 7 occupants" | pass |
| 6 passengers matches 61.113(i)(1) "no more than 6 passengers" | pass |
| Occupant cap and passenger cap mutually consistent (7 occupants − 1 pilot = 6 passengers) | pass |
| No stated value drawn from the superseded 2024 print text (6 / 6,000 / 5) | pass |
| Each value traceable to a quoted operative source, not a secondary summary | pass |

6. SCOPE

US FAA BasicMed only (14 CFR 61.113(i), 61.23(c)(3), Part 68; 49 U.S.C. 44703 note (FESSA sec. 2307, as amended by sec. 828(a)(4) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024)). No state, insurer, employer, or non-US regime limits are addressed; those can only be more restrictive and are outside this answer.

verdict.summary:
## FMCSA hours-of-service limits for a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach)

### Scope and assumptions
This answer applies to a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle operating in interstate commerce under the US federal FMCSA rules in 49 CFR Part 395. It assumes the standard rules apply and that no specific exemption or exception in 49 CFR 395.1 is being used (for example, adverse driving conditions, Alaska, or a sleeper-berth split). State intrastate rules can differ; verify the governing state rules if the operation does not cross state lines. The federal rule is the controlling baseline for interstate motorcoach operations.

### Controlling regulation
49 CFR 395.5(a) provides that no motor carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV:
- more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
- for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

### Answers
| Ask | Limit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1. How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | After 8 consecutive hours off duty, the driver may drive a passenger-carrying CMV for no more than 10 hours. Once 10 hours of driving is reached, no further driving is allowed until the driver takes another 8 consecutive hours off duty. |
| 2. After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** | The 8 hours must be consecutive and must contain no on-duty or driving time. It may be off-duty time, sleeper-berth time, or a combination. This 8-hour period resets both the 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit. |
| 3. After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | Following 8 consecutive hours off duty, the driver may not drive after accumulating 15 hours on duty. Off-duty time during the duty period does not count toward the 15 on-duty hours. After 15 on-duty hours, the driver may perform non-driving work but may not drive until another 8 consecutive hours off duty. |

### Key operational points
1. Both limits apply at the same time. The driver must stop driving when either the 10-hour driving limit or the 15-hour on-duty limit is reached, whichever comes first.
2. The 15-hour passenger limit is an on-duty accumulation, not a 15-hour elapsed window. Because off-duty time does not count toward the 15 on-duty hours, the elapsed time from the start of duty to the 15th on-duty hour can exceed 15 clock hours.
3. The 8-hour reset is not the property-carrying 10-hour reset. Passenger-carrying drivers use 8 consecutive hours off duty, a 10-hour driving limit, and a 15-hour on-duty limit. Property-carrying drivers use 10 consecutive hours off duty, an 11-hour driving limit, and a 14-hour driving window.
4. The weekly limits in 49 CFR 395.5(b) also apply separately: no driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or after 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
5. The Part 395 30-minute break requirement is a property-carrying rule (49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii)); it is not part of the passenger-carrying limits in 395.5.

### Exceptions that can change the baseline
- **Adverse driving conditions:** FMCSA guidance allows the 10-hour maximum driving time and 15-hour on-duty limit for passenger-carrying drivers to be extended by up to 2 hours when adverse driving conditions are encountered. The base answer above is the unextended limit.
- **Sleeper berth:** Under 49 CFR 395.1(g)(3), a passenger-carrying driver with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, neither less than 2 hours, totaling at least 8 hours. Absent that provision, the 8 hours must be consecutive.
- **Short-haul/recordkeeping exception:** The 150 air-mile short-haul exception in 49 CFR 395.1(e) primarily relieves record-of-duty-status requirements and has a 14-hour duty-period condition; it does not by itself change the 395.5 driving limits.
- **Alaska and other special rules:** Separate rules may apply in Alaska and to certain operations. They are not the baseline for the typical interstate motorcoach operation addressed here.

### Worked example
A driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty from 22:00 to 06:00. The driver comes on duty at 06:00, drives 4 hours, performs 2 hours of on-duty non-driving work, takes 1 hour off duty for lunch, and then drives 6 more hours. The driver has now accumulated 10 hours of driving and 12 hours on duty. The driver may not drive further because the 10-hour driving limit is reached. The driver may continue non-driving work; when the driver reaches 15 on-duty hours (after 3 more on-duty hours in this example), driving is prohibited. Non-driving work may continue after 15 on-duty hours. Before driving again, the driver must take 8 consecutive hours off duty.

### Sources
- 49 CFR 395.5 (eCFR), Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.
- FMCSA, Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers.
- FMCSA, Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service.
- FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations.
